words.label: Math Words & Symbols
words.text: Hello! Today I am your teacher for the Math Words & Symbols page. This page teaches you the special words we use in Unit 1, Numbers to 10. Words like count, how many, total, ten-frame, more, fewer, and estimate. When you know these words, the questions in this unit become much easier to understand. You will need your ears, your voice, and your fingers for typing. Take your time — there is no rush. Here is what I expect from you: read carefully, say each word out loud, and try your own sentence even if it feels hard. Mistakes are how we learn. There are four steps. Here they are. Step 1. Look at the list of words on the page. Read the first word, then read what it means beside it. Then press the Listen button to hear the word said for you. Say it with me, slowly. Do this for every word, one at a time, from the top of the list to the bottom. I expect you to go slowly and not skip any word. Step 2. Now do three things for each word. First, say the word out loud in a big voice. Second, say the meaning in your own words, not the words on the screen. Third, type a sentence that uses the word, then press Check sentence and read what the checker tells you. A good sentence shows the word doing its job, like "I count five dates." If the checker says to change something, fix it and press Check sentence again. I expect one sentence from you for every word. Step 3. When you have finished every single word, scroll to the bottom of the page. Press the button that says I know these words and symbols. Only press it when you really have done them all. That button tells the page you are ready. Step 4. Under the page there is a deck of slides. Each slide has one of the same words. Press Start on the first slide. On each slide, use the same buttons you used before: Listen, say the word, say the meaning, type your sentence, and press Check sentence. Then press the arrow on the right to move to the next slide. The little dots under the slide show you where you are. On the last slide, press the finish button. You will know the page is finished when the button I know these words and symbols has been pressed, and you have pressed the finish button on the last slide. Ready? Start with step 1, and tell me when you have listened to your first word. 🙂

lesson.label: The Lesson
lesson.text: Hello! I am your teacher today, and this is our Lesson page for Unit 1: Numbers to 10. On this page there are 5 short ideas, called concepts. They are: counting real things one at a time, the ten-frame, saying and reading and writing 0 to 10, estimating (a good guess) then counting, and comparing groups to say more or fewer. We do this page so that by the end you can count up to 10 things and never lose your place. What I expect from you: go slowly, say the numbers out loud, and touch things as you count. Mathematicians think slowly on purpose. Get these ready: a small pile of things you can count, like beans, buttons or stones. About 20 is perfect. Also a pencil and paper. You can ask your grown-up to help you find them. Here are all the steps. Step 1. Look at the first concept box on the page. Read it slowly, then press Listen so you can hear it read to you. Listening and reading together helps the words stick. Do this for each of the 5 concepts, one at a time. I expect you not to rush — one box, then the next. Step 2. Each concept has an example. Say that example out loud with your own voice. Then do it for real with your own things. For counting, put out 5 beans and touch each one as you say one, two, three, four, five. Then answer this question: how many altogether? The last number you said is the answer. Step 3. Try the other examples with your own numbers too. Make a ten-frame from paper, two rows of 5 boxes, and fill the top row first. Write a few numbers with your pencil, like 2 and 5 and 8. Take a quick peek at a small pile, guess "about how many", then count to check. Last, make two piles and say which has more and which has fewer. Step 4. When you have read all 5 concepts and tried them, go to the bottom of the page and press I studied the concepts. Only press it when you really have read them all. That button tells the page you have finished the reading part. Step 5. Now look under the page. There is a deck of slides with the same 5 concepts, one idea on each slide. Press Start on the first slide. Step 6. On each slide, use the same buttons you just used, and read or listen again. Then press the arrow on the right to move to the next slide. The little dots under the slide show you where you are, like footprints on a path. Step 7. Keep going until the last slide. On the last slide, press the finish button. That is the end of the deck. How will you know the page is finished? You have pressed Listen on all 5 concepts, you have pressed I studied the concepts, and you have pressed the finish button on the last slide. When all three are done, this page is complete. Now go and start Step 1. Come back and tell me when your 5 beans are counted, and tell me how many altogether. Take your time — there's no rush.

overview.label: Unit Overview
overview.text: Hello! I am your maths teacher today. This page is called the Unit Overview. It is like looking at a map before a trip. It shows you what Unit 1, Numbers to 10, is all about. We do this so you know what is coming, and so the lesson feels easy when we get there. You will need your eyes, your ears, and your voice. A grown-up can sit with you if you like. There are three steps. Here they all are. Step 1: Read the Unit Overview. Look at the words on the page that say what this unit is about. Where you see a little speaker picture, press Listen. Then the words will be read to you. Read along with the voice if you can. I expect you to look for two things: what you will learn, and what you will need. In this unit you will count things, use a ten-frame, say and write the numbers 0 to 10, guess before you count, and say which group has more. You will also need a small pile of things to count, like beans, stones, buttons or bottle caps. About twenty is plenty. Go and get them now, and put them in a little bowl near you. Step 2: Say in your own words what you think you will learn. Do not copy the page. Just tell it like you are telling a friend. Say it out loud to your grown-up, or type it to me. A good answer names one or two things, like this: "I will count things up to ten, and I will learn to write the numbers." Even one clear idea is a great answer. If you cannot think of one, look back at the page and pick the part you liked best. I expect real words from you, not just "I do not know". Take your time — there's no rush. Step 3: Press Continue to go to The Lesson. This is the button at the bottom of the page. Press it only after you have read the overview and said your own words. Pressing Continue takes you to the next part, where the real counting begins. I expect your counting things to be beside you before you press it, so you are all ready to start. You will know this page is finished when three things are true. You have listened to the overview, you have said in your own words what you will learn, and you have pressed Continue. Then you are on your way! Now, tell me: what do you think you will learn in this unit?

explore.label: Explore the Concept
explore.text: Hello! I am your teacher today, and this page is called Explore the Concept. On this page you will meet 6 little discoveries about numbers to 10. You will count real things, look at a ten-frame, say what number comes next, make a good guess, and compare two groups. We do this so numbers stop being just words and start meaning "how many". You will need your eyes, your finger for touching and counting, and maybe a small pile of beans or bottle caps near you. Let's go step by step. Step 1. Look at the top of the page. You will see numbered tabs: 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6. Press tab number 1 with your finger or mouse. Read the little story it shows you, and look at the picture or model. Take your time — there's no rush. What I expect: you look carefully at the picture before you think about the answer. Step 2. Now read the question under the picture. Think first, in your head or out loud. Touch each thing on the screen as you count, one touch for one thing. The last number you say is the answer. What I expect: a slow, careful count, not a quick guess. Step 3. Type your idea in the box. You can type just the number, like 5, or a few words. Then press Check my idea. What I expect: your own idea, even if you are not sure. Mistakes are how we learn. Step 4. If the page says Look again, that is okay! Press Hint and read it. The hint tells you one helpful thing. Then count once more and press Check my idea again. What I expect: you try again after the hint, calmly. Step 5. When the page says Exactly!, your tab gets a little tick. Well done! Now press tab number 2 and do the same three things: read, think, type, and press Check my idea. What I expect: the same careful counting every time. Step 6. Keep going with tabs 3, 4, 5 and 6, one at a time. Tab 4 asks you to guess first, then count — a sensible guess is a great guess, even if it is not exact. Tab 5 asks which group has more, so match them into pairs. Tab 6 has gaps in a number track, so count from 1 out loud and listen for the missing numbers. What I expect: all six tabs answered, each with a tick. Step 7. Now scroll down under the page. There is a deck of slides with the same discoveries, one on each slide. Press Start on the first slide. This is your practice round, so you can say the answers even faster. Step 8. On each slide, use the same buttons you already know: read, think, type your idea, press Check my idea, and press Hint if you need help. What I expect: you do each slide by yourself now, because you have done it once already. Step 9. To move on, press the arrow on the right side of the slide. Look at the little dots under the slide — they show you which slide you are on and how many are left. What I expect: no skipping. Do each slide in order. Step 10. On the last slide, press the finish button. That tells the page you are done. Then take a big proud breath! How you will know the page is finished: every one of the six tabs has a tick, and you have pressed the finish button on the last slide. I do not tick them for you — the page only knows you did it when you press the buttons yourself. Now go and press tab number 1. Come back and tell me what you see, and we will do it together. 🌟

method.label: Learn the Method
method.text:
Hello! Today we are on the Learn the Method page. A method is a way to work something out, step by step, like a little recipe. This page shows you 6 methods for counting, saying, reading and writing numbers to 10. We do this so your counting becomes slow, careful and correct — mathematicians think slowly on purpose. You will need your voice, and a pencil and paper nearby. Here is the whole plan. 1. Look at the first method on the page. Read its first step, or ask your grown-up to read it with you. Then press the button that says Show me the next step. I expect you to read the step BEFORE you press, not after. Take your time — there's no rush. 2. Say each step out loud as it appears. Use your own mouth and your own finger! If the step says "touch each object", touch something real — dates, beans, buttons or your fingers. A good job sounds like this: "One... two... three... four... five. Five altogether!" I expect to hear the last number said again as the total. 3. Keep pressing Show me the next step until the page says Method complete. That message means you finished that method. Do not stop in the middle. If a step feels tricky, read it once more slowly, then try it with real objects in your hand. 4. Now do the very same thing for the next method, and the next, until all 6 are done. Every method must say Method complete. I expect you to try each one with your hands or your voice, not just look at the words. Some methods ask you to write digits — get your pencil and write them, saying the shape out loud, like "2 is a curve, then a line along the bottom."

5. Under the page there is a deck of slides. Each slide shows one of the same methods again. On the first slide, press Start. This is your practice round, so it is meant to feel a little easier the second time. 6. On each slide, use the same buttons as before to move through the steps, saying them out loud again. When a slide is done, press the arrow on the right side to go to the next slide. Look at the little dots under the slide — they show you which slide you are on and how many are left. 7. On the last slide, press the finish button. That tells the page you have been all the way through. I expect you to press it yourself — I cannot mark your work done, only you can. 8. You will know the page is finished when every method has shown Method complete, and the slide deck has been finished on the last slide. Then come and tell me one thing: which method felt the easiest, and which one felt the hardest? Off you go with step 1 — press Show me the next step when you have read the first step out loud. 🌟

visuals.label: Visual Models
visuals.text:
Hello! Today we are on the Visual Models page. A visual model is a picture that shows a maths idea, so you can SEE the number, not just hear it. There are 5 models here, all about numbers to 10. By the end you will be able to look at a small group and say how many, and say which group has more. You need your eyes, your finger for pointing, and your voice for saying the numbers out loud. A grown-up can sit with you if you like. There are 6 steps. Take your time — there's no rush. Step 1: Find the first model, Counting Real Objects. Look at the objects on the screen. Point at each one with your finger and say "one, two, three..." out loud, touching each one only ONCE. If the picture moves, drag it to turn it and press its buttons to see it change. Then read the caption under it and press Listen. I expect you to say the last number loudly — that last number tells you how many altogether. Step 2: Go to the second model, the Ten-Frame. A ten-frame is a box with 2 rows of 5 cups. Press its buttons to put counters in, and fill the top row first, left to right. Read the caption and press Listen. I expect you to tell yourself two things: how many counters are in, and how many cups are still empty. Step 3: Now the third model, Saying, Reading and Writing 0 to 10. Look at each written number, 0 up to 10. Press the buttons to change the number, and say its name out loud each time. Read the caption and press Listen. I expect you to say every number name clearly, and to trace one number in the air with your finger. Step 4: Next is the fourth model, Estimating Then Counting. An estimate is a good guess before you count. Look at the group for a moment, then look away and say "about five" or "about ten". Now press the buttons or drag it, count slowly, and read the caption and press Listen. I expect you to guess FIRST and count after — a thinking guess is a good guess, even if it is not exact. Step 5: Now the last model, Comparing and Ordering. Look at the two groups. Match one from this group with one from that group, like pairs of shoes. The group with some left over has more. Drag or press its buttons to change the groups, then read the caption and press Listen. I expect you to say two sentences out loud: "This group has more" and "This group has fewer."

Step 6: When you have looked at all 5 models and pressed Listen on all 5 captions, press the button at the bottom that says I explored the models. You will know the page is finished when that button is pressed. That is how your work gets saved — I cannot press it for you! Ready? Start with Step 1, then tell me when it is done. 🌟

examples.label: Worked Examples
examples.text: Hello! Today we are on the Worked Examples page. A worked example is a maths question with all the thinking already shown. We use these to learn HOW a good mathematician counts, step by step. By the end, you will count things carefully, find missing numbers, and write digits the right way. Get a pencil, some paper, and a little pile of small things to count — beans, buttons or bottle caps. Here is what I expect from you: try each one yourself FIRST, before you peek. A wrong try that you thought about is much better than a peek. Mathematicians think slowly on purpose. Step 1. Look at the first worked example on the page. Read the question. Point at each thing with your finger and count out loud: one, two, three. Say the last number again — that is your answer. Write it on your paper. Step 2. Now press the button that says Show worked solution. Read the solution line by line. Ask yourself, "Did I count the same way?" A good check is when you can say out loud why the answer is right, not just that it matches. Step 3. If your answer was different, do not worry. Mistakes are how we learn. Count again slowly, touching each picture only once. Most little slips are counting one thing twice, or skipping one. Step 4. Do the same with the next example, and the next. Every time: try it first, then press Show worked solution. There are 12 worked examples in all. Take your time — there's no rush. Step 5. Watch the counter at the top of the page. It shows how many you have opened. Your job is to open every single one, so the counter reaches 12. Do not skip the tricky ones — those are the ones that teach you most. Step 6. Now look under the page. There is a deck of slides with the same examples, one on each slide. Press Start on the first slide. This is your practice round, so try to answer before you look. Step 7. On each slide, use the same buttons as before: try it yourself, then show the solution. Then press the arrow on the right to move to the next slide. The little dots under the slide tell you where you are — the more dots you pass, the closer you are to the end. Step 8. Keep going until you reach the last slide. On that one, press the finish button. That tells the page you are done. You will know the page is finished when the counter at the top shows all 12 opened, and you have pressed the finish button on the last slide. I do not tick it for you — you press it yourself, because it is your work. Ready? Start with example one, and tell me your answer for it. I am right here. 🙂

activities.label: Activities
activities.text:
Hello! Today I am your teacher for the Activities page. On this page you do maths with your hands, not just in your head. You will count real things, make a little model, and talk about it. This helps numbers to 10 feel real. You will need paper, a pencil, and some small things you can count, like beans, stones, bottle caps or buttons. A grown-up nearby can help you. Here is what we will do, step by step. Step 1. Look at the activity card on the page. It is called "Practise together". Press Listen to hear it read out loud. Listen all the way to the end. Then go and get your paper, your pencil, and your small counting things. I expect you to come back with your things ready on the table. Step 2. Now pick one idea from Unit 1. You could pick counting to 10, or a ten-frame, or which group has more. Then make it. You can build it with your beans or stones, or draw it on your paper. A good model is one I could look at and say, "Ah, I can see the number!" Take your time, there's no rush. Step 3. Show your model to someone at home and tell them about it. Say what you made and how many things you used. Then, on your paper, write one maths question of your own, like "How many stones?" — and write the answer too. I expect a question you made up yourself, with your own answer next to it. Step 4. Find the answer box on the page. Type what you did and what you noticed. Even one short line is good, like "I made 7 with stones and 3 cups were empty." I expect your own words, not copied words. Step 5. Press Mark complete under the activity when you have really done it. Only press it after the work is done — that button tells the page you finished. Step 6. Look under the page. There is a deck of slides with the same activity, one on each slide. Press Start on the first slide. Do the same things on each slide: listen, do it, write in the box, press Mark complete. Step 7. To move on, press the arrow on the right side of the slide. The little dots under the slide show you where you are. Count the dots if you like — that is counting practice too! Step 8. On the last slide, press Finish activities. Then press Finish activities at the bottom of the page as well, once every activity has Mark complete on it. You will know the page is finished when every activity is marked complete and you have pressed Finish activities. 🌟

Now go and get your counting things, then tell me when they are ready. I'll wait right here.

guided.label: Guided Practice
guided.text: Hello! Today I am your teacher, and this page is our practice time. This is Guided Practice for Unit 1, Numbers to 10. We count things, we find missing numbers, and we say which group has more. We practise so counting becomes easy and quick for you. You will need a pencil, some paper, and maybe 10 small things like beans or bottle caps. Your fingers work too! Here is what I expect from you: count slowly, touch each thing once, and try by yourself first. Mistakes are how we learn. Take your time — there's no rush. There are 4 steps. Here they all are. Step 1. There are 12 questions on this page. Read the first one carefully. Then work it out on paper or in your head. Touch each picture once as you count: one, two, three. The last number you say is how many. A good answer is one you counted, not one you guessed. Step 2. Now type your answer in the box. Then press Check my answer. If you feel stuck, press Give me a hint — you can get three hints. If you are still stuck, press Show next step and it shows you one line of the working. I expect you to try the hint first, before the next step. That is what good mathematicians do. Step 3. Do this for every question, one at a time, until each one is right. If an answer is wrong, do not worry. Count again slowly and try once more. When all 12 questions are right, this part is done. That is a lot of counting — you can be proud! Step 4. Under the page there is a deck of slides. They have the same questions, one question on each slide. Press Start on the first slide. Answer it with the same buttons: Check my answer, Give me a hint, Show next step. Then press the arrow on the right to go to the next slide. The little dots under the slide show you where you are. On the last slide, press the finish button. How will you know the page is finished? All 12 questions are correct, and you have pressed the finish button on the last slide. Then the page is complete. Ready? Go to question one, count it out, and tell me your answer. I will check it with you. 🙂

games.label: Games
games.text: Hello! Today we are going to play the Unit 1 games together. These games help you practise counting, reading numbers, and finding missing numbers. Playing is a fun way to make your brain quick and strong. You do not need anything special — just your eyes, your finger, and maybe some beans or buttons to count with. Here are the steps. Step 1: Pick a game and press Start game. Look at the games on your screen. Pick any one you like. Press the button that says Start game. A question will pop up with some answers to choose from. Read it slowly, work out the answer in your head first, then tap your choice. I expect you to think before you tap — no fast guessing! Every round you get right gives you a star. If you get one wrong, that is fine. Mistakes are how we learn. Step 2: Press Play again to collect more stars. When the game ends, look at your stars. If the game does not have all its stars yet, press Play again. Play the rounds one more time. Try to be a little faster and a little surer this time. When a game has all its stars, it is mastered — that means you really know it. I expect you to keep going until each game you start is mastered. Step 3: Master every game on the page. Now do the same for the next game, and the next, until every single game has all its stars. Take your time — there is no rush. If a question feels hard, count on your fingers or touch each picture once as you count. If you get stuck, come and tell me and I will give you a small hint. I expect you to try every game, not just the easy ones. How you will know you are finished: when every game shows all its stars, the page finishes by itself. You do not need to press anything extra at the end. Ready? Press Start game on your first game, then tell me which game you picked and how you did. 🌟

fluency.label: Math Fluency
fluency.text: Hello! I am your teacher today, and this page is called Math Fluency. Fluency means doing something quickly and easily, because you have practised it a lot. On this page you get 12 quick counting questions in a row. This helps your brain say numbers fast, without stopping to think hard. You will need your eyes, your finger for touching and counting, and a calm, steady head. Take a breath — you can do this. Here is what I expect from you: touch and count carefully, answer every question, and keep going even if one feels tricky. Mistakes are how we learn. Here are your steps. 1. Get ready. Sit up and look at the screen. At the top you will see your time counting up. That is just to show how fast you go — it is not a race against anyone else. 2. Read question one. Look at the picture or the numbers slowly. If there are objects, touch each one on the screen with your finger as you count: one, two, three. Count only the real things, not the little star at the front. 3. Type your answer in the box. Then press Check & continue. This sends your answer and brings the next question. 4. Keep going, one question at a time. After each answer you press Check & continue again. Do this for all 12 questions. Steady and careful beats super fast. 5. If a question is a number track with gaps, like 6, 7, blank, 9 — count out loud from the start. Your ears will hear the missing number. 6. When you finish question 12, the page will show how you did. Look at how many you got right. 7. You need most of them right to pass. If you got enough right, brilliant work — the page is done! 8. If you got fewer right, that is okay. Press Run the sprint again and do all 12 once more. This time count a little slower and touch each thing. You will know the page is finished when one sprint has enough right answers and the page says you have done it. Then you can smile — you earned that. Ready? Start question one now, and tell me when you finish your first sprint. 🌟

problems.label: Solve Real Problems
problems.text:
Hello! Today I am your teacher for the Solve Real Problems page. 🌟

This page has 6 little story problems from real life. Things like moons in the sky, anjero on a plate, goats on the road, and beans in a bowl. We do this so you can use your counting in the real world, not just on paper. By the end you will be able to count a group, say how many altogether, and say which group has more or fewer. You will need your eyes, your finger for touching and counting, and a grown-up nearby if you want one. Here is what I expect from you: count slowly, touch each thing once, and count only the things the question asks for. Take your time — mathematicians think slowly on purpose. Here are your steps. 1. Read the first problem carefully. Ask yourself, "What is this question asking me?" Sometimes it asks how many altogether. Sometimes it asks which group has more, or which has fewer. Look at the little pictures too. Careful: a star like ★ is only a marker, so do not count it. I expect you to know what the question wants before you start counting. 2. Now work it out, then type it in the box and press Check answer. Touch each picture once and count out loud: one, two, three... The last number you say is the total. In the box, write your answer and a few words about how you got it, like "I counted them one by one and got 9." If you feel stuck, press Hint first and try again yourself. I expect you to try before you press Hint. 😊

3. When the page tells you your answer is right, that problem is done. Then move on to the next problem and do the same thing: read, count, type, press Check answer. Do this for all 6 problems. If one comes out wrong, that is fine — mistakes are how we learn. Just count again slowly and try once more. 4. Now look under the page. There is a deck of slides with the same problems, one on each slide. On the first slide, press Start. Answer that slide the same way, using Check answer and Hint. Then press the arrow on the right to go to the next slide. The little dots under the slide show you how far you have come. Keep going slide by slide, and on the last slide press the finish button. How will you know the page is finished? All 6 problems will show that your answers are right, and the slide deck will be finished after you press the finish button on the last slide. Ready? Start with problem one, and tell me what it is asking you.

explain.label: Explain Your Thinking
explain.text: Hello! I am your teacher today, and this page is called Explain Your Thinking. On this page you do not just give an answer. You tell me HOW you got it. Talking about your thinking helps the maths stick in your head. You will need your eyes, your voice, and your typing finger. A grown-up can help you write your words if you like. Here is what I expect from you: try first, use the maths words, and say why your answer makes sense. Take your time. Mathematicians think slowly on purpose. There are 4 steps. Here they all are. Step 1. Read the prompt. There are 6 prompts on this page. A prompt is a question that asks you to explain. Under each one there are key ideas, like Count, How many, or Total. Read the prompt, then read the key ideas. Say them out loud if that helps. I expect you to know what the question is asking before you write. Step 2. Write your explanation in the box, then press Check mathematical ideas. Write three things: what you know, what you did, and why your answer makes sense. For example: "I touched each one and counted. The last number I said was the total." Try to use the key ideas words in your sentence. If the page says to add more, that is fine. Add one more sentence and press Check mathematical ideas again. Step 3. Press Show model explanation. This opens a good answer so you can compare. Read it and ask yourself: did I say the same big idea? Did I use the key ideas words? You do not need the same words as the model. You just need the same thinking. Then do Step 1 and Step 2 again for the next prompt, until all 6 are done. Step 4. Do the slides at the bottom. Under the page there is a deck of slides. Each slide has one of the same prompts. On the first slide press Start. Then use the same buttons on each slide: write your answer, press Check mathematical ideas, and press Show model explanation. To move on, press the arrow on the right side. The little dots under the slide show you where you are. On the last slide, press the finish button. How will you know the page is finished? When all 6 explanations use the key ideas, and you have pressed the finish button on the last slide. Then you are done! Ready? Read the very first prompt and tell me what it is asking. I am right here with you. 😊

challenge.label: Unit Challenge
challenge.text:
Hello! This page is your Unit Challenge. It is the last part of Unit 1, Numbers to 10. It has 12 questions about counting, number order, and which group has more or fewer. We do it to show what your brain has learned — it is not scary, it is a chance to shine. Get a pencil and some small things to count, like beans or bottle caps, and sit somewhere quiet. Take your time — there's no rush. Here is what I expect from you: you count carefully, you touch each thing once, and you choose the answer yourself. I will not tell you any answers — but I will help you think. That is my promise. 🙂

Step 1: Read the first question slowly. Read it twice. Ask yourself, "What is this question asking me?" Some questions ask how many. Some ask which number comes next. Some ask which group has more. Step 2: Work out your answer before you look at the choices. If it is a counting question, touch each picture once and say the numbers out loud: one, two, three. The last number you say is the total. If it is a number track, count from the start out loud and listen for the gap. Step 3: Now look at the four choices. Find the one that matches your answer. If you are not sure, cross out the ones you know are wrong first. Step 4: Choose your answer, then press Next question. Do this for every question, all the way to number 12. Go slowly. Careful counting beats fast counting every time. Step 5: At the end you will see your score. That is how many you got right. You pass when you get more than half of them right. Well done for finishing — that takes effort! Step 6: If your score is not high enough, press Try again. That is not a bad thing at all. Mistakes are how we learn. This time, count even more slowly and touch each picture once. Step 7: When your score is good enough, press Continue. That tells the page you are done. You will know the page is finished when you have pressed Continue and it moves you on. Now go and start question one. Come back and tell me your score when you finish — I would love to hear how it went!

lesson.label: The Lesson
lesson.text: Hello! Today we are learning about shapes. This page is called The Lesson. It has 7 little ideas, called concepts, about solid shapes you can hold and flat shapes you can draw. We do this so you can name shapes like cube, sphere and cylinder, and say how many sides a square has. You will need your eyes, your voice, and if you can, a ball, a tin, and a small box. Here is what to do, step by step. 1. Look at the first concept on the page. Read it slowly with your eyes. Then press Listen. A voice will read it to you. Listen all the way to the end. I expect you to listen quietly, without rushing to the next one. 2. Now find the example in that concept. Say it out loud, in your own voice. Talking helps your brain remember. I expect to hear you say the shape names, like "sphere" and "cube". 3. Try the example for real. Hold a ball and say "sphere". Hold a box and count its flat faces: one, two, three, four, five, six. If you have no box, use your finger to draw the shape in the air. A grown-up can help you find the objects. 4. Do the same three things for every concept: read it, press Listen, then say and try the example. Go one concept at a time, from the first to the seventh. Take your time — there's no rush. 5. When you have read all 7 concepts, scroll to the bottom of the page. Press the button that says I studied the concepts. Only press it when you really did read them all. That button tells the page you are done reading. 6. Under the page you will see slides. Each slide has one of the same ideas. On the first slide, press Start. Look at the slide and say the shape name out loud. 7. On each slide, use the same buttons as before. When you are ready, press the arrow on the right to go to the next slide. The little dots under the slide show you where you are. More dots filled means you are getting close to the end. 8. Keep going until the last slide. On the last slide, press the finish button. That is the end of the slides. You will know the page is finished when you have pressed I studied the concepts and pressed the finish button on the last slide. Ready? Start with step 1, and tell me when you have listened to the first concept. 🙂

words.label: Math Words & Symbols
words.text: Hello! Today we are learning our shape words. These are the words we need for Unit 2, like cube, sphere, cylinder, face and edge. When you know these words, talking about shapes gets easy. You will need your voice, your eyes, and your typing finger. Here is what we will do, step by step. 1. Read each word and its meaning. Look at the first word on the page. Read the word, then read what it means. Now press Listen. Listen carefully to how the word sounds. I expect you to listen right to the end, then say the word quietly with the voice. Do this for every word on the page. 2. Say it out loud. Now say the word in a big, brave voice. Then say the meaning in your own words, not the page's words. For sphere you might say, "a ball shape, round all over." That is exactly what I want — your own words, not copied. 3. Type a sentence, then press Check sentence. Write one sentence that uses the word. A good sentence shows you know the meaning, like "My football is a sphere." Then press Check sentence and read what the checker tells you. If it says to try again, that is fine — mistakes are how we learn. Fix it and press Check sentence again. 4. Do steps 1 to 3 for every word. Go down the list one word at a time. Do not skip any. Take your time — there's no rush. If a word feels hard, tell me and we will work on it together. 5. Press I know these words and symbols. When every word is done, scroll to the bottom and press that button. Only press it when you really have done them all. That button tells the page you finished the word list. 6. Go to the slides under the page. There is a little deck of slides below. Each slide has one word again. Press Start on the first slide to begin. 7. Do the same things on each slide. On every slide: read the word, press Listen, say the word out loud, say the meaning your way, and type your sentence. Use the same buttons you already know. You are a pro at this now! 8. Move to the next slide. Press the arrow on the right side of the slide. Look at the little dots under the slide — they show you where you are and how many are left. Keep going, one slide at a time. 9. Finish the last slide. On the very last slide, press the finish button. That is the end of the deck. You will know the page is finished when you have pressed I know these words and symbols, and you have pressed the finish button on the last slide. Then every word has a tick from you. Ready to start? Press Listen on the very first word, then tell me which word it was. 😊

overview.label: Unit Overview
overview.text:
Hello! Today we start Unit 2: Geometry. This page is our first look at the unit. It tells you what we will learn about shapes — shapes you can hold, like a ball and a box, and flat shapes you can draw, like a circle and a square. We do this page so you know where we are going before we begin. You need your eyes, your ears, and your voice. Let's go! Step 1: Read the Unit Overview. Look at the words on the screen and read them slowly. If you see a little speaker picture, press Listen and let it read to you. Read it once, then read it again. I expect you to listen right to the end and try to spot one shape word you know, like ball, box, or circle. A grown-up can read it with you if you like. Step 2: Say what you will learn, in your own words. Now close your mouth for a second and think. Then say it out loud: "In this unit I will learn about..." I expect a short sentence, not a long one. Something like "I will learn the names of shapes" is a great answer. You do not need big words — your own words are best. Step 3: Press Continue. When you have read the page and said your sentence, find the Continue button and press it. That takes you to The Lesson, where we start learning about the cube, the sphere and the cylinder. Press it only when you are ready. You will know this page is finished when you have read the overview, said your own sentence out loud, and pressed Continue. That is the whole page — well done for starting so nicely! 🌟

Now, before you press anything: can you tell me one shape you can see in your room right now?

explore.label: Explore the Concept
explore.text: Hello! Today I am your teacher, and this page is called Explore the Concept. Here is what it is. You will do six little discoveries about shapes. You will hold real things, look, think, and then type what you found. This is how we learn shapes best — with our hands and our eyes, not just our ears. By the end, you will be able to name a sphere, a cube and a cylinder, count sides, and say which shapes roll and which stack. What you need: a ball, a box or a die, and a tin can. A grown-up can help you find them. What I expect from you: try the thing first, then type your own idea in your own words. Even one or two words is fine. Guessing without looking is the only thing I do not want! Step 1: At the top of the page you will see six numbered tabs. Press tab number 1. Read the little story, and look at the picture or model on the screen. Do this slowly. I expect you to actually pick up the object it talks about and feel it in your hands. Step 2: Now read the discovery question under it. Think first — say the answer out loud to yourself. Then type your idea into the box and press Check my idea. Short words are good, like "sphere" or "6 faces". Step 3: If the page says Look again, do not worry. Mistakes are how we learn. Press Hint, read it, look at your object one more time, and try again. Step 4: When the page says Exactly!, that tab gets a tick. Well done! A tick means that discovery is done and you can move on. Step 5: Press tab number 2 and do the same three things: read, think, type, press Check my idea. Keep going like this for tab 3, tab 4, tab 5 and tab 6. Take your time — there's no rush. Step 6: Do all six. The top part of the page is finished when every tab has a tick, and no question is left empty. Step 7: Now look under the page. There is a deck of slides. They have the same six discoveries, one on each slide. This part helps the shapes stick in your memory. Step 8: On the first slide, press Start. Then answer that slide the same way as before: read, think, type, and press the check button on the slide. Step 9: To go to the next slide, press the arrow on the right side. Look at the little dots under the slide — they show you where you are and how many are left. Step 10: Keep going, one slide at a time, until you reach the last one. On the last slide, press the finish button. How will you know the page is finished? All six tabs have a tick, and you have pressed the finish button on the last slide. Then the whole page is complete. Ready? Go and press tab number 1, and tell me what you find. Let's find out.

visuals.label: Visual Models
visuals.text:
Hello! Today we are on the Visual Models page. Visual models are pictures and shapes you can look at and move. They help you SEE the shapes in this unit, not just hear about them. By the end, you will be able to name shapes and say what they can do. You just need your eyes, your finger on the screen, and your voice to say the shape names out loud. There are 3 steps. Here they are. Step 1: Look at all 6 models, one at a time. Start with the first one and take your time. If a model can move, put your finger on it and drag it to turn it around. If it has buttons, press them and watch what changes. The six models are about: solid shapes (cube, sphere, cylinder), faces and edges, rolling and stacking, flat shapes (circle, square, triangle, rectangle), counting sides and corners, and sorting shapes into groups. As you look at each one, I want you to say its shape name out loud. That is what makes it stick. Step 2: Read the caption under each model, then press Listen to hear it. A caption is the little bit of writing under the picture. Read it first with your eyes or with a grown-up, then press Listen and hear the same words. Do this for every model, all 6. I expect you to listen right to the end, not skip ahead. Good listening sounds like: quiet ears, then you say one thing you learned. Step 3: When you have looked at all 6 models and heard all the captions, press the button at the bottom that says I explored the models. Only press it when you really have seen them all. That press tells the page you are done. You will know the page is finished when you have pressed I explored the models at the bottom. Then come and tell me one thing you noticed. I would love to hear it! 😊

Ready? Start with model one, and tell me when you have looked at it.

method.label: Learn the Method
method.text: Hello! Today I am your teacher for the Learn the Method page. This page shows 6 methods. A method is a way to work something out, step by step. Here the methods teach you how to name shapes, count faces, and test which shapes roll or stack. We do it slowly, one step at a time, so your brain remembers the order. By the end you will be able to pick up a shape and say its name and its parts. What you need: your eyes, your voice, and if you can, a ball, a tin can, and a small box. What I expect from you: read each step out loud, and try it with a real object when you can. Take your time — there's no rush. Step 1. Look at the first method on the page. Read its first step out loud. Then press the button that says Show me the next step. A good job here is reading slowly and clearly, not rushing. I expect you to actually say the words out loud, even in a small voice. Step 2. Keep pressing Show me the next step until the page says Method complete. Say every new step out loud before you press again. If you can, do the step with your hands too — touch the ball, turn the box. I expect you to finish the whole method, not stop in the middle. Step 3. Now do the same for every method. There are 6 in all. Read, say it out loud, press Show me the next step, until Method complete shows for each one. If a step feels tricky, tell me and I will give you a hint. I expect all 6 methods to reach Method complete. Step 4. Look under the page. There is a deck of slides with the same methods, one method on each slide. Press Start on the first slide. Then use the same buttons on the slide to move through its steps, saying each one out loud again. Step 5. When a slide is done, press the arrow on the right side to go to the next slide. The little dots under the slide show you where you are — they help you see how many are left. Do every slide the same way: Start, then step through to the end. Step 6. On the last slide, press the finish button. That tells the page you have done them all. I expect you to press it yourself, because the page counts your work, not mine. How you will know you are finished: every method says Method complete, all the dots under the slides have been visited, and you have pressed the finish button on the last slide. Ready? Start with the first method, and tell me when you see Method complete. 🙂

examples.label: Worked Examples
examples.text: Hello! Today I am your teacher for the Worked Examples page. Here is what this page is. It has 12 shape questions. Each one shows you the full working — that means all the thinking, step by step. We do this so you can see HOW a good answer is made, not just the answer. By the end you will be able to name shapes like the cube, sphere and cylinder, count sides and corners, and say which shapes roll and which stack. What you need: your eyes, your finger for counting, and if you can, a ball, a tin and a box near you. What I expect from you: always try the question in your head FIRST, before you look at the solution. Take your time — there's no rush. Here are your steps. 1. Look at the first worked example. Read the question slowly, then read it once more. Try to answer it yourself first, out loud or in your head. Even a guess is good — trying first is what makes your brain grow. I expect you to say your own answer before you open anything. 2. Now press Show worked solution on that example. Read the solution line by line, from the top to the bottom. Ask yourself: "Did I think the same way?" If your answer matched, say "yes!" If it did not, that is fine — mistakes are how we learn. Just find the one line where your thinking went a different way. 3. Do the same for every example: read, try, then press Show worked solution. There are 12 in all. At the top of the page there is a counter. It tells you how many you have opened, like 3 of 12. Watch that number grow — it is your progress. I expect you to open all 12, not skip any, even the easy-looking ones. 4. When the counter says all 12 are open, this part of the page is done. Well done — that is a lot of good thinking! 5. Now look under the page. There is a deck of slides. The same examples are there, one shape question on each slide. This is your practice round. Press Start on the first slide to begin. 6. On each slide, do the same thing as before: read the question, try it yourself, then use the same buttons to see the working. Keep your voice going — say the shape name out loud. Saying it helps you remember it. 7. To move on, press the arrow on the right side of the slide. That takes you to the next slide. Under the slide there are little dots. The dots show you where you are in the deck, like footprints on a path. 8. Keep going slide by slide until you reach the last one. On the last slide, press the finish button. That tells the page you are done. You will know the whole page is finished when two things are true: the counter at the top shows all 12 examples opened, and you have pressed the finish button on the last slide. Ready? Start with step 1, and tell me when you have read the first question. I am right here with you. 😊

guided.label: Guided Practice
guided.text: Hello! Today I am your teacher for Guided Practice in our Geometry unit. This page gives you 12 short shape questions. We do them so your shape words become quick and easy — cube, sphere, cylinder, circle, square, rectangle, triangle. By the end you will be able to name shapes, count sides and corners, and say which shapes roll and which stack. You need your eyes, your fingers for counting, and maybe a pencil and paper. A grown-up can sit with you if you like. Here is what I expect from you: think first, then type. Try each question yourself before you ask for help. Mistakes are how we learn. Here are all the steps. Step 1: Read the first question slowly. Read it twice. Work it out in your head, or draw the shape on paper and touch each side as you count. If the question is about a real thing like a ball or a tin, picture it in your hands. A good answer is one you can explain, not one you guessed. Step 2: Type your answer in the box. Then press Check my answer. Write the shape name or the number, like sphere or 4. If you feel stuck, press Give me a hint. You can get up to three hints. If you are still stuck, press Show next step and it shows you one line of the working. Try the hint first, before the next step — that way your brain does the work. Step 3: Do this for every question, all 12. If an answer is not right, do not worry. Read the hint, think again, and type a new answer. Keep going until every question is right. That is when this part of the page is finished. Step 4: Now look under the page. There is a deck of slides with the same questions, one question on each slide. Press Start on the first slide. Answer it the same way, using the same buttons: type your answer, press Check my answer, and use Give me a hint or Show next step if you need help. Step 5: When a slide is done, press the arrow on the right to go to the next slide. The little dots under the slide show you where you are. Count the dots if you like — that tells you how many are left. Step 6: Keep going, one slide at a time, until you reach the last slide. On the last slide, press the finish button. You will know the whole page is finished when all 12 questions show a correct answer, and you have pressed the finish button on the last slide. Ready? Start with question one, and tell me your answer. I am right here with you. 😊

activities.label: Activities
activities.text: Hello! Today I am your teacher, and this is our Activities page. On this page you do maths with your hands, not just in your head. There is one hands-on activity. You will pick a shape idea from our unit, make it or draw it, and tell someone about it. By the end you will be able to name a shape and say why it is that shape. You need paper, a pencil, and a few things from home — a ball, a box, and a tin can are perfect. A grown-up can sit with you. Here are all the steps. 1. Read the activity, then press Listen. The activity is called "Practise together". It tells you what to use and what to do. Press Listen and hear the words too. Then go and get your things: paper, a pencil, and your ball, box and tin can. I expect you to have them on the table before you start. 2. Do the activity. Pick one idea from our unit — for example the sphere, the cube, the cylinder, or rolling and stacking. Draw it or build it with your objects. Then explain it to someone in your family in your own words, like "This is a cube. It has six flat faces, so it stacks." Last, make up one question of your own, such as "How many sides does a triangle have?", and answer it yourself. 3. Write in the box. Type or write what you made and what you noticed. A good answer names the shape and says one true thing about it. For example: "I drew a cylinder. It rolls on its side and stands on its flat end." One or two sentences is plenty. 4. Press Mark complete. When your activity is done and your box is filled in, press Mark complete under it. Only press it when you really did the activity — that is how the page knows your work is finished. Then press Finish activities at the bottom. 5. Now the slides at the bottom. Under the page there is a deck of slides with the same hands-on activity, one on each slide. Press Start on the first slide. 6. On each slide, use the same buttons as before: do the activity, write in the box, then press Mark complete. Take your time — there's no rush. 7. Press the arrow on the right to go to the next slide. Look at the little dots under the slide. They show you where you are in the deck. 8. On the last slide, press Finish activities. You will know the page is finished when every activity has Mark complete pressed, and you have pressed Finish activities at the bottom. Ready? Go and get your ball, your box and your tin can, then tell me when you have them. 😊

games.label: Games
games.text: Hello! Today we are playing the Shape Games. This page is full of little games about shapes. You will name shapes like the cube, the sphere and the cylinder. You will also count sides and corners. We play games because playing helps our brains remember. You need your eyes, your thinking, and maybe a ball or a box to hold. Here are the three steps. 1. Pick one game and press Start game. A question will pop up with some answers to choose from. Read it slowly, then think before you tap. If there is a clue, use it! You get one star for every round you get right. I expect you to try your best guess even when it feels tricky — never leave it blank. 2. When the game ends, press Play again. This gives you more rounds and more stars. Some questions will come back again, so you get better each time. A game is mastered when it has all its stars. I expect you to keep pressing Play again until that game is full of stars. 3. Now do the same for every game on the page. Go one game at a time, from the top. Do not rush — mathematicians think slowly on purpose. I expect you to finish one game fully before you start the next one. You will know the page is finished when every game has all its stars. Then the page finishes by itself. You do not have to press anything special! Ready? Press Start game on the first game, then tell me how the first round went. 🌟

fluency.label: Math Fluency
fluency.text: Hello! Today I am your teacher, and this page is called Math Fluency. Let's get ready together. What it is: a quick shape sprint. Twelve short questions about shapes, one at a time. A clock at the top counts your time. Why we do it: so shape names come to your mind fast, like your own name. Fast and correct is the goal. What I expect from you: try every question, answer in one or two words, and stay calm. Take your time on tricky ones — mathematicians think slowly on purpose. Mistakes are okay. They help us learn. Step 1: Look at the top of the page and find the timer. Just notice it. Do not worry about it. Being right matters more than being quick. Step 2: Read question one out loud, slowly. Reading out loud helps your brain hear the question. Step 3: Think of the real object. A ball is a sphere. A tin can is a cylinder. A box is a cube. Picture it in your hand before you answer. Step 4: Type your answer in the box. Short words are best, like sphere, cube, circle, or a number like 6. Step 5: Press Check and continue. This checks your answer and takes you to the next question. Step 6: If you were right, smile and keep going. If not, read the little message. It tells you what to fix. That message is a gift, not a telling-off. Step 7: Do the same for all twelve questions. Read, think, type, press Check and continue. One question at a time, no rushing. Step 8: For counting questions, touch each side or each face with your finger as you count. Start at one corner so you do not count twice. Step 9: For rolling questions, ask yourself: does it have a curved part? Curved parts roll. Flat parts stack. Step 10: At the end, look at your score. You need most of them right to finish the page. Step 11: If you got fewer than that, press Run the sprint again. That is normal! The second try is usually much better. Step 12: The page is finished when one sprint has enough right answers. Then you will see your good score, and you can move on. Ready? Start with question one, and tell me how it goes. I am right here. 🌟

problems.label: Solve Real Problems
problems.text: Hello! I am your teacher today, and this page is called Solve Real Problems. Here is what it is. You will look at shapes from real life, like a box, a ball, a tin, a door, a scarf. You will say the shape name, or count the sides. We do this because shapes are all around your home. When you can name them out loud, you really know them. Here is what I expect from you. Look carefully first. Say your thinking in words, like "it is round all over, so it is a sphere." Try before you press Hint. Take your time — mathematicians think slowly on purpose. Now here are your steps. 1. There are 6 problems on this page. Read the first one slowly, or ask your grown-up to read it with you. Then ask yourself: what does this problem want me to do? Sometimes it wants a shape name. Sometimes it wants you to count sides. I expect you to know which one before you write. 2. Work it out in your head, or with your finger. If you must count sides, touch each side once and count out loud: one, two, three. Then type your answer in the box. Write your thinking too, like "4 sides, I touched each one." Then press Check answer. If you feel stuck, press Hint first and try again. 3. When the page says your answer is right, that problem is done. Well done — move to the next one. If it says not right, do not worry. Mistakes are how we learn. Read the hint, look again, and try one more time. Keep going until all 6 are done. 4. Now look under the page. There is a deck of slides with the same problems, one on each slide. Press Start on the first slide. Answer it the same way, with the same buttons. Then press the arrow on the right to go to the next slide. The little dots under the slide show you where you are. On the last slide, press the finish button. You will know the page is finished when all 6 problems say your answer is right, and you have pressed the finish button on the last slide. Ready? Tell me what the first problem says, and we will look at that together.

explain.label: Explain Your Thinking
explain.text: Hello! I am your teacher today, and this page is called Explain Your Thinking. On this page you do not just say the answer. You say WHY. You will talk about shapes like the sphere, the cube and the cylinder, and tell me how you know. Talking about your thinking helps the idea stick in your brain. You need your eyes on the page and your words — a grown-up can help you type if that is easier. Here are all the steps. There are four. Step 1. Look at the first prompt. A prompt is the question on the page that asks you to explain. Read it slowly, or ask your grown-up to read it with you. Under the prompt there are key ideas — these are the special words you should try to use, like sphere, cube or face. There are 6 prompts in all, so we go one at a time. I expect you to read the prompt twice before you write anything. Step 2. Now write your explanation in the box. Tell me three things: what you know, what rule you used, and why your answer makes sense. For example, if it asks about rolling, you might say a ball is round all over, so it rolls. Try to use the key words in your writing. When you are done, press Check mathematical ideas. If the page asks for more, add one more sentence and press Check mathematical ideas again. I expect a real try, not one word. Step 3. Next, press Show model explanation. This opens a good answer so you can compare it with yours. Do not worry if the words are not the same as yours — that is fine! Just look for the key ideas. Ask yourself, did I say the same big idea? Then go back and do Step 1 and Step 2 again for the next prompt, until all 6 are done. I expect every explanation to use the key ideas. Step 4. Now look under the page. There is a deck of slides with the same prompts, one prompt on each slide. Press Start on the first slide. Use the same buttons you already know on each slide. Then press the arrow on the right to move to the next slide. The little dots under the slide show you where you are. On the last slide, press the finish button. How will you know the page is finished? When all 6 prompts have your own explanation, each one uses the key ideas, and you have pressed the finish button on the last slide. Then you are done! Take your time — there's no rush. Tell me when you have read the first prompt, and we will do it together. 🙂

challenge.label: Unit Challenge
challenge.text: Hello! Today is your Unit Challenge for Unit 2, Geometry. It is 12 short questions about shapes. It is like a friendly test that shows how much you have learned about the cube, the sphere, the cylinder, and the flat shapes like the circle, square, rectangle and triangle. By the end, you will know which shape ideas you are strong at. You do not need a pencil, but you may keep a ball, a box and a tin can beside you to look at and think with. What I expect from you: you read each question yourself, think first, then choose. I will help you think, but the answers must come from you. That is what makes it yours. Step 1. Read question one slowly. Read the question twice before you answer. Ask yourself what the question is really about: is it about rolling and stacking, or counting sides, or naming a shape? Then look at all four choices before you pick one. Step 2. Choose your answer, then press Next question. Do this for every question, one at a time, all the way to question twelve. Take your time — there's no rush. If a question feels hard, picture a real thing at home: a ball, a tin, a box, a door, a plate. If you get stuck, tell me and I will give you a hint, not the answer. Step 3. At the end you will see your score. You pass with more than half of the questions right. Look at your score and tell me how you did. I will be proud of you either way, because trying is the work. Step 4. If your score is not high enough, press Try again. That is not a bad thing at all. Mistakes are how we learn. Before you try again, come and tell me which questions felt tricky, and we will practise those shapes together first. Step 5. When your score is good enough, press Continue. That is the last button on this page. You will know the page is finished when you have answered all 12 questions, seen a passing score, and pressed Continue. Then come back and tell me one shape fact you feel really sure about now. Ready? Start with question one. 😊

lesson.label: The Lesson
lesson.text: Hello! Today I am your teacher, and this page is called The Lesson. On this page you will learn all about halves. A half is one of two equal parts of a whole. We do this so you can share things fairly, like a chapati with your brother. By the end, you will know what a whole is, what equal parts are, and that two halves make one whole. Before we start, get a pencil, some paper shapes to fold (a circle, a square, a rectangle), and ask your grown-up to sit near you. There are 5 steps. Take your time — there's no rush. Step 1. Look at the top of the page. There are 5 concepts, and each one is a short story about halves. Read the first one slowly, then press Listen to hear it read to you. I expect you to listen right to the end without skipping. Step 2. Each concept has an example. Say the example out loud, in your own voice. Then try it for real with your own things — fold a paper circle, or break a biscuit into two pieces. A good try is when the two parts match exactly. Step 3. Now do Step 1 and Step 2 again for all 5 concepts, one at a time. Read, press Listen, say the example, try it. I expect you to finish all five, not just the first one. Step 4. When you have read every concept, go to the bottom of the page and press I studied the concepts. Only press it when you really did read them all — that button is your promise to yourself. Step 5. Under the page there is a deck of slides. Each slide has one of the same concepts. Press Start on the first slide. Use the same buttons on each slide, then press the arrow on the right to go to the next slide. The little dots under the slide show you where you are. On the last slide, press the finish button. You will know the page is finished when you have pressed I studied the concepts, and the last slide shows its finish button pressed. Ready? Start with Step 1, and tell me when you have listened to the first concept. 🙂

overview.label: Unit Overview
overview.text: Hello! I am your teacher today. This page is called Unit Overview. It is like standing at the door of a new lesson and peeking inside. Our unit is Fractions: Halves. By the end of this page, you will know what a half is about and what we will learn together. You need your eyes, your voice, and a grown-up nearby if you like. There are 3 small steps. Here they all are. Step 1. Read the Unit Overview. Look at the words on the screen and read them slowly. If you see a speaker picture, press Listen and hear the words too. Reading and listening together helps the words stick. Look out for two special words: whole means the complete thing, and half means one of two equal parts. I expect you to read it all the way to the end, not just the first line. Take your time — there's no rush. Step 2. Say in your own words what you think you will learn. Say it out loud to your grown-up, or type it to me here. A good answer sounds like this: "I will learn about halves. A half is one of two equal parts, like sharing a biscuit fairly." Use your own words, not the same words as the screen. One or two sentences is plenty. I expect you to try, even if it feels wobbly — mistakes are how we learn. Step 3. Press Continue to go to The Lesson. Find the button that says Continue and press it once. Only press it after you have read the page and said your sentence. That button takes you to the next part, where we start learning properly. You will know this page is finished when you have read the overview, said what you will learn, and pressed Continue and the next page opens. Now let's begin with Step 1. Read the Unit Overview, and press Listen if you see the speaker. Tell me when you are done. 🙂

words.label: Math Words & Symbols
words.text: Hello! Today I am your teacher, and this page is called Math Words & Symbols. This page has the special maths words for our unit on halves: whole, half, equal, unequal, part, share, and divide. Words are like keys. When you know the words, the maths opens up for you. By the end you will be able to say each word, tell me what it means, and use it in your own sentence. You will need your voice, your ears, and your typing finger. What I expect from you is this: try every word, say it out loud even if it feels funny, and use your own words for the meaning. Not perfect — just yours. Take your time — there's no rush. Here are all the steps. 1. Look at the first word on the page. Read the word, then read what it means beside it. Now press Listen. Listen carefully and see if the sound matches the word in your head. Do this for the word you are on before you move along. A good job here means you looked at the word AND listened, not just clicked fast. 2. Now say the word out loud, nice and clear. Say it with me, slowly. Then say the meaning in your own words — do not copy the page. For "half" you might say, "it is one of two same-size pieces." That is a lovely answer. 3. Next, type a sentence using the word, then press Check sentence. Make it a sentence about your real life, like "I gave my brother half of my biscuit." Then read what the checker says to you. If it asks for more, fix your sentence and press Check sentence again. 4. Do steps 1, 2 and 3 again for every word on the page: whole, half, equal, unequal, part, share, and divide or split. One word at a time, no skipping. Slow and steady is the maths way. 5. When you have done every single word, press the button at the bottom that says I know these words and symbols. Only press it when you really have done them all — that button is you telling me you are ready. 6. Now look under the page. There is a deck of slides with the same words, one word on each slide. This is your practice, to make the words stick. On the first slide, press Start. 7. On each slide, use the same buttons as before: press Listen, say the word out loud, say the meaning in your own words, type your sentence, and press Check sentence. 8. When that slide is done, press the arrow on the right side to go to the next slide. Look at the little dots under the slide — they show you where you are and how many are left. 9. Keep going slide by slide. On the very last slide, press the finish button. You will know the page is finished when you have pressed I know these words and symbols, and you have pressed the finish button on the last slide. Ready? Start with word number one, press Listen, and tell me what the word is. I am right here with you. 🙂

explore.label: Explore the Concept
explore.text: Hello! Today we are exploring halves. A half is one of two equal parts of a whole. Equal means the same size. On this page you will find out about halves by yourself, one small discovery at a time. You just need your eyes, your thinking, and a grown-up nearby if you want one. Take your time — there's no rush. What I expect from you: read each little story, look hard at the picture, then type your own idea in your own words. Short is fine. Even one or two words is fine. Guessing carefully is good — mistakes are how we learn. Here are all the steps. 1. Look at the top of the page. You will see 6 numbered tabs. Each tab is one discovery. Press tab number 1 first. Now read the little story, and look at the picture or model next to it. Point at the picture with your finger and ask yourself: how many parts do I see? Are they the same size? 2. Under the story is the discovery question. Read it slowly, twice. Think first — say the answer out loud to yourself before you type. Then type your idea in the box. Use words from our unit like whole, part, half, equal or unequal. Then press Check my idea. 3. If the page says Look again, that is okay! Press Hint. The hint will point you to the right idea. Read it, change your answer a little, and press Check my idea one more time. When it says Exactly!, your tab gets a tick. Well done — that tick means you got it. 4. Now press tab number 2, and do the very same thing: read, look, think, type, press Check my idea. Keep going like this through tabs 3, 4, 5 and 6. One tab at a time, please — finish one before you open the next. 5. Watch your tabs as you go. Every tab needs a tick. When all 6 tabs have a tick, the top part of the page is done. That means you have answered every discovery question correctly. Brilliant work! 6. Now scroll down, under the page. There is a deck of slides. Each slide has one of the same discoveries. On the first slide, press Start. 7. On each slide, do the same job as before: read the question, think, type your idea, press Check my idea. If you need help, press Hint. Wait for Exactly! before you move on. 8. To go to the next slide, press the arrow on the right side. Look at the little dots under the slide. The dots show you where you are and how many slides are left. 9. Keep going slide by slide until you reach the last one. On the last slide, press the finish button. I don't tick anything for you — you press the buttons, because it is your work. You will know the page is finished when all 6 tabs have a tick, and you have pressed the finish button on the last slide. Ready? Press tab number 1, and tell me what you see in the picture. I'm right here with you. 😊

visuals.label: Visual Models
visuals.text:
Hello! Today I am your teacher for the Visual Models page. Visual models are pictures you can play with. They show what a half looks like. We do this so halves feel real to your eyes and hands, not just words. By the end, you will be able to point at a shape and say if it shows halves. What you need: your eyes, your finger or mouse, and your voice. What I expect from you: look slowly, press the buttons, and say what you notice out loud. Take your time — there's no rush. There are 7 steps. Here they are. 1. Find the first model, "A Whole and Its Parts". Look at the shape before it is split. Say out loud, "This is the whole." If the model moves, drag it with your finger or mouse to turn it, and press its buttons to split it. I expect you to tell me how many parts you made. 2. Now go to model 2, "Equal Parts vs Unequal Parts". Look at the two parts. Ask yourself, "Do they match in size?" Drag or press the buttons to change the split. I expect you to spot one picture that is fair and one that is not fair. 3. Next is model 3, "Making Halves by Folding and Drawing". Watch the shape fold. See how the two sides land on top of each other. Press the buttons to fold it a different way. I expect you to point at the fold line and say, "This line makes two halves."

4. Now model 4, "Halves Can Be Different Shapes but Equal Size". One fold makes two rectangles. Another fold makes two triangles. Drag the shape and press the buttons to try both. I expect you to say that both ways are still halves. 5. Last is model 5, "Two Halves Make a Whole". Watch the two halves slide back together. Press the buttons to pull them apart and push them back. I expect you to say the magic words: "Two halves make one whole."

6. Under every model there is a caption — the little sentence that tells you what you are seeing. Read it, then press Listen to hear it read to you. Do this for all five. I expect you to listen right to the end, then say the caption back in your own words. 7. When you have looked at all five models and heard all five captions, press I explored the models at the bottom of the page. You will know the page is finished when you have pressed I explored the models and it shows you are done. That button is yours to press — I cannot press it for you. Ready? Start with step 1 and tell me how many parts you made. 🙂

method.label: Learn the Method
method.text:
Hello! Today I am your teacher for the Learn the Method page. 😊

This page shows 6 methods. A method is a way to do something, step by step, in the right order. These methods teach you how to make halves, how to check if parts are equal, and how to put two halves back to make a whole. When we finish, you will be able to fold a shape into two halves and know if it is a true half. Here is what I expect from you: sit somewhere quiet, say each step out loud, and keep a pencil and a few paper shapes near you. A grown-up can help you fold and cut. Take your time — mathematicians think slowly on purpose. There are four things to do on this page. Here they are. Step 1: Look at the first method at the top. Read the first step it shows you. Read it out loud, slowly. Then press the button that says Show me the next step. A new step will appear. I expect you to read each new step out loud before you press again. Step 2: Keep pressing Show me the next step until the page says Method complete. Do not rush and press fast. Say every step out loud first, then press. When it says Method complete, that method is done. Well done — one finished! Step 3: Now do the same for every method. There are 6 in all. Read a step, say it out loud, press Show me the next step, and stop when it says Method complete. Then move to the next method. I expect all 6 methods to say Method complete when you are done. Step 4: Under the page there is a deck of slides. Each slide has one of the same methods. Press Start on the first slide. Then use the same buttons on that slide to see each step, just like before. Say the steps out loud again — hearing them twice helps you remember. Step 5: When a slide is finished, press the arrow on the right side to go to the next slide. Look at the little dots under the slide. The dots show you where you are and how many slides are left. Keep going, slide by slide. Step 6: On the last slide, press the finish button. That tells the page you have done them all. You will know the page is finished when all 6 methods have said Method complete, and you have pressed the finish button on the last slide. Now go and start with Step 1. Come back and tell me when your first method says Method complete, and tell me one thing it taught you. I will be right here. 🌟

guided.label: Guided Practice
guided.text: Hello! Today I am your teacher, and this is our Guided Practice page for Unit 3: Halves. Practice is where the learning sticks. You already know that a half is one of two equal parts of a whole. Now you get to use that idea again and again, until it feels easy. By the end you will be able to spot halves, make halves, and say why two equal parts are halves. You will need a pencil, some paper, and if you can, a few paper shapes to fold — a circle, a square, a rectangle. Ask your grown-up to help you cut them. Take your time. Mathematicians think slowly on purpose. Here are all the steps. 1. Read one question. There are 12 questions on the page. Start with the first one. Read it slowly, right to the end. Then work it out on paper or in your head. If it is about a shape, fold a paper shape or draw it — that helps a lot. I expect you to think first, before you type anything. 2. Type your answer, then press Check my answer. Write your answer in the box in your own words. Short is fine, like "a half" or "unequal". If the page says you are right, lovely — read the little explanation too, because it tells you why. If it says not yet, do not worry. Mistakes are how we learn. 3. If you feel stuck, press Give me a hint. You can get up to three hints. Try the first hint, then think again before you ask for the next one. That is how hints help you most. If you are still stuck, press Show next step — it shows you one line of the working, and then you finish the rest yourself. I expect you to try before you press, every time. 4. Keep going until every question is right. Work through all 12, one at a time, in order. When each one is correct, that part of the page is done. Take a small stretch after question 6 if you get tired — that is allowed! 5. Now go to the slides under the page. There is a deck of slides below, with the same questions, one on each slide.
