Press Start on the first slide. This is your chance to show the answers now live in your head. 6. Answer each slide the same way. Type your answer and press Check my answer. If you need help, press Give me a hint, and Show next step if you are still stuck. Same buttons, same good thinking. 7. Move along the slides. When a slide is done, press the arrow on the right to go to the next slide. Look at the little dots under the slide — they show you where you are and how many are left. 8. Finish the deck. On the last slide, press the finish button. That tells the page you have done them all. How will you know the page is finished? When all 12 questions show a correct answer, and you have pressed the finish button on the last slide. That is it — the page is complete. Ready? Read question one, work it out, and tell me your answer. I am right here with you. 🙂

examples.label: Worked Examples
examples.text: Hello! Today we are on the Worked Examples page for Unit 3: Fractions: Halves. A worked example is a question with all the thinking shown. It is like watching me solve it, step by step. We do this so you learn the way to think, not just the answer. By the end, you will know how to check if two parts are true halves. You will need a pencil, some scrap paper, and maybe a paper shape to fold. A grown-up can sit with you. Here is our plan. There are four steps. 1. Read the first worked example and try it yourself. Look at the question at the top of the box. Read it slowly, twice. Then say out loud, or write on your paper, what you think the answer is. It is fine to be wrong! Trying first makes your brain ready. I expect you to have a little answer in your head before you look at the solution. 2. Now press "Show worked solution" and compare. Read the solution one line at a time. After each line, ask yourself, "Did I think that too?" Put your finger on the line so you do not lose your place. I expect you to spot one thing that matches your thinking, and one thing you missed. 3. Do the same for all 12 examples. Read, try, then press "Show worked solution". At the top of the page there is a counter. It tells you how many you have opened. Keep going until every single one is open. Take your time — there's no rush. I expect you to try each question first, not just open them all quickly. 4. Now the slides at the bottom. Under the page there is a deck of slides. Each slide has one of the same examples. Press "Start" on the first slide. Use the same buttons on each slide as before. Then press the arrow on the right to go to the next slide. The little dots under the slide show you where you are. On the last slide, press the finish button. You will know the page is finished when the counter at the top shows all 12 opened, and you have pressed the finish button on the last slide. Ready? Start with step 1 now. Read the very first question, and tell me what you think the answer is. I'll be right here. 😊

activities.label: Activities
activities.text: Hello! Today I am your teacher for the Activities page. This page is where we stop reading and start doing. You will make halves with your own hands. That is the best way to remember them. You will need paper, a pencil, and a grown-up nearby to help with scissors. Here is your whole guide, step by step. 1. Look at the top of the page. There is one hands-on activity. It is called "Practise together". Read it, then press Listen to hear it read out loud. Listening while you read helps the words stick. 2. Get your things. You need paper, a pencil, and maybe a biscuit, a mango, or some little beans. Put them on the table before you start. A good learner gets ready first. 3. Now do the activity. Pick one idea from our unit about halves. You could fold a paper circle into two equal parts. You could draw a square and draw one line down the middle. Take your time — mathematicians think slowly on purpose. 4. Check your halves the clever way. Fold your shape so the two parts sit on top of each other. If the edges match exactly, you made two equal halves. If one part sticks out, try again. I expect you to fold and check, not just look. 5. Show your work to someone in your family and explain it. Say something like: "This is the whole circle. I folded it. Now it has two halves. Halves must be equal." I expect you to use the words whole, half, and equal out loud. 6. Now write in the box on the page. Write what you did and what you noticed. One or two sentences is perfect for you, like: "I folded a square. It made two equal halves." Spelling does not need to be perfect. Your thinking does. 7. When you have really done it, press Mark complete under the activity. Only press it after you have folded, explained, and written in the box. That button is your promise that the work is done. 8. Then look at the bottom of the page and press Finish activities. Press this once every activity has Mark complete on it. That tells the page you are done up here. 9. Now go to the slides under the page. They show the same activity, one on each slide. Press Start on the first slide to begin. 10. On each slide, use the same buttons as before: Listen to hear it, do the activity, write in the box, then Mark complete. Then press the arrow on the right to go to the next slide. The little dots under the slide show you where you are. 11. On the last slide, press Finish activities. Then look at the dots — when you are on the last dot and everything says complete, your page is finished. Well done, that is how you know you are all done! Now go and fold your first shape. Come and tell me what you noticed, and I will be right here waiting. 🙂

fluency.label: Math Fluency
fluency.text: Hello! Today I am your teacher for the Math Fluency page. Let's get ready. This page is a sprint. A sprint means quick questions, one after the other. There are 12 questions about halves. A half is one of two equal parts of a whole. Equal means the same size. We do this so the word "half" comes to your mind fast, without hard thinking. What I expect from you: try every question, answer in a few words, and be honest. Fast is good, but right is better. Mathematicians think slowly on purpose — so take a breath when you need one. Have a pencil and some paper shapes near you, in case you want to fold one. Here are the steps. 1. Get ready. Sit somewhere calm. Put your pencil and paper next to you. Look at the top of the page — you will see your time. The time is just for fun. It is not a race against anyone else. 2. Read question one. Read it twice. Ask yourself: are the two parts the same size? If yes, they are halves. If one is bigger, they are unequal, so they are not halves. 3. Type your answer in the box. Use short words, like "a half" or "unequal" or "3 dates". Then press Check & continue. That button saves your answer and brings the next question. 4. Look at what the page tells you. If your answer is right, smile and go on. If it is not right, read the little explanation. Say it out loud once. That helps it stick. 5. Keep going, one question at a time, until you finish all 12. Do not skip. If a question feels hard, remember the fold-and-match test: if two parts match exactly when folded, they are equal halves. 6. If you get stuck for a long time, do your best guess, press Check & continue, and read the answer note. You can always come back and try again. Mistakes are how we learn. 7. When all 12 are done, look at your score. You need most of them right to finish this page. That means only a few misses are okay. 8. If you have too few right, press Run the sprint again. This starts a fresh sprint. Before you start, tell yourself the big rule: a half is one of two equal parts of a whole. 9. On the second try, go a tiny bit slower on the questions you missed before. Slower thinking often means more right answers. 10. You will know the page is finished when a sprint has enough right answers. The page will show you that you passed. Then you can move on with a big smile. Now let's begin. Here comes question one — open it and tell me what it says, and I will help you think it through.

games.label: Games
games.text: Hello! Today we are playing the Games on our Fractions: Halves page. Games are how we practise. Every game asks you short questions about wholes, halves, equal parts and unequal parts. By the end, those words will feel easy in your head. You just need your eyes, your thinking brain, and maybe a paper shape to fold beside you. Here is what I expect from you: read each question slowly, think first, then choose. Take your time — there's no rush. It is okay to get one wrong. Mistakes are how we learn. Step 1: Pick any game on the page and press Start game. Then answer each round. Read the question twice before you tap an answer. Ask yourself the big question of this unit: are the two parts EQUAL, the same size? If they are equal, they are halves. If one is bigger, they are not halves. Every round you get right gives you a star. I expect you to think before you tap, not tap fast. Step 2: When a game ends, press Play again to collect more stars. The same game may show the questions in a new order, so read carefully again. A game is mastered when it has all its stars. If you get one wrong, that is fine — look at the little explanation, say it out loud in your own words, then Play again. I expect you to keep going until that game is full of stars. Step 3: Now do the same for every game on the page. Press Start game on the next one, answer the rounds, press Play again until it is mastered, and move on. Some games ask what a word means, like "whole" means the complete thing before it is split, and "half" means one of two equal parts. Say the meaning quietly to yourself before you choose. I expect you to finish every game, not just your favourite one. How you will know you are finished: when every game has all its stars, the page finishes by itself. You do not need to press anything extra. Ready? Press Start game on your first game, and tell me how the first round goes. 🌟

problems.label: Solve Real Problems
problems.text: Hello! Today I am your teacher for the "Solve Real Problems" page. On this page you use halves in real life. Sharing a chapati. Cutting a watermelon. Sharing dates between two children. We do this because halves are not just on paper — you use them at home every day. By the end, you will be able to look at a real thing and say if it is shared into two equal parts. What you need: your eyes, your thinking, and a grown-up nearby if you want help typing. What I expect from you: read slowly, think first, then type your own words. Even a short answer is good if it is your own. Here are all the steps. Step 1. There are 6 problems on this page. Read the first one out loud, slowly. Then ask yourself: what is this question really asking me? Take your time — there's no rush. Step 2. Now think it out. Ask yourself the big question of this unit: are the two parts the same size? If they are the same size, they are halves. If one is bigger, they are not halves. If the problem has things to share, like dates or beans, give them out one at a time, one for you, one for me, until they are gone. Step 3. Type your answer in the box. Do not just type yes or no. Tell me why too. A good answer sounds like this: "No, because one piece is bigger, so they are not equal." That "because" part is what I am looking for. Step 4. Press Check answer. If you are stuck before that, press Hint first and read it. A hint is not cheating — it is a little push. Try again after the hint. Step 5. When the page says your answer is right, that problem is done. Move to the next problem and do steps 1 to 4 again. Keep going until all 6 problems say right. Six ticks means the top part is finished. Step 6. Now look under the page. There is a deck of slides with the same problems, one problem on each slide. Press Start on the first slide. Step 7. On each slide, use the same buttons as before: think, type your answer, press Hint if you need help, then press Check answer. Step 8. When a slide is right, press the arrow on the right to go to the next slide. Look at the little dots under the slide — they show you where you are and how many are left. Step 9. On the last slide, press the finish button. How you know the page is finished: all 6 problems say your answer is right, and you have pressed the finish button on the last slide. Ready? Read problem one, then tell me what you think it is asking you. I am right here. 😊

explain.label: Explain Your Thinking
explain.text: Hello! I am your teacher today, and this page is a lovely one. This page is called Explain Your Thinking. It asks you to say WHY, not just yes or no. You will look at shapes cut into parts and tell me how you know if they are halves. We do this because a good mathematician can explain their thinking out loud. By the end, you will be able to use the words whole, half, equal and unequal in your own sentences. What you need: your eyes on the page, and a grown-up nearby to help you type. What I expect from you: a whole sentence, not one word. Try to use the word equal or unequal every time. Take your time — mathematicians think slowly on purpose. Here are all the steps, one by one. Step 1. There are 6 prompts on this page. Read the first prompt slowly. Under it you will see some key ideas, like Whole, Half and Equal. Those are the words I want you to use in your answer. Read the prompt twice before you write anything. Step 2. Now think in your head first. Ask yourself: are the two parts the same size, or is one bigger? Same size means equal, and equal means halves. One bigger means unequal, and that is NOT halves. That little check is your rule. Step 3. Click in the box and write your explanation. A good answer has three little bits: what you see, the rule you used, and what that means. Like this: "The two parts are the same size. Halves must be equal parts. So these are halves." I expect a sentence like that from you, in your own words. Step 4. Press Check mathematical ideas. This looks for your key words. If it asks for more, do not worry — that is normal. Just add one more sentence with the missing word, like "Both parts are equal", and press Check mathematical ideas again. Step 5. Now press Show model explanation. This shows you a good answer to compare with yours. Do not copy it. Just look and ask: did I say the same idea? If you missed a word, remember it for the next prompt. Step 6. Do steps 1 to 5 again for prompt 2, then 3, 4, 5 and 6. Six prompts in all. Each time: read, think, write, press Check mathematical ideas, then press Show model explanation. Step 7. Now look under the page. There is a deck of slides with the same prompts, one prompt on each slide. Press Start on the first slide to begin. Step 8. On each slide, use the same buttons as before: write your answer, press Check mathematical ideas, then press Show model explanation. Same job, just on a slide. Step 9. To move on, press the arrow on the right side of the slide. Look at the little dots under the slide — they show you which slide you are on and how many are left. Step 10. Keep going until the last slide. On that one, press the finish button. Only you can press it — that is how the page saves your good work. How will you know the page is finished? Every one of the 6 explanations is written, each one uses the key ideas, and you have pressed the finish button on the last slide. Ready? Read prompt one and tell me what you notice.

challenge.label: Unit Challenge
challenge.text: Well done for getting all the way here! This page is your Unit Challenge. It is a little quiz about halves. It shows what you have learned in this unit: what a whole is, what a half is, and how to tell equal parts from unequal parts. You just need your eyes, your thinking brain, and a grown-up nearby if you want one. I will not tell you any answers, but I will help you think. Here are the steps. Step 1. Look at question one on your screen. Read it slowly, twice. Ask yourself the magic question: are the two parts the SAME size? If yes, they are halves. If one is bigger, they are not halves. I expect you to think first, then choose. Take your time — there's no rush. Step 2. Tap the answer you think is right. Then press Next question. Do this for all 12 questions, one at a time. Some questions ask about sharing, like sharing 6 dates between 2 children. For those, share them out one at a time in your head, one for you, one for me, until they are all gone. I expect you to try every question, even the tricky ones. A good guess is better than skipping. Step 3. After the last question, your score will show on the screen. You pass when you get more than half of them right. Look at your score and see how you did. I expect you to look at the questions you got wrong and think about why. Mistakes are how we learn. Step 4. If your score is not high enough, press Try again. That is not a bad thing at all — it just means one more turn. Before you start again, say the rule out loud: a half is one of two equal parts of a whole. I expect you to go a bit slower the second time. Step 5. When your score is good, press Continue. That tells the page you are finished with the Unit Challenge. You will know the page is done when you have answered all 12 questions, seen your score, and pressed Continue. Then come back and tell me your score — I would love to hear how you did! 🌟

words.label: Math Words & Symbols
words.text: Hello! Today I am your teacher for the Math Words & Symbols page. This page holds the special words of Unit 4: Measures. These are words like taller, shorter, longer, wider, thinner, order and measure. We learn them because maths is easier when you know what the words mean. By the end, you will be able to say each word, tell me what it means, and use it in your own sentence. You will need your voice, your eyes on the screen, and a grown-up nearby if you want help typing. Take your time — mathematicians think slowly on purpose. Here are all the steps. 1. Look at the first word on the page and read it. Under the word you will see what it means in easy words. Then press Listen. Listen carefully to how the word sounds. I expect you to look at the word while you listen, so your eyes and ears learn it together. 2. Now say the word out loud. Say it clearly, like you are teaching a little brother or sister. 3. Next, say the meaning in your own words. Do not copy the page word for word. For example, for "taller" you might say, "it reaches higher up." I expect your own words, even if they are simple ones. That shows me you really understand. 4. Now type one sentence using the word, then press Check sentence. A good sentence uses the word about something real, like "My dad is taller than me." Try to use the comparing word fully — say "taller than", not just "tall". 5. Read what the checker says to you. If it says well done, smile — you got it! If it asks you to fix something, change your sentence and press Check sentence again. Mistakes are how we learn. 6. Do the same four things for every word on the page: Listen, say the word, say the meaning, type a sentence and press Check sentence. One word at a time. Do not rush ahead. 7. When you have done every single word, press I know these words and symbols at the bottom of the page. Only press it when you have really done them all — that button is your promise that you finished. 8. Now look under the page. There is a deck of slides with the same words, one word on each slide. Press Start on the first slide to begin. 9. On each slide, use the same buttons as before: Listen, then say the word, say the meaning, type your sentence, and press Check sentence. Try to make a new sentence, not the same one you used before. That makes your brain work a little harder, which is good! 10. When a slide is done, press the arrow on the right to go to the next slide. Look at the little dots under the slide — they show you where you are and how many slides are left. 11. Keep going until the last slide. On the last slide, press the finish button. You will know the page is finished when two things are true: you have pressed I know these words and symbols at the bottom of the page, and you have pressed the finish button on the last slide. Now start with step one. Press Listen on the first word, then tell me which word it is. I am right here with you. 😊

lesson.label: The Lesson
lesson.text: Hello! Today I am your teacher, and this page is called The Lesson. On this page you will learn how to compare sizes. You will learn tall and short, long and short, wide and thin. You will learn to put things in order, and to measure with blocks and paper clips. We do this so you can look at two things and say which is bigger, in a fair way. Here is what I expect from you: read slowly, say the words out loud, and try each idea with real things near you. A pencil, a cup, a spoon, a block — these are your helpers today. There are 4 things to do. Here they all are. 1. Read the 5 concepts, one at a time. Each one is a short story about size. Start with the first one, read it slowly, then press Listen to hear it read to you. Listening after reading helps the words stick. I expect you to finish one concept before you move to the next one — no jumping ahead. 2. Say the example out loud, then try it with your own things. If the example says "the date palm is taller than the bush", find two real things, like a big cup and a small cup. Stand them on the same table. Then say the whole sentence: "The big cup is taller than the small cup." I expect a full sentence, not just one word. 3. When you have read all 5 concepts, press the button at the bottom that says I studied the concepts. Only press it when you have really read every one. That button tells the page you are done reading. 4. Now look under the page. There is a deck of slides with the same 5 ideas, one idea on each slide. Press Start on the first slide. Use the same buttons on each slide. Then press the arrow on the right to go to the next slide. The little dots under the slide show you where you are. Keep going until the last slide, then press the finish button. You will know the page is finished when you have pressed I studied the concepts, and you have pressed the finish button on the last slide. Take your time — there's no rush. Tell me when you have finished step 1, and I will check in with you. 🙂

overview.label: Unit Overview
overview.text: Hello! I am your teacher today. Let's start our new unit together. This page is called Unit Overview. It is like looking at a map before a trip. It tells you what Unit 4, Measures, is about. In this unit you will learn to say which thing is taller, longer and wider. You will also measure with blocks and paper clips. What you need: your eyes, your ears, and your voice. A grown-up can sit near you if you like. There are 3 steps on this page. Here they all are. Step 1: Read the Unit Overview. Look at the words at the top of the page. Read them slowly. If you see a speaker picture, press Listen and listen carefully. You can press Listen again if you want to hear it twice. I expect you to read or listen all the way to the end, not just the first line. Take your time — there's no rush. Step 2: Say in your own words what you think you will learn. Do not copy the words on the screen. Just tell me, in your own way, like you are telling a friend. A good answer sounds like this: "I will learn about tall and short things, and I will measure with blocks." One or two sentences is plenty. I expect you to use at least one measuring word, like tall, short, long or wide. Step 3: Press Continue to go to The Lesson. Only press it after you have done Step 1 and Step 2. Continue is the button that takes you to the next part. That is where we start learning properly. You will know this page is finished when you have listened, said what you will learn, and pressed Continue. Now let's begin. Please do Step 1: read the Unit Overview, and press Listen if you see the speaker. Tell me when you are done. 🙂

explore.label: Explore the Concept
explore.text: Hello! I am your teacher today. This page is called Explore the Concept. It is all about Measures — comparing sizes. You will learn to say which thing is taller, longer, or wider. All you need is your eyes, your thinking, and a grown-up nearby if you want one. Let's begin. 1. Look at the top of the page. You will see 6 little numbered tabs. Press tab number 1. A discovery will open up. Read the little story and look at the picture or model. Take your time — I want you to really look at it, not rush. Mathematicians think slowly on purpose. 2. Now read the question under the picture. Think first, then type your idea in the box. Try to write a full sentence, like "the date palm is taller than the bush". Then press Check my idea. I expect you to try your own idea first, even if you are not sure. A try is always better than a blank box. 3. If the page says Look again, do not worry. Mistakes are how we learn. Press Hint, read it slowly, then change your answer and press Check my idea again. When it says Exactly!, that tab gets a little tick. Well done — that means you got it. 4. Now do the same for tabs 2, 3, 4, 5 and 6. One at a time, in order. Press the tab, read, think, type, press Check my idea. I expect a tick on every single tab before you stop. 5. Next, scroll down under the page. There is a deck of slides. They show the same discoveries, one on each slide. Press Start on the first slide to begin. 6. On each slide, use the same buttons as before: type your idea, press Check my idea, press Hint if you need help. Then press the arrow on the right to go to the next slide. The little dots under the slide show you how far you have come. 7. Keep going until you reach the last slide. On that one, press the finish button. That tells the page you are done. I expect you to press it yourself — that is how your work gets saved. You will know the page is finished when all 6 tabs have a tick, and you have pressed the finish button on the last slide. Now go and press tab number 1. Tell me what you see, and I will be right here. 🙂

method.label: Learn the Method
method.text: Hello! I am your teacher today, and this page is called Learn the Method. A method is a way to work something out, step by step. On this page there are 6 methods about measuring. They show you how to compare things — taller and shorter, longer and shorter, wider and thinner — and how to put things in order. We do this so you learn the right way to look, not just guess. By the end, you will be able to say things like "the date palm is taller than the bush" and know why. What you need: your eyes, your voice, and a grown-up nearby if you want one. What I expect from you: read each step, say it out loud, and take your time. Mathematicians think slowly on purpose. Here are all the steps. 1. Look at the first method on the page. Read its first step. Say it out loud in your own voice. I expect you to really say it, not just look — saying it helps your brain remember it. 2. Now press the button that says Show me the next step. A new step will appear. Read that one out loud too. Do this one step at a time, never rushing ahead. 3. Keep pressing Show me the next step until the page says Method complete. That means you have reached the end of that method. Well done — one method finished! 4. Now do the very same thing for the next method. Read step one, press Show me the next step, say each step out loud, and keep going until it says Method complete. 5. Do this for every method, until all 6 methods say Method complete. I expect you to finish all six, not stop at two or three. Take a little stretch break if you get tired. 6. While you read, try to picture it in your head. When a step says stand two things side by side, imagine your own cup and your own spoon. Even better, get two real things and try it with your hands. 7. Now look under the page. There is a deck of slides. Each slide has one method on it, just like above. Press Start on the first slide. 8. On the slide, use the same buttons as before. Press Show me the next step and say each step out loud, until that slide's method is complete. 9. Press the arrow on the right side to go to the next slide. Look at the little dots under the slide — they show you where you are and how many slides are left. 10. Keep going slide by slide. Start, read, press for the next step, then the right arrow. On the last slide, press the finish button. You will know the page is finished when all 6 methods say Method complete, and the last slide has had its finish button pressed. That is the whole page done! Ready? Start with step 1, and tell me when your first method says Method complete. I am right here. 🌟

visuals.label: Visual Models
visuals.text:
Hello! Today I am your teacher, and this page is our picture page. Visual Models means pictures that show our maths ideas. There are 5 of them. Looking at them helps you see tall, short, long, wide, thin, and how we measure with blocks. By the end, you will be able to point at two things and say which is taller, longer or wider. You need your eyes, your finger for pressing, and your voice to say the words out loud. Let's go! Step 1. Look at the first model, "Comparing Height — Tall and Short". Two things stand side by side. Run your finger up each one, from the bottom to the top. If the picture moves, drag it with your finger to turn it, and press its buttons to change it. I expect you to say out loud: "This one is taller. This one is shorter." Full sentence, please! Step 2. Go to model two, "Comparing Length — Long and Short". This one is about things lying down, like a stick or a ribbon. Check that both things start at the same line. Drag it if it moves, and press its buttons. I expect you to point to the one that reaches further and say, "This one is longer."

Step 3. Now model three, "Comparing Width — Wide and Thin". Width means how far across, from side to side. Sweep your finger across each one, left to right. The one that needs a long sweep is wider. I expect you to say, "This one is wider. This one is thinner."

Step 4. Look at model four, "Ordering by Size". Order means putting things in a line, from smallest to biggest. Find the shortest one first. Then the next shortest. Then the longest. If you can drag them, drag them into that line. I expect you to read your line out loud: "Short, longer, longest."

Step 5. Last one — model five, "Measuring with Blocks and Paper Clips". Here we count same-size blocks or clips to see how tall or how long a thing is. Press its buttons to add or change the blocks. Count them slowly, one, two, three. I expect you to say a whole sentence, like "It is 6 blocks tall."

Step 6. Under every model there is a caption. A caption is the little sentence that tells you what the picture shows. Read it, then press Listen to hear it. Listen carefully, then say the words with me. Do this for all 5 captions, not just one. Step 7. When you have looked at all 5 models and heard all 5 captions, press the button at the bottom that says I explored the models. Press it only when you really have seen them all — that is how you know the page is finished. Take your time — there's no rush. When you finish a model, tell me which one you liked best, and I will help with the next. Ready? Start with Step 1. 🙂

guided.label: Guided Practice
guided.text: Hello! Today we are doing Guided Practice for our Measures unit. This is where you practise comparing sizes. You will say which thing is taller or shorter, longer or shorter, wider or thinner. We do this so the size words become easy for you, like your own name. By the end you will be able to look at two things and say a full sentence, like "the date palm is taller than the bush." You need your eyes, your thinking, and maybe a pencil and paper. Here is what I expect from you: try each question yourself first, then answer. Take your time — mathematicians think slowly on purpose. Here are all the steps. Step 1. Look at the first question on the page. Read it slowly, twice. Picture the two things standing side by side on the same table or floor. Ask yourself: is this question about tall and short, long and short, or wide and thin? You can work it out in your head, or draw the two things on paper. I expect you to think before you type — even a quiet ten seconds is good thinking. Step 2. Type your answer in the box, then press Check my answer. Try to write a whole sentence, like "the giraffe is taller than the goat," not just one word. A whole sentence shows me you know both size words. If you are stuck, press Give me a hint — you can have up to three hints, and each one helps a little more. If you are still stuck, press Show next step, and it will show you one line of the working, so you can finish the rest yourself. Step 3. Do this for every question. There are 12 questions in all. Keep going with one question until it is right, then move to the next one. If an answer is not right, that is fine — mistakes are how we learn. Read the feedback, think again, and try once more. The page is done when all 12 questions are right. Step 4. Now look under the page. There is a deck of slides with the same questions, one question on each slide. Press Start on the first slide to begin. Answer that slide the same way as before: type your answer, press Check my answer, and use Give me a hint or Show next step if you need help. Step 5. When a slide is right, press the arrow on the right to go to the next slide. Look at the little dots under the slide — they show you where you are in the deck. Keep going, one slide at a time, and say your answer out loud too if you like. On the last slide, press the finish button. How will you know the page is finished? All 12 questions on the page are correct, and you have pressed the finish button on the last slide. That is the whole page done! Ready? Tell me what question one says, and let's look at that together.

activities.label: Activities
activities.text:
Hello! Today I am your teacher, and this page is our doing page. 😊

On this page we do a hands-on activity. That means we get real things — paper, a pencil, and objects from home — and we compare their size. We do it because measuring words like taller, longer and wider stick best when your hands are busy. By the end, you will be able to compare two things and say a full sentence like "the spoon is longer than the crayon."

What I expect from you: try it for real, not just in your head. Say your answer in a full sentence. And write something in the box, even if it is short. Here are all the steps. 1. Look at the activity card at the top of the page. It says what to use: paper, a pencil, and things from your home. Press Listen to hear it read out loud. Listen all the way to the end, then go and fetch the things it names. A grown-up can help you gather them. 2. Now do the activity. Pick one idea from our unit — tall and short, long and short, wide and thin, or putting things in order. Draw it or build it with your objects. Remember to line them up fairly at one end before you compare. 3. Show your work to someone at home and tell them about it. Say a full sentence, like "the pencil is longer than the crayon." Then make up one question of your own, such as "which is taller, my cup or my spoon?" and answer it yourself. 4. Write in the box on the page. Write your answer, or what you noticed. One good sentence is plenty for me, and drawing words like taller, longer or wider makes it even better. 5. Press Mark complete under the activity when you have really done it. Only press it after you have done the hands-on part and written in the box. That button tells the page you finished. 6. Then press Finish activities at the bottom of the page, once every activity is marked complete. 7. Now look under the page. There is a deck of slides with the same hands-on activity, one activity on each slide. Press Start on the first slide to begin. 8. On each slide, use the same buttons: Listen, then do the activity, write in the box, then Mark complete. Do the doing part for real each time — no skipping. 9. Press the arrow on the right side to go to the next slide. The little dots under the slide show you where you are, so you can see how many are left. 10. On the last slide, press Finish activities. That is the end of the deck. You will know the page is finished when every activity says complete, and you have pressed Finish activities at the bottom. Nice and clear! Now go and start with step 1 — press Listen. Tell me when you have your things ready, and I will help you pick a good idea to try. Take your time — there's no rush.

examples.label: Worked Examples
examples.text: Hello! Today we are working on the Worked Examples page for Measures. A worked example is a question with the answer already worked out for you. It shows all the thinking, step by step. We do this so you can see HOW a good answer is built, not just what it is. By the end, you will be better at saying which thing is taller, longer, or wider — and at saying WHY. You will need your eyes, your voice, and maybe a grown-up nearby. You may want a pencil and paper too. Here is what I expect from you: always THINK your own answer first, before you look at the solution. Say it out loud in a full sentence, like "the date palm is taller than the bush." That full sentence is the real learning. There are 4 steps. Here they are. Step 1. Look at the first worked example. Read the question, or ask your grown-up to read it with you. Then close your eyes for a moment and picture the two things standing side by side. Say your answer out loud in a full sentence with the word "than" in it. I expect a full sentence, not just one word. Step 2. Now press the button that says Show worked solution. Read it line by line, slowly. Compare it with what you said. Ask yourself: did I say the same thing? Did I say WHY? It is completely fine if you were not right — that is how we learn. Mathematicians think slowly on purpose. Step 3. Do this same thing for every worked example. There are 12 of them. Look at the counter at the top of the page — it tells you how many you have opened. Keep going until the counter shows all 12. Remember: think your own answer first, THEN press Show worked solution. That is what makes this work. Step 4. Now go down to the slides at the bottom of the page. There is one example on each slide. Press Start on the first slide. Use the same buttons on each slide as you did above — think first, then show the solution. Press the arrow on the right to move to the next slide. The little dots under the slide show you where you are. On the last slide, press the finish button. You will know the page is finished when two things are true: the counter at the top shows all 12 examples opened, and you have pressed the finish button on the last slide. Then the page is complete! Ready? Start with worked example one, and tell me your full sentence. I will be right here. 😊

fluency.label: Math Fluency
fluency.text:
Hello! Today I am your teacher for the Math Fluency page. This is a sprint. That means 12 quick questions about size words — taller, shorter, longer, wider, thinner. We do it so these words come to you fast, without hard thinking. You need your eyes, your brain, and maybe a grown-up nearby. Ready? Here is the whole plan. 1. Look at the top of the page. You will see your time counting. That is just to help you go quickly — it is not a race against anyone else. Take a breath and get comfy. 2. Read question one slowly, then answer it. Type your answer in the box. Then press Check & continue. I expect one clear word or short sentence, like "taller" or "The rope is longer."

3. Picture it in your head before you type. For height, ask: which one reaches higher? For length, ask: which one reaches further when both start at the same line? For width, sweep your finger across and ask: which needs the longer sweep? 4. Keep going the same way for every question. Read, think, type, press Check & continue. One question at a time. That is 12 questions in all. 5. If a question feels hard, do not stop for long. Choose your best answer and press Check & continue. You can always practise that one with me after. 6. When the sprint ends, look at your score. You need most of them right to finish this page. Getting a few wrong is normal — mistakes are how we learn. 7. If you did not get enough right, press Run the sprint again. New try, same words. Go a little slower this time and think about "which reaches further?" before you type. 8. If you got enough right, the page is done! You will see it marked as finished on your screen. You will know the page is finished when a sprint has enough right answers and the page shows it is complete. Then come and tell me your score, and I will tell you what you were strongest at. Ready? Start with question one, then tell me how it went. 😊

games.label: Games
games.text: Hello! Today we are playing the games for Unit 4, Measures. These games ask you about tall and short, long and short, wide and thin, putting things in order, and measuring with blocks. Playing them helps the words stick in your head. By the end, you will be able to look at two things and say which one is taller, longer or wider. You need only your eyes, your thinking, and your finger to tap. Here are your steps. 1. Pick one game and press Start game. Read the question slowly, all the way to the end. Then tap the answer you think is right. You get a star for every round you get right. There are four rounds in each game. I expect you to think first, then tap — not tap fast and hope. Take your time — there's no rush. 2. When a game ends, press Play again to try more rounds and earn more stars. Each game needs all its stars before it is mastered. Mastered means you got it right again and again, so we know you really know it. If you get one wrong, that is fine. Mistakes are how we learn. Read the little explanation, then press Play again and try that idea once more. 3. Keep going until every game on the page is mastered. Do them one at a time, from the top. Do not skip a game because it looks hard. If a game is tricky, tell me which one, and I will help you before you press Play again. I expect you to finish all of them, even the slow ones. Here is how you will know you are done: every game will show all its stars, and the page will finish by itself. You do not press anything special at the end. One helper for you while you play. Tall and short is up and down. Long and short is end to end, lying down. Wide and thin is across, side to side. Now go and press Start game on the first game. Tell me when your first game is done, and how many stars you got!

problems.label: Solve Real Problems
problems.text: Hello! Today I am your teacher for the "Solve Real Problems" page. On this page we use our measuring words in real life — taller, shorter, longer, wider and thinner. We do it because measuring is not just for school; we compare sizes at home, at the market and on the road every day. By the end, you will be able to look at two things and say which one is longer or wider, and say why. You will need your eyes, your thinking, and a grown-up nearby if you want to try it with real objects. Here is what I expect from you: think first, then answer in a full sentence, like "the snake is longer than the worm." Take your time — mathematicians think slowly on purpose. Step 1. There are 6 real problems on this page. Read the first one slowly, twice. Ask yourself: is this asking about tall and short, long and short, or wide and thin? Then picture the two things side by side, lined up fairly at one end. I expect you to know what the question is asking before you answer. Step 2. Now work it out in your head, or point with your finger. Type your working and your answer in the box. Your working can be short, like "I lined them up at one end. The pencil reached further." Then press Check answer. If your brain feels stuck, press Hint first and read it — a hint is not cheating, it is help. Step 3. When the page says your answer is right, that problem is done. Well done — move to the next problem and do the same thing: read, think, type, press Check answer. Keep going until all 6 problems say you are right. If one is not right, read the hint and try again. Mistakes are how we learn. Step 4. Under the page there is a deck of slides. It has the same problems, one problem on each slide. On the first slide, press Start. Answer it just like before, using the same buttons. Then press the arrow on the right to go to the next slide. The little dots under the slide show you where you are, so you can see how many are left. Step 5. Keep going slide by slide with the arrow on the right. On the last slide, press the finish button. That tells the page you have finished the whole deck. Step 6. You will know the page is finished when all 6 problems show a right answer, and you have pressed the finish button on the last slide. Then the page is complete! Ready to begin? Tell me what the first problem says, and we will look at it together.

explain.label: Explain Your Thinking
explain.text:
Hello! Let's get ready together. 🙂

This page is called Explain Your Thinking. On the other pages you picked an answer. Here you say HOW you know. You write it in words, like telling a friend. We do this because a good mathematician can say why. When you finish, you will be able to say things like "the snake is longer than the worm, and I know because we lined them up at the same end."

What I expect from you: a full sentence, not one word. Use the measuring words — taller, shorter, longer, wider, thinner. Say which one wins, and say how you know. Here is the shape of a good answer, using a different example: "The big cup is taller than the small cup. I stood them both on the same table and looked at the tops. The big cup's top reaches higher, so it is taller." That is what yours should look like. There are four things to do on this page. Here they all are. 1. Read the first prompt. Under the prompt there are key ideas — these are the words I want to see in your writing. Read the prompt twice, slowly. Then think in your head: which one is bigger, and how do I know? Take your time — there's no rush. 2. Write your explanation in the box. Say three things: what you can see, what rule you used (like "stand them on the same ground" or "line them up at one end"), and what your answer is. Then press Check mathematical ideas. If the page asks for more, that is fine — add one more sentence and press it again. A grown-up can help you type if you need. 3. Press Show model explanation. This shows a good answer so you can compare. Look for the words you used and the words you missed. Do not copy it — just notice what it does well. If it says something you forgot, remember that for the next one. 4. Do steps 1, 2 and 3 again for all six prompts. Same three buttons every time: read, write, Check mathematical ideas, then Show model explanation. Six prompts in all, so you get lots of practice. 5. Now the slides at the bottom of the page. Under the page there is a deck of slides with the same prompts, one on each slide. Press Start on the first slide. Use the same buttons on each slide as you did above. Then press the arrow on the right to go to the next slide. The little dots under the slide show you where you are — they help you see how many are left. On the last slide, press the finish button. You will know the page is finished when every one of the six explanations has been checked and uses the key ideas, and you have pressed the finish button on the last slide. Ready? Read prompt one and tell me what you think, then write it in the box. I'm right here. 🌟

challenge.label: Unit Challenge
challenge.text:
Hello! This page is your Unit Challenge. It is like a friendly test at the end of Unit 4, Measures. You will answer 12 questions about tall and short, long and short, wide and thin, putting things in order, and measuring with blocks and paper clips. It shows you how much you have learned. You just need your eyes, your thinking, and a comfy seat. Take your time — there's no rush. Here is what I expect from you. Read every question twice before you choose. Pick the answer you truly think is right, not a quick guess. And if you get stuck, ask me — I will give you a hint, but I really can't give quiz answers. 1. Get ready. Sit somewhere quiet and look at the first question on the screen. Read it slowly, all the way to the end. Read the question twice before you answer. 2. Think about the picture in your head. Ask yourself: is this question about tall and short, about long and short, or about wide and thin? Tall and short means bottom to top. Long and short means end to end, lying down. Wide and thin means side to side, across. 3. Choose your answer. Click the one answer you think is right. I expect you to have a reason in your head, like "the giraffe's head reaches higher." A reason means you really know it. 4. Press Next question. Do this after every single answer. Then read the new question twice, just like before. Keep going until all 12 questions are done. That is 12 reads, 12 thinks, 12 clicks. 5. Look at your score at the end. The screen will show how many you got right. You pass when you get more than half of them right. Well done for finishing — that is hard work! 6. If your score is not high enough, press Try again. This is not a bad thing at all. Mistakes are how we learn. Come and tell me which question was tricky, and we will practise that one together before you try again. 7. When your score is good enough, press Continue. That saves your work and takes you on. Only you can press it — I can't do that part for you. You will know the page is finished when you have answered all 12 questions, seen a score you are happy with, and pressed Continue. 🌟

Ready? Tell me when you have read question one, and I will be right here.

overview.label: Unit Overview
overview.text:
Hello! Let's get started together. 🙂

This page is called the Unit Overview. It is like looking at a map before a trip. It shows what Unit 5 is about: adding and taking away numbers up to 10. By the end of this page, you will know what you are going to learn. You need your eyes, your ears, and your voice. A grown-up can sit with you if you like. Here is what I expect from you today: look carefully, listen carefully, and say your ideas out loud. There are no wrong answers on this page. It is just a first look. There are 3 steps. Here they are. Step 1. Read the Unit Overview. Look at the words on the page. Where you see a speaker picture, press Listen. Then the words are read to you. Listen all the way to the end. You can press Listen again if you want to hear it twice. I expect you to read and listen, not rush. Take your time — there's no rush. Step 2. Say in your own words what you think you will learn. Now close your mouth for a moment and think. Then say it out loud to me or to your grown-up. You can start like this: "I think I will learn how to..." A good answer uses words like add, take away, or altogether. One or two sentences is plenty. I expect you to try, even if you are not sure. Trying is the whole point. Step 3. Press Continue to go to The Lesson. When you have read, listened, and said your idea out loud, find the Continue button and press it. That takes you to the next part, called The Lesson. Only press it when steps 1 and 2 are done. You will know this page is finished when you have listened to the overview, said out loud what you think you will learn, and pressed Continue. Now go and do Step 1. Tell me when you have listened, and we will keep going together. 🌟

lesson.label: The Lesson
lesson.text: Hello! Today I am your teacher for The Lesson page in Unit 5, Working with Numbers to 10. On this page you will meet 8 big ideas: putting groups together, adding 1 more, using a ten-frame, number bonds, taking away, testing Sumi's rule, doubles, and adding three numbers. We do this so adding and taking away stop feeling hard and start feeling easy. By the end, you will be able to say what adding and taking away mean, and show them with real things. Get ready: a pencil, some paper, and about 10 small objects you can count. Stones, buttons, bottle caps or dried beans all work well. Here are your steps. Step 1. Read the first concept slowly, then press Listen and hear it read to you. Read it with your eyes AND your ears — that helps it stick. I expect you to go slowly, one concept at a time, not rush to the bottom. Take your time — there's no rush. Step 2. Say the example out loud, in your own voice. For example: "3 add 2 equals 5." Saying it out loud turns the picture into maths words. I expect to hear a full sentence, not just a number. Step 3. Now try that same example with your own objects. Put out 3 stones, then 2 more stones, push them together, and count them all. Then change the numbers and try it again, like 4 and 3. I expect you to touch each object once as you count. Step 4. Do steps 1, 2 and 3 for every one of the 8 concepts, in order. Do not skip the tricky ones — the ten-frame one and the doubles one are the most useful of all. If one feels hard, come and tell me and we will do it together. Step 5. When you have read all 8, press the button at the bottom that says I studied the concepts. Only press it when you really have read them all. That button tells your page you have finished the reading part. Step 6. Now look under the page. There is a deck of slides with the same 8 concepts, one idea on each slide. Press Start on the first slide. This is your practice, so the ideas move from the page into your head. Step 7. On each slide, use the same buttons you used before, then press the arrow on the right to go to the next slide. Look at the little dots under the slide — they show you where you are in the deck. I expect you to finish one slide properly before you press the arrow. Step 8. Keep going, slide by slide, until you reach the last one. On the last slide, press the finish button. Then you are done! You will know the page is finished when the I studied the concepts button has been pressed and you have pressed the finish button on the last slide. Ready? Start with concept one, press Listen, and tell me when you have done it. 🙂

words.label: Math Words & Symbols
words.text: Hello! Today I am your teacher, and this page is our word page. This page has the maths words for Unit 5, like add, equals, take away and number bond. We learn them so that when you hear "how many altogether?" you know just what to do. By the end, you will be able to say each word, say what it means, and use it in your own sentence. You need your voice, your eyes, and your fingers for typing. There are four things to do. Here they all are. 1. Look at the first word and read it. Next to it you will see what the word means in simple words. Press Listen, and the word will be said out loud to you. Listen carefully to how it sounds. I expect you to look at the word while you listen, not just hear it. 2. Now say the word out loud yourself. Then say the meaning in your OWN words, not the same words on the screen. For example, for add you might say, "add means put groups together." Then type a sentence using the word in the box and press Check sentence. A good sentence shows you know the meaning, like "I add 3 dates and 2 dates." Read what the checker tells you. If it says to try again, that is fine — change one small thing and check again. Do this for every word on the page: add, altogether, equals, number sentence, take away, left, part and whole, number bond, and ten-frame. 3. When you have done all the words, press I know these words and symbols at the bottom. Only press it when every word has a sentence. This button tells the page you have finished the word list. 4. Now look under the page. There is a deck of slides with the same words, one word on each slide. Press Start on the first slide. On each slide, do the same as before: listen, say the word, say the meaning, and type your sentence. Then press the arrow on the right to go to the next slide. The little dots under the slide show you where you are. On the last slide, press the finish button. You will know the page is done when every word has a green tick or a checked sentence, you have pressed I know these words and symbols, and you have pressed the finish button on the last slide. Take your time — there's no rush. Tell me when you have pressed Listen on the first word, and we will do that word together. 🙂

explore.label: Explore the Concept
explore.text: Hello! I am your teacher today, and this page is called Explore the Concept. On this page you will discover big maths ideas by yourself. There are 6 little discoveries. They are about adding groups together, adding 1 more, the ten-frame, number bonds, and taking away. By the end, you will be able to add and take away numbers up to 10 and say how you did it. Before we start, get a small pile of counting things — stones, buttons, dried beans or bottle caps. About 10 is perfect. Good mathematicians use their hands. What I expect from you is this: try first, then type your own idea in your own words. Take your time — there's no rush. Here are all the steps. Step 1. Look at the top of the page. You will see numbered tabs: 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6. Press tab 1 with your finger or mouse. That opens the first discovery. Step 2. Read the little story on the tab, and look at the picture or model next to it. Read it slowly, twice. I expect you to be able to tell me what is happening in the picture, like "there are 3 dates here and 2 dates here". Step 3. Now find the discovery question under the story. Read the question out loud if you can. Ask yourself: is this putting groups together, or taking some away? That helps you know what to do. Step 4. Try it with your counters before you type. Put out the first group, then the second group. Push them together, or take some away, and count. Counting with real things is not cheating — it is exactly what I want you to do. Step 5. Type your idea in the box. Write the number you found, and if you can, a few words too, like "5 dates altogether". Then press Check my idea. I expect a real try from you, not a guess. Step 6. Read what the page says back to you. If it says Exactly!, well done — the tab gets a tick. If it says Look again, do not worry. Mistakes are how we learn. Step 7. If it said Look again, press Hint. Read the hint carefully, count again with your counters, then type your new idea and press Check my idea one more time. Step 8. Now press tab 2 and do the very same thing: read, look, think, count, type, press Check my idea. Then do tabs 3, 4, 5 and 6 the same way. One at a time, please — finish one before you open the next. Step 9. Look at your tabs. When all 6 tabs have a tick, the top part of the page is finished. That means every discovery question was answered right. Brilliant work! Step 10. Now scroll down under the page. There is a deck of slides there. It has the same discoveries, one on each slide. Press Start on the first slide. Step 11. On each slide, use the same buttons you already know: read the slide, type your idea, press Check my idea, and press Hint if you need help. You have done this before, so you know what to do. Step 12. When a slide is done, press the arrow on the right side to go to the next slide. Look at the little dots under the slide — they show you which slide you are on and how many are left. Step 13. Keep going until the last slide. On that one, press the finish button. Then the slides are done too. How will you know the page is finished? Two things: all 6 tabs have a tick, and you have pressed the finish button on the last slide. Remember, I do not tick anything for you — the page only knows you did the work when you press the buttons yourself. Ready? Press tab 1 and tell me what you see. I am right here with you.

visuals.label: Visual Models
visuals.text:
Hello! Today we are on the Visual Models page. Visual models are pictures that show our maths ideas — adding, taking away, and number bonds. Looking at a picture makes the maths easy to see, instead of just numbers. Here is what I expect from you: look carefully, touch and move each model, and say the maths out loud in your own words. You will need your eyes, your voice, and maybe 10 small things like stones, buttons or bottle caps to copy the models with your hands. There are 8 steps. Take your time — there's no rush. Step 1. Find the first model, Addition as Combining. Look at the two groups of things. If the model moves, drag it with your finger or mouse to turn it, and press its buttons to change it. Then say out loud how many are in each group, and how many there are altogether. I expect a full sentence, like "3 add 2 equals 5."

Step 2. Under that model there is a caption — the words that explain the picture. Read the caption, then press Listen to hear it read to you. Listen right to the end. I expect you to tell yourself one thing you learned from the caption. Do this reading-and-Listen part for every model you look at. Step 3. Go to the second model, Adding 1 More. Press its buttons to add just 1 more. Watch what number you land on each time. Read the caption and press Listen. I expect you to spot the pattern: adding 1 more always gives the next counting number. Step 4. Now the third model, The Ten-Frame for Adding. A ten-frame is a box with 10 spaces, 5 on top and 5 below. Press the buttons to put counters in, filling the top row first, left to right. Read the caption and press Listen. I expect you to count the filled spaces and the empty spaces out loud. Step 5. Next is the fourth model, Part-Whole and Number Bonds. Look at the big circle (the whole) and the two small circles (the parts). Press the buttons to split the whole different ways, and drag the model if it turns. Read the caption and press Listen. I expect you to say one bond, like "2 and 3 make 5."

Step 6. Now the fifth model, Subtraction as Take Away. Press the buttons to take some away, and watch the group get smaller. Read the caption and press Listen. I expect a take-away sentence out loud, like "7 take away 2 equals 5."

Step 7. Last is the sixth model, Is the +1 Rule Always True? This one tests Sumi's idea. Press the buttons to add 1 more from different starting numbers, like 3, then 6, then 9. Read the caption and press Listen. I expect you to decide for yourself: is Sumi correct? Say yes or no, and why. Step 8. When you have looked at all 6 models, heard all 6 captions, and tried the buttons, press the button at the bottom that says I explored the models. Only press it after you have really looked at every one — that is your honest work. You will know the page is finished when all 6 models have been explored and you have pressed I explored the models at the bottom. I don't mark it done — you do, by pressing that button. Ready? Start with Step 1 and tell me what you see in the first model. 😊

method.label: Learn the Method
method.text: Hello! Today I am your teacher, and this page is called Learn the Method. A method is a way to work something out, step by step. On this page there are 6 methods for adding and taking away. Each one shows you what to do first, then next, then next. By the end, you will know how to put two groups together, how to write a number sentence with + and =, how to add 1 more, how to use a ten-frame, and how to take away. You will need a pencil and some small things you can count. Stones, buttons, bottle caps or dried beans all work well. Your voice is important too, because I want you to say each step out loud. What I expect from you: read slowly, say every step out loud, and do the step with your counting things before you press the button. No rushing. Mathematicians think slowly on purpose. Here are all the steps. Step 1. Look at the first method on the page. Read its first step out loud. Then take your counting things and actually do it with your hands. If the step says count a group, really count it, touching each thing once. Step 2. Now press the button that says Show me the next step. A new step will appear. Read this one out loud too, and do it with your objects. I expect you to do each step, not just read it. Step 3. Keep pressing Show me the next step until the page says Method complete. When you see Method complete, say the whole thing out loud in one go, like this: "3 add 2 equals 5." That tells me you understood the method, not just the words. Step 4. Now move to the next method and do the same thing. Read step one, press Show me the next step, keep going until it says Method complete. Do this for all 6 methods, one after the other. Take your time — there's no rush. Step 5. Some methods are about taking away, not adding. For those, really move the objects away with your hand. Then count only the ones that are left. That is what take away means. Step 6. Now look under the page. There is a deck of slides. Each slide has one of the same methods on it. Find the first slide and press Start. Step 7. On the slide, use the same buttons as before. Read each step out loud, do it with your objects, and press Show me the next step until it says Method complete. Step 8. Now press the arrow on the right side of the slide. That takes you to the next slide. Look at the little dots under the slide — they show you where you are and how many slides are left. Step 9. Do every slide the same way: press Start, step through to the end, then press the arrow on the right. Keep going until you reach the last slide. Step 10. On the last slide, press the finish button. That is you telling the page you are done. How will you know the page is finished? Every method on the page has said Method complete, you have gone through all the slides, and you have pressed the finish button on the last one. When you are done, come back and tell me one thing: which method was the easiest for you? I would love to know. 🌟

examples.label: Worked Examples
examples.text: Hello! Today we are working on the Worked Examples page. A worked example is a maths question with all the working shown, step by step. We do this so you can see HOW a good answer is built, not just the answer. By the end, you will know how to add and take away numbers to 10, and how to write it down with the + , − and = signs. You will need a pencil, some paper, and 10 small things to count — stones, buttons or dry beans are perfect. Here are your steps. There are 6. Step 1: Look at the first worked example on the page. Read the question slowly. Read it twice — once to hear it, once to understand it. I expect you to say the question out loud to yourself or your grown-up. Step 2: Try it yourself first, before you look at any answer. Use your counters or draw dots on your paper. Write your answer as a number sentence, like 3 + 2 = 5. Even a guess is good — trying first is what makes your brain grow. I expect one written answer from you for that example. Step 3: Now press Show worked solution. Read the solution line by line, and put your finger on each line as you read. Compare it with your own working. Ask yourself: did I count the same way? Did I write the + and = signs? If your answer was different, that is fine — mistakes are how we learn. Just find the line where yours went another way. Step 4: Do the same for all 12 worked examples: read, try it yourself, then press Show worked solution and compare. At the top of the page there is a counter. It shows how many you have opened. Watch that number grow — it is like ticking off your work. I expect you to open every single one, not just the easy ones. Step 5: Now look under the page. There is a deck of slides with the same examples, one on each slide. On the first slide, press Start. Then use the same buttons on each slide: read, try, show the working, compare. To go on, press the arrow on the right. The little dots under the slide tell you where you are. Step 6: Keep going slide by slide until you reach the last slide. On the last slide, press the finish button. That is you telling the page you are done. I do not press it for you — the work is yours, so the button is yours too. How you will know you are finished: the counter at the top shows all 12 opened, and you have pressed the finish button on the last slide. Take your time — there's no rush. Tell me when you have read the first question, and I will help you try it. 😊

activities.label: Activities
activities.text: Hello! Today I am your teacher, and this is our Activities page. On this page you get to do maths with your hands, not just read about it. You will use real things at home to show adding and taking away. Doing it with your hands helps your brain remember it. You will need paper, a pencil, and some small things you can count — stones, buttons, bottle caps or dates. Here is what I expect from you: try it for real, count carefully, and write your own words in the box. Neat is nice, but honest thinking is better. Here are the steps. There are 4. Step 1. Read the activity, then press Listen. There is 1 hands-on activity on this page. It tells you what to use and what to do. Press Listen and hear it read to you. Then go and get the things it names — paper, a pencil, and small objects to count. Do not start until the things are in front of you. I expect you to come back with your objects ready. Step 2. Do the activity, then write in the box. The activity asks you to pick one idea from this unit — adding, adding 1 more, the ten-frame, number bonds, or take away. Build it or draw it with your objects. Then tell a grown-up in your family what your model shows. Last, write one question of your own, like "4 + 3 = ?", and solve it. Type what you did or what you noticed in the box. One or two sentences is plenty, and a number sentence like 4 + 3 = 7 is even better. Step 3. Press Mark complete, then Finish activities. When you have really done the activity and written in the box, press Mark complete under it. Then, when every activity is marked, press Finish activities at the bottom of the page. Only press it after you have truly done the work — that button is your promise that you did it. Step 4. Do the slides at the bottom. Under the page there is a deck of slides with the same hands-on activity, one on each slide. Press Start on the first slide. Use the same buttons on each slide as you did above. Press the arrow on the right to go to the next slide. The little dots under the slide show you where you are. On the last slide, press Finish activities. How will you know the page is finished? Every activity shows Mark complete pressed, your box has your writing in it, and you have pressed Finish activities at the bottom and on the last slide. Then you are done! Now go and get your counting things. Tell me when you have them, and we will begin Step 1 together. 🙂

guided.label: Guided Practice
guided.text: Hello! Today we are doing Guided Practice for Unit 5, Working with Numbers to 10. This page gives you 12 little questions about adding and taking away. We practise so that adding and taking away start to feel easy and quick. By the end, you will be able to put two groups together, take some away, and write it with the + sign, the − sign and the = sign. Get ready with a pencil, some paper, and 10 small things you can count — stones, buttons, bottle caps or dried beans. Take your time — there's no rush. Mathematicians think slowly on purpose. Here are your steps. 1. Read the first question. Read it twice, slowly. Ask yourself: am I putting groups together, or am I taking some away? Then work it out on paper, with your counters, or in your head. I expect you to try it yourself first, before you write anything in the box. 2. Now type your answer in the box and press Check my answer. Type just the number, like 7, unless the question asks for a number sentence — then write it all, like 4 + 3 = 7. If you are stuck, press Give me a hint. You can have up to three hints. If you are still stuck, press Show next step and it shows you one line of the working — then you finish the rest yourself. I expect you to try a hint before you ask for the next step. 3. If your answer is not right, that is fine. Mistakes are how we learn. Look again, count once more touching each object one time, and try again. Keep going question by question until every one of the 12 is right. That is when the top part of the page is finished. 4. Now look under the page. There is a deck of slides with the same questions, one on each slide. Press Start on the first slide. Answer it the same way: type your answer, press Check my answer, and use Give me a hint or Show next step if you need help. I expect you to try each slide on your own first. 5. When a slide is done, press the arrow on the right to go to the next slide. The little dots under the slide show you how far along you are. Do every slide, one at a time, in order. 6. On the last slide, answer it, then press the finish button. That tells the page you are done. You will know the whole page is finished when all 12 questions show as right, and you have pressed the finish button on the last slide. Ready? Read question one and tell me what you get. I'm right here. 🙂

games.label: Games
games.text: Welcome to our Games page! This is where we play little games about adding and taking away. Each game asks you short questions from Unit 5. Playing helps the answers become quick and easy in your head. All you need is your eyes, your fingers for counting, and maybe some stones or buttons nearby. There are 3 steps. Here they all are. Step 1: Pick any game on the page and press Start game. Read the question slowly, twice. Work the answer out yourself first — count on your fingers or with your stones if you like. Then press the choice you think is right. You get a star for every round you get right. I expect you to think before you tap, not tap fast. Take your time — there's no rush. Step 2: When the game ends, press Play again to earn more stars. If you got one wrong, look at the little explanation and say it out loud in your own words. A game is mastered when it has all its stars. So keep pressing Play again on that game until its stars are full. I expect you to stay with one game until it is mastered, then move on. Step 3: Now do the same for every game on the page. Choose the next game, press Start game, then Play again until all its stars are full. Master every game, one by one. If a game feels hard, that's okay — tell me which one and we will practise that idea together first. How will you know you are finished? When every game has all its stars, the page finishes by itself. You do not need to press anything extra. Then come and tell me, and we will talk about which game was your favourite. Ready? Press Start game on your first game, then tell me how it went. 🌟

problems.label: Solve Real Problems
problems.text: Hello! Today I am your teacher for the "Solve Real Problems" page. This page has 6 little story problems from real life. There are dates, beads, goats, anjero, stones and buttons. Your job is to read each story, work out the answer, and write it down. We do this because adding and taking away are not just numbers on a page — we use them at home, at the market and on the way to school. By the end you will be able to turn a story into a number sentence, like 4 + 3 = 7. Get a pencil, some paper, and 10 small things you can count — stones, buttons or bottle caps. Take your time. Mathematicians think slowly on purpose. Here are all the steps. 1. Read the first problem out loud, slowly. Then ask yourself: is this story putting groups together, or taking some away? Words like "gives her more" or "altogether" mean add. Words like "walk away" or "eaten" mean take away. I expect you to decide this before you count anything. 2. Now work it out with your counters. Make the first group, then make the second group. If it is adding, push them together and count them all. If it is taking away, move some to the side and count what is left. Say the answer out loud, like "seven dates altogether". 3. Type your working and your answer in the box, then press Check answer. Please do not type only a number. Write how you did it, like this: "4 dates and 3 dates pushed together, 4 + 3 = 7". Showing your working is what good mathematicians do. 4. If you feel stuck, press Hint. The hint does not give the answer — it gives you a nudge. Read it, try again with your counters, then press Check answer. Getting stuck is normal, and trying again is the best part. 5. When the page says your answer is right, that problem is done. Well done! Move on to the next problem and do steps 1 to 4 again. Do all 6 problems this way, one at a time, no rushing. 6. Now look under the page. There is a deck of slides with the same problems, one problem on each slide. Press Start on the first slide. 7. On each slide, use the same buttons as before: type your working, press Check answer, and press Hint if you need help. I expect the same careful working here as on the page above. 8. To move to the next slide, press the arrow on the right side. Look at the little dots under the slide — they show you which slide you are on and how many are left. 9. On the last slide, press the finish button. That tells the page you have finished the whole deck. You will know the page is finished when all 6 problems say your answer is right, and you have pressed the finish button on the last slide. Ready? Read problem one to me and tell me: is it adding, or taking away? 😊

explain.label: Explain Your Thinking
explain.text: Hello! I am your teacher today, and this page is called Explain Your Thinking. On this page you do not just say the answer. You say HOW you know. That is what mathematicians do — they tell their thinking out loud. Doing this helps the maths stick in your head. You will need your voice, your fingers or some small counters like stones, dates or bottle caps, and a grown-up nearby if you want help writing. Here is what I expect from you: use our unit words — add, altogether, equals, take away, part, whole, number bond. Say what you did, and say why it makes sense. Even one or two good sentences is great work. Here are all the steps. Step 1. Look at the first prompt on the page. There are 6 prompts in all. Read the prompt slowly, and read the key ideas listed under it. Those key ideas are your helper words — I expect you to use them in your answer. If reading is hard, ask your grown-up to read it with you. Step 2. Now think with your hands before you write. Get your counters out and act the question out. For example, if it says 5 goats and 2 goats, put 5 stones down, then 2 more, push them together, and count them all. What you do with your hands becomes the words you write. Step 3. Write your explanation in the box. Say three things: what you did, what rule you used, and why the answer makes sense. Like this: "I pushed the two groups together. Add means put groups together. I counted them all and got 7. So 5 add 2 equals 7." That is a strong answer. Step 4. Press Check mathematical ideas. This checks if you used the key ideas. If it asks for more, do not worry — that is normal. Add one more sentence, maybe the "why" part, and press Check mathematical ideas again. Step 5. Press Show model explanation. This shows a good answer so you can compare. Read it and ask yourself: what did they say that I did not say? You do not copy it. It is just a friend showing you their work. Step 6. Now do the same for prompts 2, 3, 4, 5 and 6. Same three moves every time: write in the box, press Check mathematical ideas, then press Show model explanation. Take your time — there is no rush. Step 7. Now look under the page. There is a deck of slides with the same prompts, one prompt on each slide. Press Start on the first slide. Step 8.
