On each slide, use the same buttons you already know: write your explanation, press Check mathematical ideas, then press Show model explanation. You have done this six times already, so this part will feel easy. Step 9. To go to the next slide, press the arrow on the right side. Look at the little dots under the slide — they show you which slide you are on and how many are left. Step 10. On the last slide, press the finish button. That tells the page you are done. You will know the page is finished when every one of the 6 explanations uses the key ideas, and you have pressed the finish button on the last slide. Ready? Start with step 1, and tell me your first prompt. I will help you turn your thinking into words. 🙂

fluency.label: Math Fluency
fluency.text:
Hello! Today I am your teacher for the Math Fluency page. Fluency means being quick and sure with numbers you already know. We are doing this so adding and taking away to 10 start to feel easy and fast, like saying your own name. You will need a quiet spot, your fingers, and maybe 10 small things like stones or bottle caps. Let's go step by step. 1. Get ready. Sit somewhere comfy. Put your counting things next to you. Take one big breath. There are 12 quick questions, and a timer at the top shows your time. I expect you to try your best, not to rush and guess. 2. Start the sprint. Look at question one on the screen. Read it slowly, even though it is a sprint. Ask yourself: is this putting groups together, or taking some away? Knowing that first is the most important part. 3. Answer question one. Type your answer in the box. Then press Check & continue. I expect a number, not a guess. If you are not sure, count on with your fingers, like "six... seven, eight."

4. Keep going, one question at a time. After each answer, press Check & continue to go to the next one. Do not worry about the timer. Mathematicians think slowly on purpose, and the speed comes later with practice. 5. Use your helpers when you need them. For "add 1 more", just say the next counting number. For a ten-frame question, picture the top row full, then the bottom row. For "take away", picture moving stones away and counting what is left. These little pictures make you faster. 6. Finish all 12 questions. When the last one is done, the page will show you how you did. I expect you to look at any you got wrong and tell me what happened, so we can fix it together. 7. If you need another go. You need most of them right to pass. If you got fewer than that, press Run the sprint again and do a fresh sprint. That is not failing! That is practice, and practice is how fast fingers and fast brains are made. 8. How you know the page is finished. The page is done when one sprint has enough right answers. When that happens, you will see it on the screen and you can move on. Ready? Start question one now, and tell me how it goes. I am right here. 🙂

challenge.label: Unit Challenge
challenge.text: Welcome to your Unit Challenge! This is the last part of Unit 5. It has 12 questions about adding, taking away, number bonds, and the ten-frame. We do it to show what your brain has learned. I cannot tell you any answers here, but I can help you think well. Get a pencil, some paper, and 10 small things to count like stones, buttons or bottle caps. Here is the whole page, step by step. 1. Get ready. Put your counting things next to you. Sit somewhere calm. Take a breath. I expect you to try every question, even the tricky ones. Take your time — there's no rush. 2. Read question one twice. Read the question two times before you choose. Ask yourself: is this putting groups together, or taking some away? "Altogether" means add. "Taken away" or "walk away" means subtract. 3. Work it out before you look at the choices. Use your counters or your fingers to find the answer yourself. Then look at the four choices and find the one that matches. I expect you to count carefully and touch each object once. 4. Choose your answer, then press Next question. Tap the answer you think is right. Then press the button that says Next question to move on. 5. Keep going for all 12 questions. Do the same thing each time: read twice, work it out, choose, press Next question. Some questions ask what a maths word means, like "add" or "equals" or "altogether". For those, say the word in your head and think what you do when you use it. 6. Look at your score at the end. When the last question is done, the page shows your score. You pass when more than half are right. Mistakes are how we learn, so be proud of what you got right. 7. If your score is not high enough, press Try again. This is not a bad thing! Press Try again and go through the questions once more, slowly. This time, use your counters for every single sum. 8. When your score is good, press Continue. That button finishes the page and takes you onward. I cannot press it for you — you press it yourself. You will know the page is finished when you have answered all 12 questions, seen a good score, and pressed Continue. Come back and tell me how it went. I would love to hear which question was the hardest for you! 🌟

overview.label: Unit Overview
overview.text: Hello! I am Wehel Tutor, and today I am your teacher for Unit 6: Position. This page is our Unit Overview. It is like standing at the door and peeking into the room before we go in. Position means where something is — on, under, above, below, behind, in front of, between. By the end of this unit you will say where things are, and use words like 1st, 2nd and 3rd. For this page you just need your eyes, your ears, and your voice. Maybe a grown-up sitting near you too. Here are our 3 steps. Step 1: Read the Unit Overview. Look at the words at the top of the page that tell you what this unit is about. If you see a little speaker picture, press Listen and let it read to you. Listen right to the end, then read it once more with your eyes. I expect you to spot at least one position word you already know, like on or under. Step 2: Say in your own words what you think you will learn. Say it out loud, to your grown-up or to me. A good answer sounds like this: "I think I will learn words that tell where things are." One or two sentences is plenty. I expect your own words, not the page's words — that is how I know you really understood. Step 3: Press Continue to go to The Lesson. When you have read and talked, find the Continue button and press it. That takes you into the real lesson, where we start with on and under. Do not press it too fast — press it when you can tell me one thing this unit is about. You will know this page is finished when you have listened, said your own sentence, and pressed Continue and landed on The Lesson. Now go ahead with Step 1. Press Listen, then come back and tell me one position word you heard. Take your time — there's no rush.

lesson.label: The Lesson
lesson.text: Hello! I am your teacher today. Let's learn about Position. Position means where something is. We will learn words like on, under, above, below, behind, in front of, and between. We will also learn first, second and third. By the end, you will be able to say where a toy is, and follow a "put it under the mat" kind of instruction. You will need a pencil, and a few small things you can move: a cup, a spoon, a ball or a stone. Here is what I expect from you today. Go slowly. Say the words out loud. Move real objects with your hands, not just your eyes. There are 4 things to do on this page. 1. Read the 6 concepts, one at a time. On the page there are 6 short lessons. Read the first one slowly. Then press Listen and hear it read to you. Listening while you read helps the words stick. Do not rush to the next one. I expect you to finish one concept fully before you start the next. 2. Say the example out loud, then do it with your own things. Each concept has an example, like "the cup is on the mat". Say that sentence out loud in a big clear voice. Then pick up your own cup and put it on your mat. Say it again with your thing: "My cup is on the table." I expect your hands to move, not just your mouth. Do this for every concept. 3. When you have read all 6, press I studied the concepts. This button is at the bottom of the page. Only press it after you have really read and tried all six. It tells the page that you have finished the reading part. I expect you to be honest with yourself here. 4. Now do the slides at the bottom. Under the page there is a deck of slides. Each slide has one concept, the same as before. Press Start on the first slide. Then use the same buttons on each slide to work through it. When a slide is done, press the arrow on the right to go to the next slide. Look at the little dots under the slide — they show you where you are. On the last slide, press the finish button. How will you know the page is finished? You will have pressed Listen on all 6 concepts, said each example out loud with your own objects, pressed I studied the concepts, and pressed the finish button on the last slide. Take your time — there's no rush. Tell me when you are ready to start step 1, or if you want me to explain any word first.

words.label: Math Words & Symbols
words.text: Hello! I'm your teacher today, and this page is all about our position words. Position words tell us where something is. On this page you will meet the words we use all through Unit 6, like on, under, above, below, between, first and last. We do this so that when you talk about your toys, your shoes or your food, you can say exactly where they are. You need your voice, your eyes, and a chair to sit in. Let's begin! Here is what I expect from you: try every word, even the tricky ones, and say them out loud. Take your time — mathematicians think slowly on purpose. Step 1: Look at the first word on the page. Read the word, then read what it means. Now press Listen and hear the word said out loud. Listen carefully to how it sounds. Do this for the word at the top before you move down the list. Step 2: Now say the word out loud yourself. Say it clearly, like the Listen button did. Then say the meaning in your own words — not the same words on the page, but your words. For example, for "under" you might say, "it means below something, like my shoes under my bed." I expect to hear your own idea, not just reading. Step 3: Now type a sentence using that word, then press Check sentence. A good sentence has a thing, the position word, and another thing. Like this: "The cup is under the table." Then read what the checker tells you. If it says to fix something, fix it and try again — mistakes are how we learn. Step 4: Do steps 1, 2 and 3 again for every word on the page. The words are on, under, above, below, behind, in front of, next to, beside, between, first, last, ordinal number, and order. Go one word at a time. Do not rush ahead — finish one word before you start the next. Step 5: When you have listened, said, and written a sentence for every single word, press I know these words and symbols at the bottom. Only press it when every word is done. That button tells the page you have finished the word list. Step 6: Now look under the page. There is a deck of slides. Each slide has one of the same words on it. Press Start on the first slide to begin. Step 7: On each slide, use the same buttons you already know. Press Listen, say the word out loud, say the meaning in your own words, then type your sentence and press Check sentence. You are practising the same word again — and that is good, because saying a word twice helps it stick. Step 8: When one slide is done, press the arrow on the right to go to the next slide. Look at the little dots under the slide. They show you where you are and how many slides are left. Step 9: Keep going, one slide at a time, until you reach the very last slide. On that last slide, press the finish button. Well done — that is the end of the deck. How will you know the page is finished? You will have pressed I know these words and symbols at the bottom of the word list, and you will have pressed the finish button on the last slide. Then every word has been heard, said, and used in your own sentence. Ready? Start with the very first word and press Listen. Tell me when you have done it, and I'll be right here. 🌟

visuals.label: Visual Models
visuals.text:
Hello! Today we are on the Visual Models page. Here is what that means: a visual model is a picture that shows an idea, so you can see it with your eyes. This page has 5 pictures about position — words like on, under, above, below, between, and first, second, third. We do this because position words are much easier to learn when you can watch something move. By the end, you will be able to look at two things and say where one of them is. What I expect from you: look at every model, not just one. Say the position word out loud each time. Take your time. There is no rush. Step 1. Find the first model at the top of the page. Look at it carefully. If it can move, use your finger or mouse to drag it and turn it around. If it has buttons, press them and watch what changes. A good look means you can tell me what moved and where it went. Step 2. Under that model there is a caption. A caption is the little bit of writing that tells you about the picture. Press the Listen button to hear it read out. Listen once, then say the position word out loud yourself, like this: on, or under. Step 3. Now go to the second model. Do the same thing: drag it, press its buttons, then press Listen. This one is about above and below. Remember, above and below do not touch. A bird above a tree is high in the sky. Step 4. Go to the third model. Drag it and press Listen. This one shows that where you stand changes your answer. Watch what happens to in front of and behind when the view moves. That is a tricky one, so look twice. Step 5. Go to the fourth model. Press its buttons and press Listen. This one is about order: first, second, third. Point at each thing and count out loud, starting from the front. Step 6. Go to the fifth and last model. Drag it, press its buttons, and press Listen. This one is about giving and following position instructions, like "put the cup under the mat."

Step 7. When you have looked at all 5 models and heard all 5 captions, scroll to the bottom. Press the button that says I explored the models. You will know the page is finished when you have pressed I explored the models at the bottom. That button is how the page saves your work, so it must be you who presses it, not me. Now start with Step 1, and tell me when it is done. 😊

explore.label: Explore the Concept
explore.text: Hello! Today we are learning about position. Position means where something is — like on, under, above, below, between, in front of and behind. We will also learn 1st, 2nd, 3rd, which tell us which one in a line. This page has 6 little discoveries. You will read a small story, think, and type your own idea. By the end you will be able to say where things are, using the right word. You need your eyes, your thinking brain, and maybe one toy to move around. Let's go! Step 1. Look at the top of the page. You will see little numbered tabs: 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6. Press tab number 1. Now read the little story and look at the picture or model. Read it slowly. If reading is tricky, ask your grown-up to read it with you. I expect you to look carefully before you answer — mathematicians think slowly on purpose. Step 2. Under the story there is a question. Read it twice. Think about where the thing is: is it touching? is it higher? is it in the middle of two things? Then type your idea in the box. A good answer uses a position word, like "under the table" or "above the tree". Even a few words is fine — I just want your real thinking. Step 3. Press Check my idea. If it says Exactly!, well done — that tab gets a tick. If it says Look again, do not worry. Mistakes are how we learn. Press Hint, read the little clue, then change your answer and press Check my idea again. Step 4. Now press tab number 2 and do the same thing: read, think, type, press Check my idea. Then keep going — tab 3, tab 4, tab 5, tab 6. One tab at a time, please. Take your time — there's no rush. I expect all six tabs to have a tick. Step 5. Now scroll down, under the page. There is a deck of slides. They show the same six discoveries, one on each slide. Press Start on the first slide. Step 6. On each slide, use the same buttons as before: read, type your idea, press Check my idea, and press Hint if you need help. Then press the arrow on the right to go to the next slide. The little dots under the slide show you where you are. Step 7. Keep going slide by slide until the last one. On the last slide, press the finish button. That tells the page you are done. How you will know you are finished: every one of the 6 tabs has a tick, and you have pressed the finish button on the last slide. Ready? Press tab number 1 and tell me what your first discovery says. 😊

examples.label: Worked Examples
examples.text:
Hello! I am your teacher today, and this page is one of my favourites. This page is called Worked Examples. It has 12 little maths questions about position words, like on, under, above, below, between, and 1st, 2nd, 3rd. Each question comes with the full working — that means someone shows you their thinking, step by step. We do this so you can see HOW a good answer is built, not just what the answer is. By the end, you will be able to look at a picture or a line of things and say exactly where something is. What you need: your eyes, your voice, and maybe one small toy or a cup to move around. What I expect from you: try each one yourself FIRST, before you peek. A brave guess is much better than a quick peek. Mistakes are how we learn. Here are all the steps. Step 1. Look at the very first worked example. Read the question, or ask your grown-up to read it to you. Say your answer out loud before you press anything. I expect a full sentence, like "The cup is under the table" — not just one word. Step 2. Now press the button that says Show worked solution. Read the working line by line, slowly. Ask yourself, "Did I think the same way?" If yes, say "Yes!" out loud. If not, that is fine — find the one line where your thinking went a different way. Step 3. Do the same for every one of the 12 examples: read, say your answer, then press Show worked solution and compare. Take your time — mathematicians think slowly on purpose. If one feels tricky, move a real object with your hands to help you see it. Step 4. Look at the counter at the top of the page. It counts how many examples you have opened. Keep going until every single one is open. Do not skip any, even the easy-looking ones — the easy ones keep your words strong. Step 5. Now scroll down under the page. There is a deck of slides with the same examples, one on each slide. On the first slide, press Start. Step 6. On each slide, use the same buttons as before: read the question, say your answer out loud, then press Show worked solution. One slide, one answer, no rushing. Step 7. To move on, press the arrow on the right side of the slide. Look at the little dots under the slide — they show you where you are in the deck. Keep going, slide by slide. Step 8. On the last slide, press the finish button. That tells the page you are done. How will you know the page is finished? Two things: the counter at the top shows all 12 examples opened, and you have pressed the finish button on the last slide. 🌟

Ready? Start with Step 1, then come back and tell me your answer to the very first example. I will be right here.

guided.label: Guided Practice
guided.text: Hello! Today I am your teacher for Guided Practice. This page is where we practise the position words from Unit 6 — words like on, under, above, below, between, and the order words 1st, 2nd, 3rd. We practise because saying a word once is not enough; your brain remembers it when you use it. By the end you will be able to say exactly where something is, and which one is first, second or third. Get a pencil and some paper, and a small toy or a cup you can move if you want to try it for real. Here are your steps, one at a time. 1. Read the first question slowly. Read it twice. Then work it out — in your head, or by drawing it on your paper. You can also act it out with your cup: put it on the table, then under the table, and see which one matches. I expect you to think first, before you type anything. Mathematicians think slowly on purpose. 2. Now type your answer in the box and press Check my answer. Write the position word, like "under" or "between" or "3rd". If you are not sure, press Give me a hint. You can have up to three hints. If you still feel stuck, press Show next step and it shows you one line of the working. I expect you to try a hint before you look at the next step — that way the thinking stays yours. 3. Do this for every question, all 12 of them. If an answer is not right, that is fine — mistakes are how we learn. Read the question again, ask yourself "is it touching, or not touching?", and try again. Keep going on each question until it is right. When all 12 are right, that part of the page is done. 4. Now look under the page. There is a deck of slides with the same questions, one question on each slide. Press Start on the first slide. Answer it the same way: type your answer, press Check my answer, and use Give me a hint or Show next step if you need help. Then press the arrow on the right to go to the next slide. The little dots under the slide show you where you are. On the last slide, press the finish button. You will know the page is finished when all 12 questions are right and you have pressed the finish button on the last slide. I do not tick it for you — you press it yourself, because it is your work. Ready? Start with question one, and tell me your answer. I am right here. 😊

method.label: Learn the Method
method.text:
Hello! I am your teacher today. This page is called Learn the Method. A method is a way to work something out, step by step. On this page you will meet six methods about position. They teach you words like on, under, above, below, between, next to, and the order words first, second, third. Doing them will help you say exactly where something is. What I expect from you: say each step out loud, and use your hands or a small toy to try it for real. Take your time. Slow is good — mathematicians think slowly on purpose. Here are your steps. Step 1. Look at the first method on the page. Read the first step, or ask your grown-up to read it with you. Say it out loud in your own voice. Then press Show me the next step to see the step after it. Step 2. Keep pressing Show me the next step until you see the words Method complete. Say every step out loud as it appears. If a step says to put a date on a plate, try it with something small you have — a stone, a spoon, a toy. Doing it with your hands makes the word stick. Step 3. Now do the same for every method on the page. There are six. After each one, wait until it says Method complete before you move to the next one. I expect all six to reach Method complete, not just the first one. Step 4. Look under the page. There is a deck of slides with the same methods, one method on each slide. Press Start on the first slide. Step 5. On each slide, use the same buttons as before to walk through the steps to the end. Keep saying the position word a little louder than the other words, like this: "The cup is UNDER the table."

Step 6. Press the arrow on the right to go to the next slide. Look at the little dots under the slide — they show you how far you have come. Do every slide the same way. Step 7. On the last slide, press the finish button. That tells the page you have done them all. How you know the page is finished: all six methods say Method complete, and you have pressed the finish button on the last slide. 🌟

Ready? Start with step 1, then come back and tell me when your first method says Method complete.

games.label: Games
games.text: Welcome to our Games page! This is the fun part of Unit 6: Position. You will play little games about position words like on, under, above, below, behind, in front of, next to and between. You will also use ordinal numbers, like 1st, 2nd and 3rd. Playing helps the words stick in your head, so you can say where things are all by yourself. You need nothing but your eyes, your thinking and maybe a toy to move around. Here is what I expect from you today: read each question slowly, think before you tap, and try your best on your own. Mistakes are how we learn — so a wrong answer is fine, we just look at it and try again. There are 3 steps. Here they are. Step 1. Pick any game on the page and press Start game. A question will pop up with some choices. Read it twice, then picture it in your head — is the thing touching, higher, lower, or in the middle? Then tap the answer you think is right. You get a star for every round you get right. I expect you to think first, then tap — not tap fast to see what happens. Step 2. When a game ends, press Play again to earn more stars. A game is mastered when it has all its stars. So if you missed a star, play that game again and try to fix the one you got wrong. I expect you to keep going on a game until all its stars are filled, even if it takes two or three tries. Take your time — there's no rush. Step 3. Do the same for every game on the page. Go one game at a time, and master each one before you move to the next. There are games about on and under, above and below, behind and in front of, next to and beside, between, first and last, and ordinal numbers. I expect you to try every single game, even the ones that look tricky. How will you know the page is finished? When every game has all its stars, the page finishes by itself. You will see all the games shining with full stars — that means you did it! Now press Start game on your first game. Tell me which game you picked, and I'll cheer you on. 🌟

fluency.label: Math Fluency
fluency.text: Hello! I am your teacher today. Let's get ready for Math Fluency. Math Fluency is a quick sprint of 12 short questions about position. Position words tell us where something is, like on, under, above, below, behind, in front of, next to and between. We also use 1st, 2nd, 3rd — the words that tell us which one in a line. We do this sprint so these words come to your mind fast, without stopping to think hard. You will need your eyes, your thinking brain, and maybe one small toy on your table to help you picture things. Here is what I expect from you: try every question, make a picture in your head first, then answer. Fast is good, but careful is better. Mistakes are how we learn. Here are your steps. 1. Look at the top of the page. You will see your time counting. That is just for fun — it does not mean you must rush. Take a small breath and get ready. Then read question one slowly. 2. Answer the first question. Type your answer in the box, then press Check & continue. Do this for each question, one at a time, all the way to question twelve. That is twelve turns of typing and pressing Check & continue. 3. Answer each question well like this: picture the two things in your head. Is it touching? Then it is on or under. Is it not touching? Then it is above or below. Does it have something on BOTH sides? Then it is between. Only one neighbour? Then it is next to. 4. For the line questions, always start counting from the front of the line. Point with your finger and say it out loud: first, second, third. This stops you counting from the wrong end. 5. When you finish all twelve, the page will show how many you got right. You need most of them right to pass the sprint. Look at your score and see how you did. 6. If you got fewer than you needed, that is okay — it just means one more go. Press Run the sprint again. The questions will feel easier the second time, because your brain has met them already. Come tell me any word that felt tricky, and we will practise it together. You will know the page is finished when one sprint has enough right answers. Then you have done it — well done! Ready? Start with question one, and tell me how it goes. 🙂

activities.label: Activities
activities.text:
Hello! Today I am your teacher for the Activities page. This page has one hands-on activity. That means you do not just read — you touch, move and make things. We do this because position words like on, under, above, below and between are easiest to learn with real objects in your hands. By the end, you will be able to show a position word and talk about it. You will need paper, a pencil, and a few small things from home — a cup, a spoon, a toy, a stone. A grown-up can sit with you. Here is what to do, step by step. Step 1: Read the activity, and press Listen to hear it read out loud. Listen carefully. Then go and get the things it names. I expect you to have your paper, pencil and small objects on the table before you start. Take your time — there's no rush. Step 2: Now do the activity. Pick one idea from this unit, like "under" or "between". Make it real: put the spoon under the cup, or put a stone between two cups. You can also draw it on your paper. I expect you to say the position word out loud as you place the object, like this: "The spoon is UNDER the cup."

Step 3: Show your model to someone in your family and tell them about it. Use a full sentence with the position word in it. Then write or draw one question of your own, like "Where is the stone?", and answer it yourself. Even one short sentence is great work. Step 4: Write your answer in the box. Tell me what you made and what you noticed. A good answer names the two objects and the position word, like "The cup is on the mat." Your grown-up can help you write it. Step 5: Press Mark complete under the activity when you have finished it. Only press it when you have really done the activity — that is your honest work. Step 6: When the activity is marked, press Finish activities at the bottom of the page. Step 7: Now look under the page. There is a deck of slides with the same activity, one on each slide. Press Start on the first slide. Do the same things there: listen, do it, write in the box, press Mark complete. Step 8: Press the arrow on the right to go to the next slide. The little dots under the slide show you where you are. Do each slide the same way, one at a time. On the last slide, press Finish activities. You will know the page is finished when every activity says complete and you have pressed Finish activities at the bottom, and the last slide is finished too. Ready? Go and get your things, then tell me when you have them. 🙂

challenge.label: Unit Challenge
challenge.text: Welcome to your Unit Challenge! This is the last part of Unit 6: Position. It is like a friendly game where you show what you know about words like on, under, above, below, behind, in front of, between, and 1st, 2nd, 3rd. We do it so you can see how much you have learned. You will need your eyes, your thinking brain, and maybe a grown-up sitting near you. I will not tell you any answers — but I will help you think. Take your time — there's no rush. 1. Read question one on your screen. Say it out loud, slowly, if that helps. Make a picture in your head: where is the thing? On top? Underneath? Higher up and not touching? In the middle of two things? Then tap the answer you think is right, and press Next question. I expect you to look at all the choices before you pick one. 2. Keep going, one question at a time, until you have done all 12 questions. After each pick, press Next question. Do not rush! Mathematicians think slowly on purpose. For every question, ask yourself: is it touching or not touching? Touching the top is on. Not touching and higher is above. 3. For the questions about lines and order, use your finger. Point at the first one and say "first", then "second", then "third". Always start counting from the front of the line. I expect you to count out loud, not just guess. 4. For questions about words, like "What does between mean?", think of your own example first. Picture yourself standing in the middle of two chairs. That helps you pick the right meaning. 5. When you finish the last question, your score will pop up. You pass with more than half of them right. Look at your score and see how you did. 6. If your score is not high enough, do not worry. Mistakes are how we learn. Press Try again and go through the questions once more. This time, read each question twice before you choose. 7. When your score is good, press Continue. That is the last button on this page. You will know the page is finished when you have pressed Continue and the page moves on. Then come back and tell me your score — I would love to hear how you did! 🌟

explain.label: Explain Your Thinking
explain.text: Hello! I am your teacher today. Let me tell you about this page. This page is called "Explain Your Thinking." You will not just say the answer. You will say WHY. You tell me where something is, and which position word you used, like on, under, above, below, between, or next to. This helps the words stick in your head, and it makes you a strong little mathematician. Mathematicians think slowly on purpose. What I expect from you: try first, use your own words, and use the key ideas words in your answer. Short is fine. One or two sentences is plenty. A grown-up may sit with you and help you type. Get a pencil too, if you like to draw the picture first. Here are all the steps. 1. There are 6 prompts on this page. A prompt is a small question. Read the first prompt slowly. Under it you will see the key ideas — those are the special words, like above, below, or between. Read those words too. I expect you to point at each key idea word and say it out loud before you write. 2. Now write your answer in the box. Say three things: what you see, which position word you used, and why that word is the right one. Like this shape: "The fish is below the boat, because it is lower down and it is not touching the boat." Then press Check mathematical ideas. I expect you to use at least one key idea word in your writing. 3. If the page asks for more, do not worry. That just means one small piece is missing. Add one more sentence — maybe say why the OTHER word is wrong, like "It is not on the boat, because on means touching." Then press Check mathematical ideas again. I expect you to try again, not to give up. Mistakes are how we learn. 4. Next, press Show model explanation. This opens a good example answer. Read it and see what is the same as yours. Do not copy it — you already wrote yours! I expect you to tell me one thing the model answer said that you also said. That means you got it right. 5. Now do the same for prompt 2, then 3, 4, 5 and 6. Read, write in the box, press Check mathematical ideas, then press Show model explanation. Take your time — there's no rush. Six prompts is a lot for one day, so you can stop and come back. 6. Now look under the page. There is a deck of slides with the same prompts, one on each slide. On the first slide, press Start. This is your chance to say the same ideas again, and saying them again makes them stronger. 7. On each slide, use the same buttons as before: write your answer, press Check mathematical ideas, then press Show model explanation. I expect a little more from you here, because you have already practised these ideas once. 8. To move on, press the arrow on the right side of the slide. Look at the little dots under the slide — they show you where you are and how many are left. On the last slide, press the finish button. You will know the page is finished when all 6 prompts have your explanation, each one uses the key ideas words, and you have pressed the finish button on the last slide. I do not tick it off — you do, by pressing the buttons yourself. Ready? Read prompt 1 and tell me what you see. I am right here with you. 🌟

problems.label: Solve Real Problems
problems.text:
Hello! I'm your teacher today, and this page is one of my favourites. 😊

This page is called Solve Real Problems. It has six little stories from real life — things like getting ready in the morning, standing in a line at the market, or putting your shoes under your bed. Your job is to use our position words (on, under, next to, between, in front of, behind) and our order words (1st, 2nd, 3rd, last) to work out the answer. We do this because position words are not just for the page — you use them every day at home. Here is what I expect from you: read slowly, say the story out loud if it helps, and always tell me why, not just the answer. A grown-up can sit with you and read the words. Here are all the steps. Step 1: Read the first problem carefully, right to the end. Then ask yourself, "What is this question really asking me?" Sometimes it asks where something is. Sometimes it asks which one is 1st, 2nd or 3rd. Say the question back in your own words before you answer. That is what I expect first — understanding, not speed. Step 2: Work it out with your hands or your eyes. You can line up real things, like spoons or toys, or draw little circles in a row. If the story is about order, point and count out loud: first, second, third. Mathematicians think slowly on purpose, so take your time. Step 3: Type your working and your answer in the box. Your working is just how you got there, in your own simple words, like "I counted the ones in front" or "the plate has one thing on each side". Then press Check answer. I expect a position word or an order word in your answer, not only a number. Step 4: If you feel stuck, press Hint. A hint is not cheating — it is a helping hand. Read the hint, then try again by yourself. If it is still hard, tell me and we will do one small bit together. Step 5: When the page says your answer is right, that problem is done. Now do the same thing for problem 2, then 3, 4, 5 and 6. Same three moves every time: read, work it out, type it and press Check answer. Step 6: Now look under the page. There is a deck of slides with the same six problems, one problem on each slide. This is your practice round, to make the words stick. Press Start on the first slide. Step 7: On each slide, use the same buttons you already know: type your answer, press Check answer, and press Hint if you need help. Then press the arrow on the right to go to the next slide. The little dots under the slide show you where you are — like a line of children, one dot for each slide. Step 8: Keep going, one slide at a time, until you reach the last slide. On the last slide, press the finish button. Well done — that closes your practice deck. How will you know the page is finished? All six problems say your answer is right, and you have pressed the finish button on the last slide. Then the whole page is complete. Ready? Read me problem number one, and tell me what you think it is asking. I'm right here. 🙂

words.label: Math Words & Symbols
words.text: Hello! Today I am your teacher for the Math Words & Symbols page. This page has the special words for Unit 7, our sorting unit. Words like sort, set, more, fewer, and Venn diagram. When you know these words, you can say what you did with your buttons and stones — not just do it. That is what makes it maths! You will need your voice, your eyes, and your hands for typing. A grown-up can sit near you if you like. Here is what to do, step by step. Step 1: Look at the first word at the top of the page. Read the word. Then read what it means beside it. Then press Listen. Listen carefully to how it sounds. I expect you to look at the word while you listen, not away from the screen. Step 2: Now say the word out loud, in a big clear voice. Then say what it means in YOUR own words — not the same words as the page. For example, for "sort" you might say, "sort means put things in piles." I expect your own words, even if they are wobbly. That is how I know you really understand. Step 3: Now type a sentence with that word in it. Make it about your real life — your toys, your food, your family. Something like, "I sort my socks into big and small." Then press Check sentence. Read what the checker tells you. If it says to fix something, fix it and press Check sentence again. I expect one full sentence, starting with a capital letter and ending with a full stop. Step 4: Now do the very same three things for the next word. Listen, say it, say the meaning your way, type a sentence, press Check sentence. Keep going down the page until every word is done. Take your time — there is no rush. Mathematicians think slowly on purpose. Step 5: When every word has a green tick or a checked sentence, press I know these words and symbols at the bottom. Only press it when you have really done them all. That button tells the page you are ready. Step 6: Now look under the page. There is a little deck of slides. Each slide has one of the same words. Press Start on the first slide. This is like a game to help the words stick in your head. Step 7: On each slide, use the same buttons as before. Press Listen. Say the word out loud. Say the meaning your way. Type your sentence and press Check sentence. Do this on every slide, one at a time. Step 8: When a slide is done, press the arrow on the right side to go to the next slide. Look at the little dots under the slide. The dots show you where you are and how many are left. Step 9: Keep going until you reach the last slide. On the last slide, press the finish button. Well done — that is the whole deck! How will you know the page is finished? Every word has a checked sentence, the I know these words and symbols button has been pressed, and you have pressed the finish button on the last slide. Now go and start with step 1. When you have done the first word, come back and tell me your sentence — I would love to read it. 🙂

overview.label: Unit Overview
overview.text: Hello! I am your teacher today. Let's look at this page together. This page is called the Unit Overview. It is like a little map for Unit 7, Statistics. It tells you what we will learn: sorting things into groups, counting them, and comparing which group has more. We do this first so you know where we are going. You just need your eyes, your ears, and your voice. Maybe a grown-up nearby too. There are 3 steps. Here they all are. Step 1: Read the Unit Overview. Look at the words at the top of the page. Read them slowly. If you see a little speaker picture, press Listen and hear the words out loud. It is fine to press Listen twice. I expect you to read or listen all the way to the end, not just look at the pictures. Step 2: Say what you will learn, in your own words. Do not copy the words on the screen. Just tell me, or tell your grown-up, one thing you think you will do in this unit. A good answer sounds like this: "I will put things into groups and count them." One sentence is enough. I expect you to try, even if it is not perfect. Step 3: Press Continue. When you have read the page and said your sentence, find the Continue button and press it. That takes you to The Lesson, where the real sorting fun starts. Do not press it before you say your sentence. You will know the page is finished when you have read or listened to the overview, said your own sentence out loud, and pressed Continue. Now let's begin with Step 1. Read the Unit Overview, and press Listen if there is a speaker. Tell me when you are done.

lesson.label: The Lesson
lesson.text: Hello! Today I am your teacher, and this page is called The Lesson. On this page you will learn about sorting. Sorting means putting things into groups. We do this because it helps us see what is the same and what is different, and then we can count and compare. By the end you will be able to sort a pile of things, say your rule out loud, and count which group has more. Before we start, get a small pile of things you can touch: buttons, stones, bottle caps, or dry beans. Have a grown-up nearby if you need help. There are 4 parts to this page. Here they all are. Step 1. Read the 6 little lessons, called concepts. Read them slowly, one at a time. On each one, press Listen so you can hear the words read to you while you follow along. The 6 concepts are: what a set is, counting and comparing sets, the sorting circle called a Venn diagram, two circles and the middle that means both, what this unit is about, and how to choose a good sorting rule. I expect you to finish one concept before you go to the next one. No rushing — mathematicians think slowly on purpose. Step 2. Say each example out loud, then do it with your own things. For example, put your buttons into a red pile and a not-red pile. Then say the rule out loud: "They are all red." Then count each pile by touching each button once. Saying it out loud is the part that makes it maths, so I really do want to hear your voice. Try one new thing each time: sort by colour, then mix them up and sort the very same things by size. Step 3. When you have read all 6 concepts and tried all the examples, go to the bottom of the page and press the button that says I studied the concepts. Only press it when you have really read every one. That button tells us you are ready. Step 4. Now look under the page. There is a deck of slides with the same 6 concepts, one on each slide. On the first slide, press Start. Do the same buttons on every slide. Then press the arrow on the right to go to the next slide. The little dots under the slide show you where you are, like footprints. Keep going until the last slide, and there you press the finish button. You will know the page is finished when you have pressed I studied the concepts and you have pressed the finish button on the last slide. Then all the dots are behind you and the page is done. Ready? Start with Step 1, concept one, and press Listen. Tell me when you have read it, and I will check what you learned before we move on. 🙂

explore.label: Explore the Concept
explore.text: Hello! Today we are doing Explore the Concept in Unit 7, Statistics. In this activity you look at six little discoveries about sorting things into groups. We do it so you learn to make sets, count them, and say which has more. By the end you will be able to sort objects by one rule and explain your rule out loud. You will need your eyes, your thinking, and if you can, a small pile of buttons or stones near you. Ready? Here are the steps. 1. Look at the top of the page for the numbered tabs. Press tab number 1. Read the little story it shows you, and look at the picture or model carefully. Take your time — I expect you to really look, not just click. Ask yourself: what is the same about these things? 2. Under the picture there is a discovery question. Read it, then think for a moment before typing. Type your idea in the box in your own words, then press Check my idea. A good answer names the rule, like "they are all red" — not just "yes". 3. If it says Look again, do not worry. Mistakes are how we learn. Press Hint, read it, then change your answer a little and press Check my idea once more. When it says Exactly!, that tab gets a tick. That tick means well done! 4. Now press tab number 2 and do the same thing: read, look, think, type, press Check my idea. Keep going through tabs 3, 4, 5 and 6, one at a time. The page is finished when every one of the six discoveries has a tick. 5. Now scroll down under the page. There is a deck of slides with the same discoveries, one slide each. On the first slide, press Start. This part is practice, so I expect you to try again in your own words, not copy. 6. On each slide, use the same buttons: type your idea, press Check my idea, and press Hint if you need help. Then press the arrow on the right to go to the next slide. The little dots under the slide show you where you are. 7. On the last slide, press the finish button. That tells the page you are done. I do not tick it for you — you press it yourself, because it is your work. You will know the page is finished when all six tabs have a tick and you have pressed the finish button on the last slide. Start with tab 1 now, and tell me your idea when you have typed it. Take your time — there's no rush.

method.label: Learn the Method
method.text: Hello! Today I am your teacher for the "Learn the Method" page. This page shows 6 methods. A method is a way to do something step by step, like a little recipe. Our methods are all about sorting things into groups, counting them, and comparing them. By the end, you will know how to sort a pile of things and say which pile has more. You will need your eyes, your voice, and if you like, a small pile of buttons, stones or beans to move with your hands. Take your time — there is no rush. Here are the steps. 1. Look at the first method at the top of the page. Read step one out loud. Then press the button that says Show me the next step. A new step will appear. I expect you to read each step with your voice, not just with your eyes — saying it helps your brain remember it. 2. Keep pressing Show me the next step until the page says Method complete. Say every step out loud as it appears. If you can, do the step with real objects, like moving buttons into two piles. That is what a really good learner does here. 3. Now do the same thing for every method. There are 6 in all. Press Show me the next step, read out loud, and keep going until each one says Method complete. Go one method at a time. I expect all 6 to be finished, not just the easy ones. 4. Now look under the page. There is a deck of slides with the same methods, one method on each slide. On the first slide, press Start. Then use the same buttons on the slide to move through the steps, saying them out loud again. 5. When one slide is done, press the arrow on the right to go to the next slide. The little dots under the slide show you where you are. Do every slide the same way: press Start, read the steps out loud, then move on. 6. On the last slide, press the finish button. That tells the page you are all done. You will know the page is finished when all 6 methods say Method complete, and you have pressed the finish button on the last slide. Ready? Start with step one, and tell me when your first method says Method complete. I am right here with you. 😊

visuals.label: Visual Models
visuals.text:
Hello! Today I am your teacher for the Visual Models page. 🌟

Visual models are pictures of our maths ideas. On this page there are 6 of them. They show sorting, sets, more and fewer, and sorting circles. Looking at pictures helps the idea stick in your head. Here is what I expect from you: look slowly, touch and move each picture, and say what you notice out loud. There is no writing to do. Take your time — there's no rush. There are 8 steps. Here they all are. Step 1. Get ready. Sit with the screen in front of you. If you can, put a small pile of buttons, beans or bottle caps next to you. Then you can copy the picture with real things. Ready? Scroll to the top of the page. Step 2. Look at model 1, "What Is a Set". A set is a group of things that belong together. Look at the picture and find the group. If the picture moves, drag it with your finger or mouse to turn it. If it has buttons, press them and watch what changes. Then say out loud: "These belong together because..." and finish the sentence. That is what I expect — one short reason. Step 3. Look at model 2, "Counting and Comparing Sets". This one is about more and fewer. Count each group by touching each thing once. Then say which group has more and which has fewer. Drag or press any buttons to change the groups, then count again. A good job here means you counted, not guessed. Step 4. Look at model 3, "The Venn Diagram — One Sorting Circle". A Venn diagram is a sorting circle. Things that fit the rule go inside. Things that do not fit stay outside. Find the rule for the circle, then point to one thing inside and say why it is inside. Then point to one thing outside and say why. Step 5. Look at model 4, "Two Circles and the Middle". This one is the tricky one, so go slowly. Two circles overlap. The middle part means both. Find one thing in the middle and say: "It is here because it fits both rules." If it moves, drag things into the circles and check each one. Step 6. Look at model 5, "What This Unit Is About", and model 6, "Sorting Objects Into Two Sets by One Rule". Model 5 shows the whole unit: sort, count, compare. Model 6 shows one rule making two sets, like red and not red. Press any buttons on them and watch what changes. Then tell me one thing you noticed. Step 7. Read the caption under every model. The caption is the words under the picture. Then press the Listen button and hear it read to you. Listen with your eyes on the words. Do this for all 6 models, not just one or two. Step 8. Press "I explored the models" at the bottom of the page. Only press it when you have looked at all 6 and pressed Listen on all 6. That button tells the page you are done. How will you know the page is finished? When all 6 models have been looked at, all 6 captions have been heard, and you have pressed "I explored the models". Then the page is complete. One last question for you, when you get there: which model was your favourite, and why? Come back and tell me. 😊

examples.label: Worked Examples
examples.text: Hello! Today we are working on the Worked Examples page for Unit 7, Statistics. A worked example is a question with all the thinking shown, step by step. We do this so you can see how a good sorter thinks: choose one rule, sort into two sets, count each set, then compare. By the end, you will be able to sort things and say your rule out loud. You will need your eyes, your voice, and a small pile of things to move, like buttons, beans, or bottle caps. Here are the steps. 1. Look at the first worked example. Read the question first, before anything else. Try it yourself with your objects or in your head. I expect a first try from you, even a small one — a guess is fine, because mistakes are how we learn. 2. Now press Show worked solution. Read Step 1, then Step 2, then Step 3, slowly. Compare it with your own thinking, one line at a time. I expect you to spot one thing: did your rule match theirs? Say yes or no out loud. 3. Do the same for every example. There are 12 of them. The counter at the top shows how many you have opened. Open all 12, and try each one before you press Show worked solution. That trying part is the real learning. 4. Now go under the page. There is a deck of slides with the same examples, one on each slide. Press Start on the first slide. 5. On each slide, use the same buttons as before: read the question, try it, then press Show worked solution. Take your time. Mathematicians think slowly on purpose. 6. Press the arrow on the right to go to the next slide. The little dots under the slide show you where you are. Keep going, one slide at a time. 7. On the last slide, press the finish button. That tells the page you have done the whole deck. You will know the page is finished when the counter at the top shows all 12 opened, and you have pressed the finish button on the last slide. I am here the whole time. When you have done step 1, tell me your rule and I will check it with you. 😊

guided.label: Guided Practice
guided.text: Hello! Today we are doing Guided Practice for Unit 7, Statistics. This page gives you 12 little sorting questions. You will sort things into groups, count them, and say which group has more. We do this so the ideas from the lesson become easy for you. Get a pencil and some paper. A grown-up can sit near you if you like. Here is our plan, step by step. 1. Read the first question slowly. Read it twice, like a good mathematician. Then work it out on paper or in your head. You can draw dots or circles to help you count. I expect you to look carefully and count each thing only once. 2. Type your answer in the box, then press Check my answer. Most answers here are just a number, like 4, or a short sentence, like "they are all red". If you feel stuck, press Give me a hint. You can get up to three hints. If you are still stuck, press Show next step and it shows you one line of the working. I expect you to try first, then use a hint — hints are for helpers, not for skipping. 3. Do the same for every question, all twelve of them. If an answer is not right, that is fine. Mistakes are how we learn. Read the question again, fix your answer, and press Check my answer again. Keep going until each question is right. 4. Now look under the page. There is a deck of slides with the same questions, one question on each slide. Press Start on the first slide. Answer it the same way, and use the same buttons: Check my answer, Give me a hint, Show next step. Then press the arrow on the right to move to the next slide. The little dots under the slide show you where you are. On the last slide, press the finish button. You will know the page is finished when all twelve questions are right and you have pressed the finish button on the last slide. Take your time — there's no rush. Tell me when you have read question one, and we will look at it together. 😊

activities.label: Activities
activities.text: Hello! Today I am your teacher, and this is our Activities page. On this page you do maths with your hands, not just in your head. You will sort real things into sets, count them, and say which set has more. We do this because sorting is easier to learn when you can touch it and move it. By the end, you will be able to sort a pile one way, say your rule out loud, and count each set. Get these ready first: paper, a pencil, and a small pile of things from home. Buttons, bottle caps, stones, beads or dry beans are perfect. Ask your grown-up if you may use them. There are four steps. Here they all are. Step 1. Look at the hands-on activity on the page. It is called "Practise together". Press Listen to hear it read to you. Listen once, then get the things it names. What I expect: you have your paper, your pencil, and your little pile of objects on the table before you start. Step 2. Now do the activity, then write in the box. Pick one idea from our unit, like sorting by colour. Sort your objects into two sets, such as red and not red. Count each set, and say which has more. Then draw or write it in the box. A good answer says the rule and the numbers, like this: "I sorted by colour. 5 red, 3 not red. Red has more." Then tell a family member what you did — explaining out loud is the real maths part! Step 3. When you have written in the box, press Mark complete under that activity. Do this only after you really did the sorting, not before. When every activity has its Mark complete pressed, press Finish activities at the bottom of the page. Step 4. Now look under the page. There is a deck of slides with the same hands-on activities, one slide each. Press Start on the first slide. Use the same buttons on each slide: Listen, write in the box, then Mark complete. Press the arrow on the right to move to the next slide. The little dots under the slide show you where you are. On the last slide, press Finish activities. How you will know you are finished: every activity shows as complete, the dots have all been visited, and you have pressed Finish activities. Take your time — there's no rush. Tell me when you have your objects ready, and I will stay right here with you. 🙂

problems.label: Solve Real Problems
problems.text: Hello! Today I am your teacher for the Solve Real Problems page. On this page you will sort real things, like pegs, oranges, bread and cups. Sorting means putting things into groups by one rule. We do this so you can use your maths at home and at the market, not just on paper. By the end you will sort things, count each group, and say which group has more. You will need a pencil, some paper, and your thinking voice. A grown-up can sit with you if you like. There are 6 problems. Here is how we do them, step by step. 1. Read the first problem slowly. Then read it again. Ask yourself two things: what are the things, and what is the rule? For example, the rule might be wooden or plastic. I expect you to say the rule out loud before you write anything. 2. Now work it out. Count each group by touching each one, or draw little circles on your paper. Then type in the box what you did and your answer, like this: I sorted by wood or plastic. 5 wooden and 4 plastic. Then press Check answer. I expect a number AND a few words about your rule, not just a number. 3. If your brain feels stuck, that is okay. Press Hint. The hint gives you a little push, not the answer. Read it, then try again by yourself. Mistakes are how we learn. 4. When the page says your answer is right, that problem is finished. Well done! Move down to the next problem and do the same three things: read, work it out, press Check answer. 5. Keep going until all 6 problems say right. Take your time. Mathematicians think slowly on purpose. 6. Now look under the page. There is a deck of slides with the same problems, one problem on each slide. Press Start on the first slide. 7. On each slide, use the same buttons you already know: type your answer, press Check answer, and press Hint if you need help. I expect you to try first, then use the hint. 8. To move to the next slide, press the arrow on the right side. Look at the little dots under the slide. They show you where you are and how many are left. 9. On the last slide, press the finish button. That tells the page you are all done. You will know the whole page is finished when all 6 problems say your answer is right, and you have pressed the finish button on the last slide. Ready? Start with problem one. Read it twice, then tell me the rule you will use. 😊

games.label: Games
games.text:
Hello! Today we play the Unit 7 games. These games are about sorting — putting things into groups called sets. You will also count sets and say which has more or fewer. Playing helps the words stick in your head, so they feel easy later. You need your eyes, your thinking brain, and maybe a grown-up nearby. Take your time — there is no rush. Here are the steps. 1. Look at the games on the page. Pick one you like. Press Start game. A question will come up with some answers to choose from. Read it slowly, then pick the answer you think is right. Do this for every round. Each round you get right gives you a star. I expect you to think before you tap — not just tap fast. If you get one wrong, that is okay. Mistakes are how we learn. 2. When the game ends, press Play again. This gives you more chances to win stars. A game is mastered when it has all its stars. If a question feels hard, read it twice and ask yourself, "What is the rule?" I expect you to keep playing that game until all its stars are yours. 3. Now do the same for every game on the page. Press Start game, answer the rounds, then press Play again until that game has all its stars too. Then move to the next one. I expect you to try every game, even the ones that look tricky. You can come and tell me about any question that puzzles you, and we will look at it together. You will know the page is finished when every game has all its stars. The page finishes by itself then — you do not press anything special. 🌟

Ready? Pick your first game and press Start game. Tell me which one you chose!

fluency.label: Math Fluency
fluency.text: Hello! Today we are doing Math Fluency. It is like a little running race, but with your brain. You will get 12 quick questions about sorting, sets, more and fewer, and sorting circles. We do this so the words and ideas from Unit 7 come to you fast, without hard thinking every time. All you need is your eyes, your fingers for counting, and maybe a grown-up sitting nearby. Here is what I expect from you: read each question, say the answer in your head first, then type it. Quick is good, but right is better. Mathematicians think slowly on purpose — so do not panic about the clock at the top. Step 1. Look at the top of the page and find the timer. It counts your time. Just say hello to it and then forget it. It is there to cheer you, not to scare you. Step 2. Read question one all the way to the end. Read it twice. Ask yourself: is this question about sorting, about counting, or about which set has more? Step 3. Work out your answer before you type. If the question says something like "6 shells, 4 are striped, how many are not striped?", use your fingers or draw little dots on paper. Counting on paper is allowed and clever. Step 4. Type your answer in the answer box. Type just the answer, like "4" or "inside the circle". Keep it short and clear. Step 5. Press Check & continue. This tells the page you are ready and moves you to the next question. Step 6. Look at what the page tells you. If you were right, smile and keep going. If not, read the little note it gives you. Mistakes are how we learn. Step 7. Do the same for every question, one at a time, all the way to question twelve. Do not skip ahead. One question, one answer, press Check & continue. Step 8. When you finish all 12, look at your score. You need most of them right to pass the sprint. Getting nearly all of them is the goal. Step 9. If you got fewer than that, press Run the sprint again. This is not a punishment! It is a second try, and second tries make you faster. Before you start again, tell me which questions were tricky and I will help you. Step 10. You will know the page is finished when you complete a sprint with enough answers right. The page will show you that you have done it. Then you can be very proud. Ready? Tell me when you have read question one, and say what you think it is asking. 😊

challenge.label: Unit Challenge
challenge.text: Well done for getting all the way here! This page is your Unit Challenge. It is 12 questions about everything we learned in Statistics: sorting things into sets, saying your rule, counting each set, saying which has more and which has fewer, and using sorting circles. We do it to see what your brain has already learned. You do not need anything special — just your eyes, your thinking, and a grown-up nearby if you want one. I will not tell you answers, but I will show you how to think. Here are all the steps. Step 1. Read the first question slowly. Read it twice. Ask yourself: what is this question really asking? Sometimes it asks how many, sometimes it asks which set has more, sometimes it asks where an object goes. I expect you to read every word before you choose. Step 2. Look at the four choices. Read all four, not just the first one. Some choices look right but are not. I expect you to check each one before you pick. Step 3. Pick your answer, then press Next question. Take your time — there is no rush. Mathematicians think slowly on purpose. Step 4. For sorting questions, find the rule first. The rule is one thing, like red or not red. Ask: does this object fit the rule, yes or no? If they tell you the total and how many fit, the rest are the ones that do not fit. Step 5. For counting questions, count carefully. Touch each thing on the screen with your finger as you count. Say the numbers out loud. That way you never count one thing twice. Step 6. For more and fewer questions, look at the two numbers. The bigger number means more. The smaller number means fewer. If both numbers are the same, the sets are equal. Step 7. For sorting circle questions, remember the circle has a rule. Things that fit the rule go inside. Things that do not fit stay outside. If there are two circles, ask two questions: does it fit this rule, and does it fit that rule too? If both are yes, it goes in the middle. Step 8. Keep going, one question at a time, pressing Next question after each one. Twelve questions in all. If one feels hard, that is okay — choose your best answer and move on. Step 9. At the end you will see your score. More than half right means you passed. Look at your score and see how you did. Step 10. If your score is not high enough, press Try again. That is not a bad thing! Mistakes are how we learn. Try again means you get another go, and this time you will know more. Step 11. When your score is good, press Continue. That is the last button on this page. You will know the page is finished when you have answered all 12 questions, seen your score, and pressed Continue. Take a breath and start with question one. I am right here if you get stuck — just tell me which question, and I will give you a hint. 😊

explain.label: Explain Your Thinking
explain.text:
Hello! Today I am your teacher, and this page is called "Explain Your Thinking."

On this page you do not just sort things. You say WHY. You tell me the rule you used, and why your answer makes sense. Talking about your thinking is what real mathematicians do. You will need your eyes, your words, and maybe a grown-up to help you type. Here is what I expect from you. Use the maths words: sort, set, same, different, more, fewer, compare. Say your rule out loud first, then write it. Two or three little sentences is plenty. Take your time — there's no rush. Now here are all the steps, one at a time. Step 1: Read the first prompt. There are 6 prompts on this page. Under each one you will see some key ideas — those are the special words I want you to use. Read the prompt slowly, twice. Then say the answer out loud to yourself before you write anything. I expect you to know what the question is asking before your pencil moves. Step 2: Write your explanation in the box. Tell me three things: what you see, what rule you used, and why your answer makes sense. For example you might write, "I looked at each button. My rule was red or not red. The red ones go together because they are the same colour." Then press Check mathematical ideas. If the page asks for more, add one more sentence and press it again. I expect you to try your own words first, not copy anyone. Step 3: Press Show model explanation. This shows you a good answer so you can compare. Do not worry if yours has different words — that is fine! Just check one thing: did you say the rule? If you forgot it, go back and add it. Then do steps 1, 2 and 3 again for prompt 2, then 3, then 4, 5 and 6. Step 4: Now look under the page. There is a deck of slides with the same prompts, one on each slide. On the first slide, press Start. Do the same as before: read, write your explanation, press Check mathematical ideas, then Show model explanation. When that slide is done, press the arrow on the right to move to the next slide. The little dots under the slide show you how far you have come. On the last slide, press the finish button. You will know the page is finished when all 6 explanations use the key ideas, and you have pressed the finish button on the last slide. Ready? Start with prompt 1, and tell me when you have read it. 🙂

overview.label: Unit Overview
overview.text: Hello! I am your teacher today. This page is called the Unit Overview. It is like looking at a map before a trip. It tells you what Unit 8 is about — Time! By the end of this unit you will know the days of the week, the parts of the day, and how to read a clock. You need your eyes, your ears, and your voice. Let's start with something small. 1. Read the Unit Overview. Look at the words on the screen. Read them slowly, out loud if you like. If you see a little speaker picture, press Listen and listen carefully. You can press Listen again if you want to hear it twice. I expect you to read it all the way to the end, not just the first line. Look for the words days, clock, and time — they will tell you what is coming. 2. Say what you will learn, in your own words. Do not copy the words on the screen. Just say it your own way, like telling a friend. For example: "I will learn the days of the week and how to read a clock." One or two sentences is plenty. You can say it out loud to your grown-up, or type it to me and I will listen. I expect a real try — even a short answer is a good answer. 3. Press Continue to go to The Lesson. Continue is the button at the bottom of the page. Press it once when you are ready. That takes you to the next part, where we start learning for real. Do not press it before you have read the overview — the map first, then the trip! You will know this page is finished when you have read the overview, said in your own words what you will learn, and pressed Continue. Then The Lesson opens, and that means you did it. Take your time — there's no rush. When you are ready, tell me one thing you think you will learn in this unit. 🙂

lesson.label: The Lesson
lesson.text:
Hello! Today I am your teacher for the Lesson page in Unit 8: Time. ⏰

This page has 5 short ideas, called concepts. They teach you the days of the week, the parts of the day, the two clock hands, o'clock times, and half past times. By the end, you will be able to say the days in order and read a clock. You need your eyes, your voice, and a grown-up nearby if you want one. Let's start. Step 1. Look at the first concept on the page. Read it slowly, word by word. Then press Listen and hear it read to you. Listening while you look helps the words stick. I expect you to read it, not skip it. Step 2. Read the example in that concept out loud. Saying it out loud helps your brain remember it. Say it clearly, like you are teaching a little brother or sister. Step 3. Now try it your own way. If the concept is about days, say the days of the week out loud: Monday, Tuesday, Wednesday, Thursday, Friday, Saturday, Sunday. If it is about the clock, hold up one short finger for the hour hand and one long finger for the minute hand. I expect you to use your own words, your own fingers, or a clock at home. Step 4. Do the same three things for concept 2, concept 3, concept 4 and concept 5. Read it, press Listen, say the example out loud, then try it yourself. Take your time — there's no rush. Mathematicians think slowly on purpose. Step 5. When you have read all five concepts, go to the bottom of the page. Press the button that says I studied the concepts. Only press it after you really read them all. That button tells the page you are done reading. Step 6. Under the page there is a deck of slides. It has the same five ideas, one idea on each slide. Look at the first slide and press Start. This begins your slide practice. Step 7. On the slide, use the same buttons as before. Read the slide, press Listen if it is there, and say the idea out loud. I expect you to say something out loud on every slide, even if it is just one word. Step 8. Press the arrow on the right to go to the next slide. Look at the little dots under the slide. The dots show you which slide you are on and how many are left. Step 9. Keep going: read, say it out loud, then press the arrow. Do this until you reach the last slide. On the last slide, press the finish button. You will know the page is finished when you have pressed I studied the concepts and pressed the finish button on the last slide. Now go and do Step 1, then come back and tell me what your first concept was about. I'll be right here! 😊

words.label: Math Words & Symbols
words.text: Hello! Today I am your teacher for the Math Words & Symbols page in our Time unit. This page holds our time words, like week, clock, hour hand, minute hand, o'clock and half past. We learn them so that when you read a question about time, the words feel like old friends. By the end, you will be able to say each word, tell me what it means, and use it in your own sentence. You will need your voice, and a grown-up nearby if you want help with typing. Here is what I expect from you: try every word, say them out loud (not in your head), and make your own sentences — not copied ones. There are 4 steps. Take your time. 1. Look at the first word on the page. Read the word, then read what it means. Now press Listen and hear how it sounds. Listen carefully, then say it back the same way. Do this for one word at a time, from the top of the list down. I expect you to press Listen for every word, even the easy ones. 2. Now make the word yours. First say the word out loud. Then say the meaning in your own words, not the words on the screen — like "hour hand means the short hand." Then type one sentence using the word, such as "The hour hand points to 5." Press Check sentence and read what the checker tells you. If it says to fix something, change your sentence and press Check sentence again. I expect a real sentence about your own day — your breakfast, your school, your clock at home. Do step 1 and step 2 for every word on the list. 3. When you have finished every word on the list, go to the bottom of the page and press I know these words and symbols. Only press it when you have really done them all — that button is your promise to yourself. It tells the page you are ready. 4. Now look under the page. There is a deck of slides, with one word on each slide. Press Start on the first slide. Use the same buttons here as before: Listen to hear the word, say it out loud, say the meaning, type your sentence, and press Check sentence. Then press the arrow on the right to move to the next slide. The little dots under the slide show you how far you have come. Keep going, one slide at a time, until the last slide — and there, press the finish button. You will know the page is finished when two things are true: the I know these words and symbols button has been pressed, and you have pressed the finish button on the last slide. Ready? Start with step 1, and tell me when you have listened to your first word. 🙂

explore.label: Explore the Concept
explore.text: Hello! Today I am your teacher for Time. This page is called Explore the Concept. It has six little discoveries about days of the week, parts of the day, and clocks. We do it so you can find the ideas yourself, not just be told them. By the end you will name the days in order, say morning, afternoon and evening, know the short hand and the long hand, and read o'clock and half past. What I expect from you: think first, then type your own idea in words. A good answer is short and clear, like "Tuesday" or "the short hand". Guessing fast is not the goal. Mathematicians think slowly on purpose. Have a pencil and paper near you, and a grown-up close by if you want help reading. Here are all the steps. Step 1. Look at the top of the page. You will see numbered tabs: 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6. Press tab 1 with your finger or mouse. That opens the first discovery. Step 2. Read the little story at the top of the tab, and look at the picture or model with it. Say what you see out loud. This part is not a test — it is just looking. I expect you to look for at least a few seconds before you answer. Step 3. Now read the discovery question. Read it twice. Ask yourself: what is it really asking? For days, it helps to say the days out loud from Monday. For clocks, always ask first, where is the long hand? Step 4. Type your idea in the box. Use a word or a few words, not just a number guess. Then press Check my idea. Step 5. If it says Look again, do not worry. Mistakes are how we learn. Press Hint, read it slowly, then change your answer and press Check my idea one more time. Step 6. When it says Exactly!, the tab gets a little tick. Well done! That tick means that discovery is finished. Step 7. Press tab 2 and do the same thing: read, look, think, type, press Check my idea. Then do tabs 3, 4, 5 and 6 the same way, one at a time. I expect all six tabs to have a tick. Step 8. Now scroll down under the page. There is a deck of slides with the same discoveries, one on each slide. Press Start on the first slide. Step 9. On each slide, use the same buttons as before: type your idea, press Check my idea, press Hint if you need help. Step 10. When a slide is done, press the arrow on the right to go to the next slide.
