Look at the little dots under the slide. They show you where you are and how many are left. Step 11. On the last slide, press the finish button. That tells the page you are done. I cannot tick it for you — you press it yourself. How will you know the page is finished? Every one of the six tabs has a tick, and you have pressed the finish button on the last slide. Ready to start? Press tab 1, then tell me what you see. 😊

visuals.label: Visual Models
visuals.text:
Hello! Let's get started together. 😊

This page is called Visual Models. It has 5 pictures that show the big ideas of our unit, Time. Some of them move — you can turn them and press their buttons. We do this so you can SEE time, not just hear about it. By the end, you will know the days of the week, the parts of a day, and the two hands on a clock. What I expect from you: look slowly at each model, touch it and try its buttons, and say the words out loud. There are 7 steps. Take your time — there's no rush. 1. Find the first model, The Days of the Week. Look at the seven days in a line. Point at each one with your finger and say it out loud: Monday, Tuesday, Wednesday, Thursday, Friday, Saturday, Sunday. If the model moves, drag it or press its buttons to see the days change. A good job here is saying all seven days in the right order without stopping. 2. Now go to the second model, Parts of the Day — Morning, Afternoon, Evening. Look at the three parts. Press any buttons on it to see the pictures change. For each part, tell me one thing YOU do then — like breakfast in the morning. I expect three little answers from you: one for morning, one for afternoon, one for evening. 3. Next is the third model, Meeting the Clock — the Two Hands. Look at the round clock face and the numbers 1 to 12. Find the short hand and the long hand. If you can drag the hands, drag them round slowly and watch them move. Say it out loud with me: short hand is the hour hand, long hand is the minute hand. 4. Now the fourth model, Reading O'clock Times. Press its buttons or drag the short hand to make different times. Watch carefully: the long hand stays on 12 every time. Read three times out loud, like "3 o'clock". I expect you to notice that only the short hand moves. 5. Then the fifth model, Reading Half Past Times. Move the long hand down to the 6. Look at where the short hand sits — it is between two numbers. We say the smaller number, so "half past 7", not "half past 8". Try two half past times out loud. 6. Under every model there is a caption — that is the little bit of writing that tells you about the picture. Read it, then press Listen to hear it read to you. Do this for all 5 models, one by one. Listening and reading together helps the words stick in your memory. 7. Last step! When you have looked at all 5 models and pressed Listen on each caption, press the button at the bottom that says I explored the models. Only press it when you have really done them all — that button is your work being saved, and only you can press it. You will know the page is finished when you have seen all 5 models, heard all 5 captions, and pressed I explored the models at the bottom. Ready? Start with step 1 and tell me when the days of the week are done. 🌟

method.label: Learn the Method
method.text: Hello! Today I am your teacher, and this page is called Learn the Method. A method is a way to do something step by step, like a little recipe. This page has 6 methods about time. They show you how to put the days of the week in order, how to use today, tomorrow and yesterday, how to sort morning, afternoon and evening, how to sort school days and weekend days, how to name the parts of a clock, and how to tell the short hour hand from the long minute hand. We do this so time stops feeling tricky. By the end, you will know the steps to work out a day or a time all by yourself. You need your eyes, your voice, and your finger for pressing. A grown-up can sit with you. What I expect from you is this: say every step out loud, do not rush, and finish all 6 methods. Here are your steps. Step 1: Look at the first method at the top of the page. Read the first step, or ask your grown-up to read it with you. Say it out loud in your own voice. Good work looks like this: your mouth moves, not just your eyes. Step 2: Now press the button that says Show me the next step. A new step will come. Say that one out loud too. Take your time — there is no rush. Step 3: Keep pressing Show me the next step until you see the words Method complete. That tells you this method is finished. Before you move on, try to say the whole method back in your own words. That is how it sticks in your head. Step 4: Now do the very same thing for the next method. Read step one, press Show me the next step, keep going to Method complete. Do this for all 6 methods, one after the other. Do not skip one, even if it looks easy. Step 5: Now scroll down to the bottom of the page. There is a deck of slides there. The same 6 methods are here again, one method on each slide. This is your practice. Step 6: On the first slide, press Start. Then use the same buttons as before to move through the steps, right to the end of that slide. Say each step out loud again. Step 7: Press the arrow on the right side to go to the next slide. Look at the little dots under the slide — they show you where you are. More dots to go means more slides to do. Step 8: Keep going slide by slide. On the last slide, press the finish button. Well done — that is the end. How will you know the page is finished? Every method at the top must say Method complete, and you must have pressed the finish button on the last slide. Then you are done! Now go and do Step 1. Come back and tell me the first method you finished, and I will check it with you. 🙂

guided.label: Guided Practice
guided.text: Hello! Today we are doing Guided Practice for our Time unit. That means you get to try questions all by yourself, with me right here to help. We are doing this so the days of the week, the parts of the day, and the clock hands all become easy for you. By the end, you will be able to say the days in order and read o'clock and half past times. You will need a pencil, some paper, and your thinking brain. Take your time — mathematicians think slowly on purpose. Here is what to do, step by step. 1. Read the first question carefully. Read it twice, slowly. Then work it out on paper or in your head. For days questions, say the days out loud from Monday. For clock questions, always ask yourself first: where is the long hand? On 12 means o'clock. On 6 means half past. I expect you to think first, before you type. 2. Type your answer in the box, then press Check my answer. Write it neatly, like "Thursday" or "4 o'clock". If you feel stuck, press Give me a hint. You can get up to three hints, one at a time — try again after each one. If you are still stuck, press Show next step and it will show you one line of the working. I expect you to try a hint before you look at the next step. That is how your brain grows. 3. Do this for every one of the 12 questions, until each one shows as right. If an answer is wrong, do not worry — mistakes are how we learn. Read the question again, use a hint, and try once more. The page is done when all 12 questions are correct. 4. Now look under the page. There is a deck of slides with the same questions, one question on each slide. On the first slide, press Start. Answer that slide the same way as before, using Check my answer, Give me a hint, and Show next step. 5. When a slide is right, press the arrow on the right side to go to the next slide. Look at the little dots under the slide — they show you where you are and how many are left. Keep going, one slide at a time. I expect you to answer every slide, not skip any. 6. On the last slide, press the finish button. That tells the page you have finished all your work. You will know the page is finished when all 12 questions are correct and you have pressed the finish button on the last slide. Ready? Start with question one, and tell me your answer. I am right here with you. 🙂

examples.label: Worked Examples
examples.text: Hello! Today we are working on the Worked Examples page for Unit 8: Time. A worked example is a question with the answer already worked out, step by step. We look at these to see HOW a good thinker gets to the answer, not just what the answer is. By the end, you will be better at days of the week, parts of the day, and reading o'clock and half past times. You will need your eyes, your thinking, and a grown-up nearby if you want help reading. Here we go. 1. Look at the first worked example. Read the question out loud, slowly. Do not press anything yet. I want you to try it in your own head first. Say your answer out loud, even if you are not sure. Guessing bravely is allowed here — this page is for learning, not for marks. 2. Now press Show worked solution. Read the solution line by line, from the top. Compare it with what you said. Ask yourself: did I think the same way? If you did — brilliant! If you did not, that is fine. Mistakes are how we learn. 3. Do the very same thing for every worked example on the page. There are 12 of them. Read, think, say your answer, then press Show worked solution and check. Take your time — there's no rush. 4. Look at the counter at the top of the page. It counts how many examples you have opened. Keep going until every single one is opened. When the counter shows all 12, this part of the page is done. 5. Now scroll down under the page. There is a deck of slides with the same examples, one on each slide. On the first slide, press Start. 6. On each slide, do the same job as before: read the question, think of your answer, then press the button to see the worked solution. Say your answer before you look. That is the important part! 7. To move on, press the arrow on the right side of the slide. Look at the little dots under the slide — they show you where you are in the deck. More dots filled means you are getting closer to the end. 8. On the last slide, press the finish button. That tells the page you have been all the way through. You will know the page is finished when the counter at the top shows every example opened, and you have pressed the finish button on the last slide. Ready? Start with worked example number one, and tell me your answer before you press Show worked solution. I'll be right here.

activities.label: Activities
activities.text:
Hello! Today I am your teacher, and this page is our doing page. We have been learning about time — the days of the week, the parts of the day, and the two hands on a clock. On this page you do not just read about time. You make something, you talk about it, and you write one small answer. By the end you will be able to show what you know about time with your own hands and your own words. Get a pencil, some paper, and something from home you can use — like a paper plate, a bottle cap, or some small cards. Here are all the steps. Do them one at a time, slowly. Mathematicians think slowly on purpose. 1. Find the activity and listen to it. There is 1 hands-on activity on this page. Read the box that says what to use and what to do. Then press Listen so you can hear it read out loud. Listening and reading together helps the words stick. What I expect: you know what you need before you start. Go and get those things — paper, a pencil, and any household objects it names. 2. Choose your time idea. The activity asks you to pick one idea from our unit. You could pick the days of the week, or the parts of the day, or a clock. Pick the one you like best. What I expect: you can say your idea out loud in one sentence, like "I choose the clock."

3. Build or draw your model. Now make it! If you chose the clock, draw a round face, write the numbers 1 to 12 around the edge, and add a short hour hand and a long minute hand. If you chose the days of the week, make seven cards and lay them in order from Monday to Sunday. What I expect: your work is neat enough for someone else to understand, and the short hand really is shorter than the long hand. 4. Explain your model to a family member. Show your work to a grown-up or a brother or sister. Tell them what each part is. For a clock, say "This is the face, these are the numbers, this short hand is the hour hand and this long hand is the minute hand." What I expect: you use the real words — face, numbers, hour hand, minute hand, or the day names in the right order. 5. Write one question of your own, and solve it. Think of a small time question, like "The long hand is on 12 and the short hand is on 4 — what time is it?" or "What day comes after Tuesday?" Write it on your paper. Then write your own answer under it. What I expect: your question is about time, and your answer matches your model. 6. Write in the box on the page. Under the activity there is a box for your answer. Type what you made and what you noticed. One or two sentences is plenty, like "I made a clock. I noticed the short hand is the hour hand." What I expect: your own words, not copied words. 7. Press Mark complete. When you have really done the activity and written in the box, press Mark complete under that activity. Only press it when the work is done — that button is your promise that you did it. What I expect: honest work first, then the button. 8. Press Finish activities at the bottom. When every activity has Mark complete pressed, scroll to the bottom of the page and press Finish activities. This saves the record that you did your work. What I expect: nothing left unmarked before you press it. 9. Now the slides at the bottom. Under the page there is a deck of slides. Each slide has the same hands-on activity, one per slide. Press Start on the first slide to begin. What I expect: you look at the slide and read it before you touch anything else. 10. Work through the slides. Use the same buttons on each slide as you did above — do the activity, write in the box, then Mark complete. When a slide is done, press the arrow on the right to go to the next slide. Look at the little dots under the slide — they show you where you are and how many are left. What I expect: you finish one slide properly before you move on. 11. Finish the last slide. On the last slide, press Finish activities. That is the end of the deck. What I expect: you do not skip a slide just to get to the end. How will you know the page is finished? Every activity will show Mark complete pressed, you will have pressed Finish activities at the bottom of the page, and you will have pressed Finish activities on the last slide too. When all three are done, you are finished. Take your time — there's no rush. Come back and tell me which idea you chose, and I will help you build it. 🙂

fluency.label: Math Fluency
fluency.text:
Hello! Today I am your teacher for the Math Fluency page. 🌟

Fluency means "quick and sure". This page gives you 12 quick questions about time. You already know these things from Unit 8: the days of the week, morning, afternoon and evening, the two clock hands, o'clock and half past. The sprint helps those answers come fast, like knowing your own name. What I expect from you: answer each question by yourself, in your own words. Try to be quick, but being right matters more than being fast. If a question is tricky, take a breath and say the days in order, or ask yourself "where is the long hand?"

Here are the steps. Step 1. Look at the top of the page. You will see a timer. It counts your time while you work. Do not worry about it. It is just there to cheer you on, not to scare you. Step 2. Read question one carefully. Read it twice. Then type your answer in the box. Write it simply, like "Saturday" or "3 o'clock" or "the short hand". Step 3. Press Check & continue. The page will tell you if you got it right, and then bring the next question. Do this for every question, one at a time, until all 12 are done. Step 4. If an answer is not right, that is fine. Mistakes are how we learn. Read the little note the page gives you, then keep going to the next question. Step 5. Here is my hint for clock questions. Look at the long hand first. Long hand on 12 means o'clock. Long hand on 6 means half past. Then read the short hand for the hour. Step 6. Here is my hint for day questions. Say the days out loud in order: Monday, Tuesday, Wednesday, Thursday, Friday, Saturday, Sunday. Stop at the day you need. "After" means the next one. "Before" means the one just gone. Step 7. When all 12 are done, the page shows your score. You need most of them right to pass the sprint. Look and see how many you got. Step 8. If you did not get enough right, press Run the sprint again. Trying again is not failing. It is practising, and practice is how fast answers are made. Step 9. Do the questions again the same careful way, one at a time, pressing Check & continue each time. You will know the page is finished when one sprint has enough right answers and the page tells you so. That is it — you are done! Now go and start question one. Take your time — there's no rush. Come back and tell me how you did! 😊

games.label: Games
games.text:
Hello! Today I am your teacher for the Games page in our Time unit. 🌟

These games are quick, fun quizzes about everything we learned: the days of the week, morning and afternoon and evening, and reading a clock. We play them so the answers become fast and easy in your head. By the end, you will be able to say the days in order and read o'clock and half past times without stopping to think. All you need is your finger to tap, and your thinking brain. There are three steps. Step 1: Pick one game and press Start game. Then read each round and choose your answer. You get one star for every round you get right, so take your time and read the whole question before you tap. If a round is tricky, whisper the days in order, or ask yourself: where is the long hand? On 12 it is o'clock, on 6 it is half past. I expect you to try every round yourself, even the hard ones. Mistakes are how we learn. Step 2: When the game ends, press Play again to earn more stars. Playing again is not a punishment — it is practice, like kicking a ball again and again. Each time, try to answer a little faster and get more rounds right. A game is mastered when it has all its stars. I expect you to keep pressing Play again on that game until all its stars are filled. Step 3: Now do the same for every game on the page. Go one game at a time, from the top: press Start game, answer the rounds, then press Play again until that game has all its stars. Do not jump around — finish one, then move to the next. I expect you to keep going gently, and to stop for a rest if your brain feels tired. Take your time — there's no rush. You will know the page is finished when every game shows all its stars. The page finishes by itself then — you do not need to press anything extra. Ready? Press Start game on the first one, then come back and tell me how many stars you got. 😊

problems.label: Solve Real Problems
problems.text: Hello! Today we are doing "Solve Real Problems." These are little stories about real life — a market day, a jar of stones, a trip in the morning. Your job is to use what you know about days of the week and parts of the day to work each one out. We do this because time words are not just for the page — you use them at home every day. By the end, you will be able to say which day comes next and which part of the day something happens in, all by yourself. You need your eyes, your thinking brain, and maybe a finger to count the days. There are four things to do. Here they all are. 1. There are 6 story problems on the page. Read the first one slowly. Read it twice — once to hear the story, once to find the question. Ask yourself: "What is this asking me?" Sometimes it asks a day. Sometimes it asks morning, afternoon or evening. Sometimes it asks how many. I expect you to know what the question wants before you answer. 2. Now work it out in your head, or count on your fingers. A good trick is to say the days out loud in order: Monday, Tuesday, Wednesday, Thursday, Friday, Saturday, Sunday. Then type your answer in the box, and write a few words about how you got it. Then press Check answer. If your brain feels stuck, press Hint — that is not cheating, that is being smart. I expect your own thinking in the box, not just one word. 3. When the page tells you your answer is right, that problem is done. Give yourself a little smile, then move on to the next story. Do all 6 the same way: read, think, type, press Check answer. If one is not right, do not worry. Mistakes are how we learn. Read the story again and try once more. 4. Under the page there is a deck of slides. It has the same problems, one story on each slide. Press Start on the first slide. Answer it just like before, using the same buttons. Then press the arrow on the right to go to the next slide. Look at the little dots under the slide — they show you where you are. Keep going, one slide at a time. On the last slide, press the finish button. You will know the page is finished when all 6 problems show as right, and you have pressed the finish button on the last slide. Then it is all done! Ready? Read problem number one and tell me what you think it is asking. Take your time — there's no rush.

explain.label: Explain Your Thinking
explain.text:
Hello! I am so glad you are here. Today I am your teacher for the "Explain Your Thinking" page in our Time unit. Here is what this page is. There are 6 questions. Each one asks you to say HOW you know your answer, not just the answer. We do this because a good mathematician can say why. Saying why makes the idea stick in your head. By the end, you will be able to explain days of the week and clock times in your own words. What I expect from you: full sentences, using our time words like week, before, after, today, tomorrow, yesterday, hour hand, minute hand, o'clock and half past. Ask your grown-up to help you type if writing is tricky. Take your time. Mathematicians think slowly on purpose. There are 8 steps. Here they all are. 1. Look at the first prompt on the page. Read it slowly, twice. Under the prompt you will see the key ideas. Those are the words I want to hear in your answer. Point at each one with your finger and say it out loud. 2. Before you write, say your answer out loud to yourself or your grown-up. Something like, "Tomorrow is Monday, because Monday always comes after Sunday." Talking first makes writing much easier. 3. Now write your explanation in the box. Try to say three things: what you know, what rule you used, and why your answer makes sense. A good answer sounds like this: "I say the days in order. Monday, Tuesday, Wednesday. So the day after Tuesday is Wednesday."

4. Press the button that says Check mathematical ideas. This checks if you used the key ideas. If it asks for more, do not worry. That is normal. Just add one more sentence with a key idea in it, then press Check mathematical ideas again. 5. Now press Show model explanation. This shows a good answer so you can compare. Look for one thing they said that you did not say. That is your learning for that question. You do not have to copy it word for word. 6. Do steps 1 to 5 again for all 6 prompts. One prompt at a time, please. Some are about days of the week. Some are about o'clock and half past. Remember our clock rule: long hand on 12 means o'clock, long hand on 6 means half past. 7. Now look under the page. There is a deck of slides with the same prompts, one slide each. On the first slide, press Start. Then use the same buttons you already know on every slide. To move on, press the arrow on the right side. The little dots under the slide show you which one you are on. 8. Keep going slide by slide until the last one. On the last slide, press the finish button. Well done, that is the whole page. You will know the page is finished when all 6 explanations use the key ideas, and you have pressed the finish button on the last slide. Ready? Tell me when you have read the first prompt, and tell me what the key ideas under it say. 😊

challenge.label: Unit Challenge
challenge.text:
Welcome to your Unit Challenge! This is the last part of our Time unit. It is 12 questions about everything we learned. Days of the week. Today, tomorrow and yesterday. Morning, afternoon and evening. The two clock hands. O'clock times and half past times. We do this so you can show what you know. It is not scary. It is like a game that says, "Look how much you learned!"

Here is what I expect from you: read each question twice, think slowly, then pick your answer. Mathematicians think slowly on purpose. And this one is important — the answers must come from you. I will help you think, but I will not tell you which one to click. You will need your thinking brain, and maybe your fingers for counting days. Let's go! Step 1. Read question one carefully. Read it twice. Then look at all four choices before you pick one. Do not grab the first one you see! Click the answer you think is right, then press Next question. Do this for all 12 questions, one at a time. Step 2. While you work, use your helpers. For a day question, say the days out loud in order: Monday, Tuesday, Wednesday, Thursday, Friday, Saturday, Sunday. For a clock question, ask yourself one thing first: where is the long hand? On 12 means o'clock. On 6 means half past. Then the short hand tells you the hour. Step 3. If a question feels hard, take a breath. Take your time — there's no rush. You can tell me "I'm stuck on this one" and I will give you a small hint or a similar question to practise. I will never tell you the answer, because I want you to feel proud when you get it yourself. Step 4. Keep pressing Next question until you finish all 12. Try to answer every single one. Even a careful guess is better than an empty box. Step 5. At the end, your score appears on the screen. Look at it together with your grown-up. You pass when more than half are right. That means 7 or more out of 12. Step 6. If your score is not high enough, that is okay — mistakes are how we learn. Press Try again and go through the questions once more. This time, go slower on the ones that felt tricky. You can chat with me first and we will practise those parts together. Step 7. When your score is good enough, press Continue. That saves your work and moves you on. You will know the page is finished when you have pressed Continue after a passing score. Then come back and tell me your score — I would love to hear how you did! 🌟

overview.label: Unit Overview
overview.text:
Hello! I am your teacher today. 🙂

This page is called the Unit Overview. It is like looking at a map before a trip. It tells you what Unit 9, "Numbers to 20", is all about. We do this so you know what is coming and feel ready. By the end of this page, you will be able to say what you are going to learn. You need your eyes, your ears, and your voice. A grown-up can sit with you if you like. There are 3 steps. Here they all are. Step 1: Read the Unit Overview. Look at the words at the top of the page. If you see a little speaker picture, press Listen and hear the words read to you. Follow along with your finger while you listen. I expect you to listen all the way to the end, and to notice the big idea: this unit is about counting all the way to 20. If a word feels hard, that is okay — just tell me and we will look at it together. Step 2: Say in your own words what you think you will learn. Do not copy the words on the screen. Say it your own way, out loud, to me or to your grown-up. A good answer sounds like this: "I will count to 20, and I will learn the teen numbers like thirteen and fourteen." One or two sentences is plenty. I expect you to try, even if it is not perfect — trying is the whole job here. Step 3: Press Continue to go to The Lesson. When you have listened and said your idea out loud, find the Continue button and press it. That takes you to the next part, called The Lesson. I expect you to press it only after Step 1 and Step 2, so you are ready. You will know this page is finished when you have listened to the overview, said in your own words what you will learn, and pressed Continue. That is it! Let's start with Step 1. Press Listen, then tell me one thing you heard. Take your time — there's no rush.

lesson.label: The Lesson
lesson.text: Hello! Today we are learning Numbers to 20. This page is called The Lesson. It has seven small ideas about counting past ten, teen numbers, writing numbers, comparing, estimating and patterns. By the end you will be able to count to 20 and say that a teen number is one ten and some ones. You need your eyes, your voice, and a few small things to count, like buttons, stones or dates. Let's start! Step 1. Read the first concept slowly. It is a short story about numbers with an example. Then press Listen and hear it read to you. Read with your finger under the words if that helps. I expect you to read it, listen to it, and be able to tell me one thing you learned. Do this for each concept, one at a time. Step 2. Now say the example out loud. Use your own voice, nice and clear. Then try it with real things. For example, put ten buttons in a line, add four more, and count: ten, eleven, twelve, thirteen, fourteen. I expect you to touch each thing as you count, and to say the number name out loud, not just in your head. Step 3. Keep going until you have read all seven concepts. Do not rush — mathematicians think slowly on purpose. When every concept is read, listened to, and tried out loud, press the button at the bottom that says I studied the concepts. I expect you to press it only after all seven are done, honestly. Step 4. Now look under the page. There is a deck of slides. Each slide has one of the same concepts. Press Start on the first slide. Do the same on each slide: read it, listen, say the example out loud. Then press the arrow on the right to move to the next slide. The little dots under the slide show you how far you have come. Step 5. Keep pressing the arrow until you reach the last slide. On the last slide, press the finish button. I expect you to visit every slide, not skip any. If a slide feels hard, stay there a little longer and try it with your buttons or stones. You will know the page is finished when you have pressed I studied the concepts, and you have pressed the finish button on the last slide. Then come back and tell me one number word you can now say all by yourself. Take your time — there's no rush. 🙂

explore.label: Explore the Concept
explore.text: Hello! Today I am your teacher, and this page is called Explore the Concept. Here is what it is. This page has 6 little discoveries about numbers to 20. Each one shows you a picture or a model, then asks you one question. We do it so you can find the answer yourself, not just be told. By the end you will be able to count to 20, say the teen numbers, and tell which number is greater. You need your eyes, your thinking brain, and a grown-up nearby if you want help typing. What I expect from you: think first, then type your own idea. A short answer is fine. Guessing fast is not our way — mathematicians think slowly on purpose. Here are the steps. 1. Look at the numbered tabs at the top: 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6. Press tab 1. Read the little story, and look hard at the picture or model. I expect you to look before you answer. Ask yourself: what do I see? How many? 2. Now read the discovery question under the picture. Say it out loud if that helps. Then think of your answer in your head. A good answer is short, like a number or one word. 3. Type your idea in the box. Then press Check my idea. I expect your own idea, even if you are not sure. A brave try is a good try. 4. If it says Look again, do not worry. Mistakes are how we learn. Press Hint, read it slowly, then change your answer and press Check my idea one more time. 5. When it says Exactly!, that tab gets a tick. Well done! Say the answer out loud once more so your brain remembers it. 6. Now press tab 2 and do the same three things: look, think, type, then Check my idea. Keep going like this for tab 3, tab 4, tab 5 and tab 6. I expect every tab to have a tick at the end. 7. Now go under the page. There is a deck of slides. They show the same discoveries, one on each slide. Press Start on the first slide. 8. On each slide, use the same buttons as before: type your idea, press Check my idea, and press Hint if you need a little help. Take your time — there is no rush. 9. When a slide is done, press the arrow on the right to go to the next slide. Look at the little dots under the slide. They show you where you are and how many are left. 10. On the last slide, press the finish button. That tells the page you have done them all. How will you know the page is finished? All 6 tabs have a tick, and you have pressed the finish button on the last slide. That is your finish line. Ready? Press tab 1 and tell me what you see in the picture.

words.label: Math Words & Symbols
words.text: Hello! Today I am your teacher for the Math Words & Symbols page. This page teaches you the special maths words in Unit 9, like teen numbers, ten, ones, greater than and estimate. We learn them because words are our maths tools. When you know the words, you can say what you are thinking, and you can understand every question in this unit. By the end, you will be able to say each word, say what it means in your own words, and use it in a sentence. What you need: your eyes, your voice, and your fingers for typing. What I expect from you: say the words out loud, not just in your head. Do every word, not only the easy ones. Take your time — mathematicians think slowly on purpose. There are 4 steps. Here they are. Step 1: Read each word and its meaning, then press Listen. Start at the top word. Read the word, then read what it means. Then press Listen and hear how it sounds. Listen twice if you like. I expect you to look at the word while you listen, so your eyes and ears learn it together. Step 2: Say the word out loud, then say the meaning in your own words, then type a sentence and press Check sentence. First say the word loudly and clearly. Next, say the meaning in YOUR words — not the same words on the screen. For example, for "ten" you might say, "ten is when I fill a whole ten-frame." Then type one short sentence using the word, like "Fifteen is a teen number." Press Check sentence, and read what the checker says to you. If it asks you to try again, that is fine — mistakes are how we learn. Do this for every word on the page. Step 3: Press I know these words and symbols at the bottom. Only press it when you have done every single word. Before you press, check yourself: can you say each word and what it means without looking? If one word feels wobbly, go back and do it again first. I expect honesty here — this button tells your teacher what you really know. Step 4: Do the slides under the page. Under the page there is a deck of slides. Each slide has one word. Press Start on the first slide. Then use the same buttons as before: Listen, say it out loud, and type your sentence with Check sentence. When that slide is done, press the arrow on the right to go to the next slide. The little dots under the slide show you where you are. Keep going, one slide at a time, until the last slide. On the last slide, press the finish button. How will you know the page is finished? You will have pressed Listen and Check sentence on every word, you will have pressed I know these words and symbols, and you will have pressed the finish button on the last slide. When all the dots are behind you, you are done! Now go and start with Step 1. Tell me when the first word is done, and tell me the sentence you made. I will be right here. 😊

method.label: Learn the Method
method.text: Hello! Today I am your teacher, and this page is called Learn the Method. A method is a way to work something out, step by step. On this page there are 6 methods for Numbers to 20. They show you how to count to 20, how to say the teen names, how to write the numbers, how to show a teen number as one ten and some ones, how to use place value cards, and how to compare two amounts. We do this so the steps get easy and you can do them on your own. What I expect from you: say every step out loud, take your time, and do not rush to the end. If you have counters, beans, buttons or stones nearby, keep them close so you can try a step with your hands. Take your time — there's no rush. Step 1. Look at the first method at the top of the page. Read its first step, or ask your grown-up to read it with you. Then say it out loud in your own voice. I expect to hear your voice saying the step, not just your eyes looking at it. Step 2. Now press the button that says Show me the next step. A new step will appear. Read this one out loud too. Good work means you say the numbers slowly and clearly, like eleven, twelve, thirteen. Step 3. Keep pressing Show me the next step again and again. Stop when the page says Method complete. That means you have seen the whole method from start to end. Well done — that is one method finished! Step 4. Now do the same for the next method. Read the first step out loud, then press Show me the next step until it says Method complete. Do this for every method, all 6 of them. Try to do the little action too, like filling a ten-frame with 10 things and adding a few more. Step 5. Now look under the page. There is a deck of slides. It has the same 6 methods, but one method on each slide. This is your practice round. Step 6. On the first slide, press Start. Then use the same buttons as before to move through the steps, and say each step out loud. When that slide is done, press the arrow on the right side to go to the next slide. Step 7. Look at the little dots under the slide. The dots show you where you are. More dots to the right means more slides still to do. Keep going, one slide at a time, saying each step out loud. Step 8. On the last slide, press the finish button. That is the end of the slides. Only you can press these buttons, so make sure you press them yourself — that is how the page saves your work. How you will know the page is finished: every one of the 6 methods says Method complete, and you have pressed the finish button on the last slide. Ready to begin? Start with the very first method, and tell me when it says Method complete. 🙂

examples.label: Worked Examples
examples.text:
Hello! Today I am your teacher, and this page is called Worked Examples. Here is what it is. A worked example is a maths question with all the thinking written out for you. You try it first. Then you look at how it was done. This helps you learn the way to think, not just the answer. All of them are about our numbers to 20. What I expect from you: try every question yourself BEFORE you look at the solution. Say your answer out loud or write it on paper. A grown-up can sit with you. Take your time — mathematicians think slowly on purpose. You will need a pencil and paper. There are 4 steps. Here they all are. Step 1: Look at the first worked example. Read the question. Then work it out yourself on your paper. Say each number out loud as you count. I expect to see a real try — even a wobbly try is a good try. Do not peek yet! Step 2: Now press Show worked solution. Read it slowly, line by line, next to your own work. Ask yourself: did I do the same steps? If your answer is different, that is fine. Mistakes are how we learn. Find the one line where yours went a different way. Step 3: Do the same for every question on the page. There are 12 of them. Read, try, then press Show worked solution and compare. Look at the counter at the top — it counts how many you have opened. Keep going until every single one is open. Take a little stretch break in the middle if you need one. Step 4: Now go under the page to the deck of slides. They show the same examples, one on each slide. Press Start on the first slide. Do the same thing here: try it, then press the button to see the solution. Press the arrow on the right to move to the next slide. The little dots under the slide show you where you are. On the last slide, press the finish button. How will you know the page is finished? Two things. The counter at the top shows all 12 opened, and you have pressed the finish button on the last slide. Then you are done! 🌟

Ready? Start with worked example number one, and tell me your answer when you have tried it.

visuals.label: Visual Models
visuals.text: Hello! Today I am your teacher for the Visual Models page. Visual models are pictures that show numbers. On this page you will see six of them. They help you SEE what "one ten and some ones" really looks like. By the end, teen numbers will feel much easier. You need your eyes, your voice, and a finger to press and drag. Ready? Here are your steps. 1. Look at model one, Counting on to 20. This one shows counting past ten: eleven, twelve, thirteen, all the way to twenty. If it moves, drag it slowly with your finger to turn it. Press any buttons on it to make it change. I want you to say the numbers out loud as you look. Take your time — there's no rush. 2. Look at model two, Teen Numbers as One Ten and Some Ones. This is the most important one. Look for the frame that is completely full — that full frame is one ten. Then count the extra ones next to it. Say it like this: "Fourteen is one ten and four ones." I expect you to say that sentence out loud at least once. 3. Look at model three, Saying, Reading and Writing Number Words to 20. This one shows the number words. Say each word slowly: thir-teen, four-teen, fif-teen. Listen for the "-teen" at the end. It means "and ten". I want you to notice that eleven and twelve are special — they have no "-teen". 4. Look at model four, Comparing and Ordering Numbers to 20. Find the number line. The number further along the line is the greater one. Point to two numbers and say, "This one is greater. This one is less." Good work if you can say both sentences. 5. Look at model five, Estimating Then Counting. Look at the group of things for just a moment, then guess. Say "about ten" or "about fifteen". Then count them one by one to check. A close guess is a good guess, even if it is not exact. 6. Look at model six, Number Patterns — Twos, Tens, Odd and Even. Try counting in twos: two, four, six, eight, ten. Then think about pairs. If everything has a partner, the number is even. If one is left over alone, it is odd. 7. Now read the caption under each model. The caption is the little bit of writing below the picture. Press Listen to hear it read to you. Do this for all six, one at a time. Listening and reading together helps the words stick. 8. When you have looked at all six models and heard all six captions, press the button at the bottom that says I explored the models. You will know the page is finished when you have pressed I explored the models. That button saves your work, so it must be you who presses it, not me. Shall we begin with step one? Tell me when you have looked at model one. 😊

guided.label: Guided Practice
guided.text: Hello! I am your teacher today, and this is our Guided Practice page for Unit 9, Numbers to 20. Here we practise what we have learned: counting to 20, teen numbers like fourteen and seventeen, one ten and some ones, comparing numbers, and estimating. Practice is how the numbers get stuck in your head. By the end you will be able to count and write numbers to 20 all by yourself. You need a pencil, some paper, and something small to count with — beans, buttons or stones. Take your time. Mathematicians think slowly on purpose. Here are the steps. 1. Look at the first question on the page. Read it, or ask your grown-up to read it with you. Now work it out on your paper or in your head. You can draw dots, or move your counters, or count on your fingers. I expect you to try the question yourself first, before you type anything. 2. Type your answer in the box. Then press Check my answer. If you feel stuck, press Give me a hint — you can get up to three hints. If you are still stuck, press Show next step, and it shows you one line of the working. Try the hint first, then the next step. That way your brain does the thinking, and the buttons only give you a little help. 3. Keep going like this for every question. There are twelve questions in all. If an answer is not right, that is okay — mistakes are how we learn. Read the question again, use a hint, and try once more. I expect every question to end up right before you stop. Twelve green ticks means you did it. 4. Now look under the page. There is a deck of slides with the same questions, one question on each slide. Press Start on the first slide. Answer it the same way, using the same buttons: Check my answer, Give me a hint, Show next step. 5. When a slide is right, press the arrow on the right side to go to the next slide. The little dots under the slide show you where you are, like footprints. Keep going, one slide at a time, and answer them all. 6. On the last slide, press the finish button. That tells the page you are done. I cannot press it for you — you must press it yourself, because it saves your good work. You will know the page is finished when all twelve questions are right and you have pressed the finish button on the last slide. Ready? Start with question one, and tell me what it says. I will be right here with you.

games.label: Games
games.text:
Welcome to the Games page! This is where we play with numbers to 20. Games help you practise counting, teen numbers, and comparing. Playing is real learning — your brain gets faster each time. By the end, you will feel sure about numbers 11 to 20. You need your eyes, your thinking brain, and maybe some counters or your fingers to help you count. Take your time — there's no rush. Here are the steps. Step 1. Look at the games on your screen. Pick one you like. Press Start game. A question will pop up. Read it, think, then tap your answer. If you get it right, you earn a star! Keep going until the game ends. I expect you to think first, not tap fast. Count on your fingers if it helps. Mathematicians think slowly on purpose. Step 2. When the game finishes, press Play again. This gives you more chances to earn stars. A game is mastered when it has all its stars. If you got one wrong, that's okay — mistakes are how we learn. Read the little explanation, then try that question again next round. I expect you to play again until your game is full of stars. Step 3. Now do the same for every game on the page. Press Start game on the next one, answer the rounds, and press Play again until it is mastered too. I expect you to keep going, one game at a time, and not skip the tricky ones. The tricky ones are the ones teaching you the most! How will you know you are finished? The page finishes by itself when every game is mastered — when all the games have all their stars. You do not have to press anything special at the end. One last thing: if a question feels hard, come and tell me. I can give you a hint — but the answer has to come from you. 🌟

Ready? Press Start game on your first game and tell me how it goes!

activities.label: Activities
activities.text: Hello! Today we are doing the Activities page for Unit 9, Numbers to 20. An activity is a doing job, not a reading job. You will use real things you can touch, like buttons, stones or beans. Doing helps your hands and your eyes learn the numbers, not just your ears. By the end, you will be able to show a teen number, like 14, as one ten and some ones, and explain it to someone at home. Get these ready: paper, a pencil, and a small pile of little things you can count. A grown-up nearby can help you read the words. Here are the steps. Step 1. Look at the first activity box on the page. There is only one hands-on activity, so this is the one. Read it, then press Listen to hear it read out loud. Listen all the way to the end, then go and get the things it names. I expect you to come back with your paper, your pencil, and your counting things on the table. Step 2. Now do the activity. Pick one idea from this unit, like "14 is one ten and four ones". Make it with your things: put ten in one group, then four more beside it. Draw it on your paper too. Then say it out loud to someone in your family: "Fourteen is one ten and four ones." Take your time. There is no rush. Step 3. Write in the box on the page. Write your number, and what you noticed. A good answer says the number and both parts, like "16 is one ten and 6 ones." Even a short line is good, as long as it is your own. You can ask your grown-up to help you spell. Step 4. Press Mark complete under the activity. Only press it after you really did it and wrote in the box. That button tells the page you are done with that one. Step 5. When the activity is marked, press Finish activities at the bottom of the page. That finishes the top part. Step 6. Now look under the page. There is a deck of slides. Each slide has the same hands-on activity, one per slide. Press Start on the first slide. Step 7. On each slide, use the same buttons as before: Listen, then do it, then write in the box, then Mark complete. Do the doing part properly again, with your things. Practice is what makes it stick. Step 8. Press the arrow on the right to go to the next slide. Look at the little dots under the slide. They show you where you are, and how many are left. Step 9. On the last slide, press Finish activities. You will know the page is finished when every activity is marked complete and you have pressed Finish activities at the bottom. Now go and do Step 1. Tell me when you have your things, and we will keep going together. 🙂

fluency.label: Math Fluency
fluency.text: Hello! I am your teacher today, and this page is called Math Fluency. Fluency means quick and sure. It is like knowing your own name — you do not stop and think, you just know. On this page you will do a sprint. A sprint is 12 fast questions about numbers to 20: counting on, counting back, teen number names, one ten and some ones, and which number is greater. Why do we do it? Because when counting to 20 feels easy and fast, harder maths later feels easy too. You need a pencil and paper nearby, and your fingers are allowed to help! What I expect from you: try your best on every question, type a real answer even when you are not sure, and stay calm. Fast is nice, but right is better. Here are the steps. Step 1. Look at the top of the page. You will see your time counting. Do not worry about it. Take a breath and get ready. Step 2. Read the first question carefully. Read it twice. Ask yourself: does it want me to count forward, count back, or say a number name? Step 3. Work it out in your head or on your fingers. For counting on, start at the number given and say the next ones out loud, like ten, eleven, twelve. For "one ten and some ones", think of one full ten-frame, then count the extra ones. Step 4. Type your answer in the box. Type just the answer, like 17 or fourteen. Check you did not swap the digits — the 1 for the ten goes first, so fourteen is 14, not 41. Step 5. Press Check & continue. The page will tell you if you were right, and then give you the next question. Step 6. If it was right, smile and keep going. If it was wrong, read the little note it gives you. Mistakes are how we learn. Do not stop — the next question is waiting. Step 7. Do this same thing for all 12 questions: read, think, type, press Check & continue. One question at a time, all the way to the last one. Step 8. At the end you will see how many you got right. You need most of them right to finish the page. Step 9. If you got fewer than that, press Run the sprint again. This is good news, not bad news! You will practise the tricky ones and get faster. Come and tell me which ones were hard, and we will work on them together. Step 10. When a sprint has enough right answers, the page is finished. That is how you know you are done. Now off you go — start with question one, and tell me how it goes. Take your time — there's no rush.

problems.label: Solve Real Problems
problems.text:
Hello! Today we are doing the Solve Real Problems page together. 🌟

This page has 6 little story problems. Each story is about real life, like counting goats, mangoes, buttons or seats on a bus. We are doing them so you can use your counting to 20 in real places, not just on paper. By the end, you will be able to read a story, work out what it asks, and count on or back to find the answer. Get a pencil and paper next to you. You can also use your fingers, or 20 small things like beans or buttons. Take your time — mathematicians think slowly on purpose. Here are all the steps. 1. Read the first problem out loud, slowly. Then ask yourself one question: what is this story asking me to find? Sometimes it asks "what comes next?" and sometimes it asks "how do you say this number?" I expect you to read it twice before you start. Read the question twice before you answer. 2. Now work it out on your paper. If the story counts up, count on one number at a time. If the story counts down, count back one number at a time. You can touch each finger or each bean as you say the number. I expect you to say every number out loud, and not skip any. 3. Type your working and your answer in the box, then press Check answer. Working means showing how you got there, like "12, 13, 14". A good answer has both: how you counted, and the number you finished on. I expect your own thinking in that box, even if it is short. 4. If you feel stuck, press Hint. The hint gives you a little push, not the answer. Read it, then try again on your paper. Being stuck is normal — it means your brain is working. 5. When the page says your answer is right, that problem is done. Give yourself a little cheer! Then move down to the next problem and do steps 1 to 4 again. There are 6 problems in all, so you will do this 6 times. 6. If your answer is not right, do not worry. Mistakes are how we learn. Look again at where you started counting — many children start at the wrong number. Fix that one thing and press Check answer again. 7. Now look under the page. There is a deck of slides with the same problems, one problem on each slide. On the first slide, press Start. This is your practice round, so you can show what you learned. 8. On each slide, use the same buttons as before: work it out, type your answer, press Check answer, and press Hint only if you need it. I expect you to try first, before any hint. 9. To go to the next slide, press the arrow on the right. Look at the little dots under the slide — they show you which slide you are on and how many are left. 10. On the last slide, press the finish button. That tells the page you are all done with the slides. You will know the page is finished when all 6 problems say your answer is right, and you have pressed the finish button on the last slide. Ready? Read problem one out loud, then tell me what you think it is asking. I am right here with you.

explain.label: Explain Your Thinking
explain.text: Hello! I am your teacher for this page. Let's get ready. This page is called Explain Your Thinking. It asks you to say HOW you know an answer, not just the answer. Talking about your thinking makes your maths brain strong. You will need your voice, a grown-up to help you type, and maybe some stones or buttons to count. What I expect from you: a full sentence, not one word. Try to use our unit words, like teen numbers, ten, ones, and greater than. Take your time. Mistakes are how we learn. Step 1. Look at the first prompt on the page. Read it out loud, or ask your grown-up to read it to you. Under the prompt there are key ideas, like ten and ones. Those are the words I want to hear in your answer. Step 2. Say your answer out loud first, before you write. For example: "Seventeen is one ten and seven ones, because one full ten-frame is ten, and seven more counters makes seventeen." Saying it first makes writing much easier. Step 3. Now write your explanation in the box. Write what you know, what rule you used, and why your answer makes sense. Even one or two clear sentences is good work for Grade 1. Step 4. Press Check mathematical ideas. If the page asks for more, do not worry. Add one more sentence with a key idea in it, then press Check mathematical ideas again. Step 5. Press Show model explanation. This shows a good answer. Compare it with yours. Ask yourself: did I use the same maths words? You do not need the same words exactly. Your own words are welcome. Step 6. Do the same thing for all 6 prompts. Read, say it out loud, write, press Check mathematical ideas, then press Show model explanation. One prompt at a time, no rushing. Step 7. Now look under the page. There is a deck of slides with the same prompts, one prompt on each slide. Press Start on the first slide. Step 8. On each slide, use the same buttons as before: write your explanation, press Check mathematical ideas, then press Show model explanation. Then press the arrow on the right to go to the next slide. The little dots under the slide show you where you are. Step 9. On the last slide, press the finish button. That tells the page you are done. How you will know the page is finished: every one of the 6 explanations uses the key ideas, and you have pressed the finish button on the last slide. Ready to begin? Tell me the first prompt, and we will think it through together. 😊

challenge.label: Unit Challenge
challenge.text:
Hello! I am your teacher today, and this is your Unit Challenge for Unit 9: Numbers to 20. 🌟

This is the last part of the unit. It checks what you have learned: counting to 20, teen number names, one ten and some ones, comparing numbers, and estimating. You do not need to be perfect. You just need to try your best and think carefully. Get ready with a pencil and paper. You can draw dots or ten-frames to help you. Your fingers help too! Take your time — there's no rush. Here is what you will do, step by step. Step 1: Answer the 12 questions. There are 12 questions on this page. Read one question, then read it again. Ask yourself: what is it really asking? Then choose your answer and press Next question. Do this for every question, one at a time. Step 2: How to think about each question. For counting questions, say the numbers out loud in order. For "one ten and some ones", picture one full ten-frame, then count the extra ones. For "which is greater", think about the number line — the number further along is greater. For estimating, pick a sensible guess, not a wild one. I will help with hints if you get stuck, but the answers must come from you. Step 3: See your score at the end. When the last question is done, the page shows your score. You pass when more than half are right. Look at your score and tell me how you did — I would love to hear. Step 4: Press Try again if you need to. If your score is not high enough, that is okay. Mistakes are how we learn. Press Try again and go through the questions once more, slower this time. Tell me which ones felt hard, and we will practise those together first. Step 5: Press Continue. When your score is good enough, press Continue. That finishes the page. You will know the page is finished when you have answered all 12 questions, passed your score, and pressed Continue. Now, are you ready to start question one? Tell me when you have pressed into the first question. 😊

overview.label: Unit Overview
overview.text: Hello! Today we start Unit 10. It is all about 3D shapes — solid shapes you can hold, like a ball, a tin, and a box. This first page is our "look ahead" page. It tells us what we will learn. Doing this helps your brain get ready, like stretching before you run. You will need your eyes, your voice, and a grown-up nearby if you like. There are 3 steps. Here they are. Step 1. Read the Unit Overview. Look at the words at the top of the page that tell you what this unit is about. If you see a little speaker, press Listen and hear the words read out loud. Read slowly and point with your finger. I expect you to spot at least one shape name you know, like cube or ball. Step 2. Say what you think you will learn. Use your own words, out loud, to a grown-up or to me. You can start with, "In this unit I will learn about..." A good answer names solid shapes, or says something like "shapes that roll and shapes that stack". It does not have to be perfect — I just want your own thinking. Step 3. Press Continue. When you have read and talked, press the Continue button. That takes you to The Lesson, where we start learning properly. I expect you to press it yourself when you feel ready. You will know this page is finished when you have read the overview, said one sentence about what you will learn, and pressed Continue. Let's start with Step 1. Read the Unit Overview now, and press Listen if there is a speaker. Tell me when you are done. 🙂

words.label: Math Words & Symbols
words.text: Hello! Today I am your teacher for the Math Words & Symbols page. This page teaches you the special words of Unit 10, our 3D shapes unit. Words like cube, sphere, face and roll. Knowing these words helps you talk about shapes like a real mathematician. You will need your voice, your eyes, and your fingers for typing. Let's go, one step at a time. 1. Look at the first word on the page. Read the word, then read what it means. Take your time — there is no rush. I expect you to look at both parts: the word AND its meaning. 2. Press Listen. This makes the word say itself out loud. Listen carefully. I expect you to hear it at least once. Press Listen again if you want. 3. Now say the word out loud yourself. Say it with me, slowly. Speaking it helps your mouth remember it. 4. Now say the meaning in your own words. Do not copy the page word for word. For example, for cube you might say, "a box shape with six flat square sides, like a die." I expect your own words, even if they are simple. 5. Now type a sentence using the word, then press Check sentence. A good sentence shows you know the meaning. "My ball is a sphere" is good. "I like sphere" is not, because it does not show what a sphere is. Try to use something from your home in your sentence — a tin, a box, a ball. 6. Read what the checker says about your sentence. If it says to fix something, fix it and press Check sentence again. Mistakes are how we learn. 7. Do steps 1 to 6 again for every word on the page. Listen, say it, say the meaning, type a sentence, check it. I expect every word to get its turn — no skipping. 8. When every word is done, press I know these words and symbols at the bottom. Only press it when you truly have done them all. 9. Now look under the page. There is a deck of slides with the same words, one word on each slide. Press Start on the first slide. 10. On each slide, use the same buttons as before: Listen, say the word, say the meaning, type your sentence, press Check sentence. Try to make a different sentence this time. That is good practice for your brain. 11. Press the arrow on the right to go to the next slide. Look at the little dots under the slide — they show you how far you have come and how many are left. 12. On the last slide, press the finish button. That tells the page you have finished the whole deck. You will know the page is finished when you have pressed I know these words and symbols, and you have pressed the finish button on the last slide. Ready? Start with step 1 and tell me when you have read your first word. Which word is it?

lesson.label: The Lesson
lesson.text: Hello! Today we are learning about 3D shapes — solid shapes you can hold in your hand. This page is called The Lesson. It has 5 short ideas about shapes like the cube, the sphere and the cylinder. We do it so you can name these shapes and say what they do — roll or stack. By the end, you will be able to point around your room and name the solid shapes you see. What you need: a die or a small block, a ball, a tin, and a grown-up nearby to help. What I expect from you: read slowly, touch real objects, and say the shape names out loud. Here are your steps. Step 1. Read the 5 concepts, one at a time. On each one, press Listen and hear it read to you. Read along with the voice. Do not rush — mathematicians think slowly on purpose. A good job here means you can tell me one thing you learned from each concept. Step 2. Say the example out loud, then try it for real. If the concept talks about a cube, hold your die and count its flat faces: one, two, three, four, five, six. If it talks about a ball, push it and watch it roll. I expect you to touch a real object for every concept, not just look at the picture. Step 3. When you have read all 5 concepts, press the button that says I studied the concepts at the bottom. Only press it after you have really read them all. That button tells the page you have finished the reading part. Step 4. Now look under the page. There is a deck of slides with the same ideas, one idea on each slide. On the first slide, press Start. Step 5. On each slide, use the same buttons as before, then press the arrow on the right to go to the next slide. Look at the little dots under the slide — they show you where you are in the deck. Take your time on every slide. Step 6. On the last slide, press the finish button. That is the end of the deck. You will know the page is finished when you have pressed I studied the concepts and pressed the finish button on the last slide. Now go and start with concept one. When you have read it, come back and tell me one thing you learned. I'm right here! 😊

explore.label: Explore the Concept
explore.text: Hello! Today we are learning about 3D shapes — solid shapes you can hold, like a ball, a tin and a box. This page is called Explore the Concept. You will look at 6 little discoveries, think about them, and type your own idea for each one. By the end you will be able to name solid shapes and say why some roll and some stack. You will need a pencil, and if you can, a ball, a tin and a small box on the table next to you. Ready? Here are all the steps. Step 1. At the top of the page you will see numbered tabs, one for each of the 6 discoveries. Press tab 1 first. Read the little story on it, and look carefully at the picture or model. Take your time — there's no rush. I expect you to really look, not just click. Step 2. Now read the discovery question. Think first. If you have the real object near you, pick it up and feel it — that is the best way to find the answer. Then type your idea in the box in your own words. A good answer says the shape name and one reason, like "it is a ... because ...". Step 3. Press Check my idea. If it says Exactly!, well done — the tab gets a tick. If it says Look again, don't worry. Mistakes are how we learn. Press Hint, read it, then change your answer a little and try once more. Step 4. Press tab 2 and do the very same thing: read, look, think, type, press Check my idea. Then do tabs 3, 4, 5 and 6 the same way. One tab at a time, please — finish one before you open the next. Step 5. Keep going until all 6 tabs have a tick. That is what "done" looks like at the top of the page: six little ticks, and no question left empty. Step 6. Now scroll down under the page. There is a deck of slides there. It has the same discoveries, but one on each slide. Press Start on the first slide. Step 7. On each slide, use the same buttons as before: read it, type your idea, press Check my idea, and press Hint if you need help. Say your answer out loud too — that helps it stick in your head. Step 8. When a slide is done, press the arrow on the right to go to the next slide. Look at the little dots under the slide. They show you where you are and how many are left. Step 9. On the last slide, press the finish button. That tells the page you are done. I can't press it for you — the record of your good work has to come from you. You will know the page is finished when all 6 tabs have a tick, and you have pressed the finish button on the last slide. Now go and press tab 1. When you have typed your first answer, come back and tell me what you wrote — I would love to hear it!

visuals.label: Visual Models
visuals.text: Hello! Today I am your teacher for the Visual Models page. This page has six little pictures and shapes of the big ideas in our 3D shapes unit. You can drag them to turn them around and press their buttons. We do this so the shapes stop being just words and start feeling real to your eyes. By the end, you will be able to name a cube, cuboid, sphere, cylinder, cone and pyramid, and say which ones roll and which ones stack. Get a pencil, and if you can, grab a die, a tin and a ball to hold while you look. There are 7 steps. Here they all are. 1. Model 1 is "Solid (3D) shapes take up space". Look at it first, then drag it slowly with your finger or mouse to turn it all the way round. Press any buttons on it to see it change. Then read the caption under it and press Listen to hear the words. I expect you to tell me one thing: a 3D shape is solid and you can hold it, and a 2D shape is flat like paper. 2. Model 2 is "Cubes and cuboids — faces and edges". Drag it to turn it, and touch each flat side on the screen as you count out loud: one, two, three, four, five, six. Press Listen under the caption too. I expect you to count six faces on the cube, and then say what is the same and what is different about the cube and the cuboid. 3. Model 3 is "Spheres and cylinders — curved surfaces". Turn this one round and look for a flat part. Press its buttons, then read the caption and press Listen. I expect you to see that the sphere has no flat part at all, but the cylinder has two flat round ends and a curved side. 4. Model 4 is "Cones and pyramids — shapes with a point". Drag it round and look at the very top of each shape. Read the caption and press Listen. I expect you to find the point on both, and to notice the cone's side is curved and smooth, but the pyramid's sides are flat triangles. 5. Model 5 is "Sorting — rolls, stacks and everyday objects". Press its buttons and watch which shapes roll and which stay still. Read the caption and press Listen. I expect you to say the rule in your own words: curved surface on the table means it rolls, flat face on the table means it stacks. 6. Model 6 is "Cones and Pyramids Are Like Squeezed Shapes". Turn it and press its buttons to watch the shape squeeze to a point. Read the caption and press Listen. I expect you to finish this sentence for me: a cuboid squeezed to a point becomes a ______. 7. Now check you have done all six. Every model turned, every caption read, every Listen pressed. Then press the button at the bottom that says I explored the models. Only press it when you really have looked at all six — that press is your work being saved, so it must come from you. You will know the page is finished when all six models have been looked at and the I explored the models button has been pressed. Take your time — there's no rush. Come back and tell me when you are done, and I will ask you one small question to see what stuck. 🙂

method.label: Learn the Method
method.text: Hello! Today I am your teacher for the Learn the Method page. This page shows 6 methods. A method is a way to do something step by step, like a recipe. These methods teach you how to name solid shapes, count their flat faces, feel a curved surface, and sort shapes that roll or stack. We do this so your hands and your mouth learn the shapes, not just your eyes. By the end you will be able to hold a real object and say its shape name all by yourself. What you need: a die or a small block, a tin, a ball or an orange, a box, and your voice. What I expect from you: say every step out loud, and try it with a real object when the step asks you to. Take your time — there's no rush. Here are all the steps. 1. Look at the first method on the page. Read its first step. Do what it says with a real thing in your hand if you can. Then press Show me the next step. I expect you to read slowly and touch the object, not just look at the words. 2. Keep pressing Show me the next step. Say each new step out loud as it appears. Keep going until the page says Method complete. That message means you finished that method — well done! 3. Now do the same thing for the next method. Read the first step, press Show me the next step, and keep pressing until it says Method complete. I expect you to say the shape names out loud: cube, cuboid, sphere, cylinder, cone, pyramid. 4. Do this for every one of the 6 methods. Finish each one all the way to Method complete. Do not skip a method, even if it looks easy. Easy ones are quick wins! 5. Now look under the page. There is a deck of slides. Each slide has one of the same methods on it. This is your practice round. 6. On the first slide, press Start. Then use the same buttons on the slide to move through the steps, one at a time, until that slide's method is done. Say the steps out loud again. 7. Press the arrow on the right to go to the next slide. Look at the little dots under the slide — they show you where you are. More dots left means more slides to do. 8. Keep going slide by slide. Press Start, step through, then the arrow on the right. On the last slide, press the finish button. That is the end. You will know the page is finished when all 6 methods say Method complete, and you have pressed the finish button on the last slide. Ready to start? Tell me when the first method says Method complete, and tell me one shape you held in your hand. 🙂

examples.label: Worked Examples
examples.text:
Hello! Today I am your teacher for the Worked Examples page. Here is what this page is. It shows 12 shape questions. Each one has the full working, which means all the thinking steps, written out. We do this so you can see HOW a good answer is built, not just what the answer is. By the end, you will be able to name 3D shapes, count faces, and say which shapes roll and which stack. What you need: your eyes, your voice, and if you can, a die, a tin, a box and a ball to hold. Take your time — mathematicians think slowly on purpose. Here are your steps. Step 1. Look at the first worked example. Read the question by yourself first, out loud if you like. Do NOT press anything yet. Think about your own answer, and say it out loud or write it down. I expect you to try first, even if you are not sure. A guess made with thinking is a great start. Step 2. Now press Show worked solution. Read it line by line, slowly. Compare it with what you said. Ask yourself: did I get the same answer? Did I think the same way? I expect you to notice one thing — either "I got it!" or "Ah, I forgot that bit."

Step 3. Do the same for every example: read, think, then press Show worked solution. There are 12 in all. At the top of the page there is a counter, a little number that shows how many you have opened. I expect you to open all 12, not just the easy ones. Keep going until the counter shows every one is open. Step 4. Now look under the page. There is a deck of slides, with the same examples again, one on each slide. On the first slide, press Start. Step 5. On each slide, use the same buttons as before: read the question, try it yourself, then show the solution. When you are ready, press the arrow on the right to move to the next slide. The little dots under the slide tell you where you are, like footprints. Step 6. Keep going through the slides. On the last slide, press the finish button. Well done — that is the whole deck! How you will know the page is finished: the counter at the top shows all 12 examples opened, and you have pressed the finish button on the last slide. One more thing I expect from you: if a shape name feels tricky, come and tell me and we will look at it together. Ready? Start with Step 1, and tell me your answer to the first example. 😊

activities.label: Activities
activities.text: Hello! Today I am your teacher, and this is our Activities page for Unit 10, 3D Shapes. An activity means you learn by doing, not just by looking. You will pick a real solid shape, make it or draw it, and talk about it. By the end, you will be able to name a 3D shape and say what it is like. You will need paper, a pencil, and some things from home — like a die, a tin, a ball, or a box. Here is what I expect from you: try it with real objects in your hands, use our shape words (cube, cuboid, sphere, cylinder, cone), and write your own words in the box, even if the spelling is not perfect. Take your time — there's no rush. Step 1. Look at the activity card on the page. There is 1 hands-on activity. Read it, then press Listen to hear it read to you. Now go and get the things it names: paper, a pencil, and one or two solid objects from your home. A good start is: you come back with real things in your hands, ready to touch and turn them. Step 2. Now do the activity. Choose one idea from our unit, like a cube or a cylinder. Draw it or build it, then show it to your grown-up and tell them about it. Say something like, "This is a cylinder. It has two flat round ends and a curved side." Then think of one question of your own, like "How many faces does my box have?", and answer it. Step 3. Write in the box on the page. Write what you made and what you noticed. A good answer has the shape name and one thing about it, for example: "I made a cube. It has 6 flat faces and it stacks." That is exactly what I am looking for. Step 4. Press Mark complete under the activity when you have really done it. Only press it after you have made your model and written in the box. When every activity is marked, press Finish activities at the bottom of the page. Step 5. Now look under the page. There is a deck of slides with the same hands-on activities, one on each slide. Press Start on the first slide. Step 6. On each slide, use the same buttons you already know: Listen to hear it, do the activity, write in the box, then Mark complete. Then press the arrow on the right to go to the next slide. The little dots under the slide show you where you are. Step 7. Keep going until the last slide. On the last slide, press Finish activities. You will know the page is finished when every activity says complete, and you have pressed Finish activities at the bottom and on the last slide. Off you go with Step 1 — tell me when you have your objects, and I will check in with you. 😊

guided.label: Guided Practice
guided.text: Hello! Today we practise our 3D shapes together. This page is called Guided Practice. That means you try the questions, and I help you when you need me. By the end, you will be able to name shapes like the cube, the sphere and the cylinder, and say which ones roll and which ones stack. You will need a pencil, some paper, and if you can, a die, a tin and a ball to hold. Here are the steps. 1. Read the first question slowly. Say it out loud if that helps. Then work it out on paper or in your head. If the question is about a real thing, like a ball or a box, pick it up and feel it. Count the flat faces with your finger. Take your time — there is no rush. I expect you to think first, before you type. 2. Type your answer in the box. Then press Check my answer. Write the shape name in full, like cube or cylinder, not just one letter. If you get stuck, press Give me a hint. You can have up to three hints. If you are still stuck, press Show next step, and it shows you one line of the working. I expect you to try a hint before you ask for the step — that way your brain does the work. 3. Do this for every question, all twelve. If an answer is not right, that is fine. Mistakes are how we learn. Read the hint, think again, and type a new answer.
