Keep going on each question until it is right. The page is finished when all twelve are right. 4. Now look under the page. There is a deck of slides with the same questions, one question on each slide. Press Start on the first slide. Answer it the same way, with the same buttons: Check my answer, Give me a hint, Show next step. Then press the arrow on the right to move to the next slide. The little dots under the slide show you where you are. On the last slide, press the finish button. You will know the page is finished when all twelve questions are right and you have pressed the finish button on the last slide. Ready? Start with question one. Read it, work it out, and tell me your answer. I am right here. 🙂

fluency.label: Math Fluency
fluency.text: Hello! I am your teacher today, and this page is called Math Fluency. Fluency means knowing something so well that you can say it quickly. On this page you will get 12 quick questions about our 3D shapes — the cube, cuboid, sphere, cylinder, cone and pyramid. We do this so the shape names pop into your head fast, without you having to stop and think hard. What I expect from you is your best try on every question, and honest answers that come from your own head. A grown-up can sit with you to read the questions if you like. Here are all the steps, one by one. 1. Get ready first. Sit somewhere comfy. Put a cube near you if you can — a die, a stock cube, or a square block. Holding a real shape helps your brain remember. 2. Look at the top of the page. There is a timer there. It counts your time. Do not worry about it! Fast is nice, but right is better. 3. Read question one. Read it twice, slowly. Ask yourself: is this shape flat or solid? Does it roll or stack? How many flat faces does it have? 4. Type your answer in the box. Use one clear word when you can, like sphere, cube, cuboid, cylinder, cone, ROLL or STACK. Spelling does not have to be perfect, but try your best. 5. Press Check & continue. This tells the page you are done with that question and brings the next one. 6. If your answer was right, smile and keep going. If it was not right, read the little message the page gives you. It tells you why. Learning from it is just as good as getting it right. 7. Do the same for all 12 questions. Read, think, type, press Check & continue. One question at a time, no rushing. Mathematicians think slowly on purpose. 8. If you get stuck on one, picture a real thing at home. A ball is a sphere. A tin is a cylinder. A box is a cuboid. A die is a cube. A party hat is a cone. 9. At the end, the page shows how many you got right. You need most of them right to pass the sprint. 10. If you got fewer than you needed, press Run the sprint again. That is not a fail — that is practice. Try to remember the ones that tricked you last time. 11. Keep going until one sprint has enough right answers. Then the page marks itself finished for you. 12. You will know you are done when the page says the sprint is passed and does not ask you to run it again. That is your finish line! Now go ahead and start question one. When you finish your sprint, come back and tell me your score — I would love to hear how it went. 🌟

problems.label: Solve Real Problems
problems.text: Hello! Today we are going to do the "Solve Real Problems" page together. On this page, shapes come out of the book and into real life — a football, a tin, a lunch box, a party hat. Your job is to look at each little story and think like a shape detective. By the end, you will be able to name a 3D shape you see at home and say why it rolls or stacks. You will need your eyes, your thinking, and a real object to hold if one is nearby. Here are your steps. Step 1. Read the first problem slowly, all the way to the end. Ask yourself: what is this question really asking me? Sometimes it asks for a shape name, like cube or sphere. Sometimes it asks "will it roll?" I expect you to say the question back in your own words before you answer. Take your time — there's no rush. Step 2. Now work it out in your head, or with a real object in your hands. Then type your answer in the box and press Check answer. A good answer has two parts: what it is, and why. Not just "sphere", but "sphere, because it is round all over with no flat part". If you get stuck, press Hint first and try again — that is what the Hint button is for. Step 3. When the page tells you your answer is right, that problem is finished. Move on to the next one. There are 6 problems in all. Do them one at a time, in order, so your brain stays calm and clear. Step 4. Now look under the page. There is a deck of slides with the same problems, one problem on each slide. Press Start on the first slide to begin. Use the same buttons here: type your answer, press Check answer, and press Hint if you need help. Step 5. When a slide is done, press the arrow on the right to go to the next slide. Look at the little dots under the slide — they show you where you are and how many are left. Keep going, one slide at a time. Step 6. On the last slide, press the finish button. That tells the page you have finished all of them. You will know the whole page is finished when all 6 problems say your answer is right, and you have pressed the finish button on the last slide. Ready? Tell me the first problem you see, and what you think it is asking. I'm right here with you. 🙂

games.label: Games
games.text: Hello! Today we are playing the shape games for Unit 10. These games ask you quick questions about 3D shapes — the cube, the cuboid, the sphere, the cylinder, the cone and the pyramid. We play them so the shape names and their faces stick in your head. By the end, you will be able to name a shape fast and say if it rolls or stacks. All you need is your eyes, your thinking, and maybe a die or a tin to hold. There are 3 steps. Step 1: Pick a game and press Start game. Then read each round carefully and choose your answer. Take your time — there's no rush. Every round you get right gives you a star. I expect you to think first, not just tap quickly. If a round is tricky, look for the clue and ask yourself: is this shape flat all over, or does it curve? Step 2: When the game ends, press Play again. This gives you another go and more stars. A game is mastered when it has all its stars. I expect you to keep trying, even if you miss one. Mistakes are how we learn — read why an answer was right, then try again. Step 3: Do the same for every game on the page. Press Start game, answer the rounds, press Play again until each game has all its stars. I expect you to finish one game before starting the next, so your brain stays on one idea at a time. You will know the page is finished when every game has all its stars — the page finishes by itself. You do not need to press anything extra at the end. Ready? Pick your first game and press Start game. Tell me when you have your first round on the screen! 🌟

challenge.label: Unit Challenge
challenge.text: Hello! Today you are doing the Unit Challenge for our 3D shapes unit. It is 12 questions about solid shapes — cube, cuboid, sphere, cylinder, cone and pyramid. We do it to show what your brain has learned about faces, curved surfaces, rolling and stacking. I will not tell you any answers, because these are yours to solve. But I will show you how to think, and I know you can do this. Take your time — there's no rush. Here is the whole page, step by step. 1. Get ready first. Sit somewhere quiet. If you can, put a die, a small box and a ball next to you. If a question feels hard, you can pick one up and look at it. I expect you to have your things ready before you start. 2. Read question one. Read it twice, slowly. Look at all four choices before you pick. I expect you to think first, then choose — not just tap the first one you see. 3. Choose your answer, then press Next question. Only press Next question when you are happy with your choice. Then question two comes up. Do the same thing every time. 4. Keep going until all 12 questions are done. One question, one answer, then Next question. I expect you to finish every single one, even the tricky ones. 5. Here is how to think about the shape questions. Ask yourself: is it round all over, or does it have flat faces? Round all over means a sphere. Flat square faces means a cube. Flat rectangle faces means a cuboid. 6. Here is how to think about counting questions. Do not guess. Touch each flat face one at a time and turn the shape as you count. That way you never count the same face twice. 7. Here is how to think about rolling and stacking. Ask: what part is touching the table? A curved part rolls. A flat part stays still and can stack. 8. Here is how to think about pattern questions. Say the pattern out loud, like a little song. Your ears will hear what comes next. 9. If you get stuck, do not worry. Read the question again and ask yourself what it is really asking. You may also ask me for a hint — I will give you a small clue, never the answer. 10. At the end you will see your score. You pass when you get more than half right. I expect you to look at your score bravely, whatever it says. Mistakes are how we learn. 11. If your score is not high enough, press Try again. That is not a bad thing — it just means your brain wants one more turn. Go slower the second time. 12. When your score is good, press Continue. That tells the page you have finished. You will know the page is finished when you have answered all 12 questions, seen your score, and pressed Continue. Come and tell me your score when you are done — I would love to hear how it went! 🌟

explain.label: Explain Your Thinking
explain.text: Hello! Today I am your teacher for the "Explain Your Thinking" page. On this page you do not just say the answer. You say WHY. You use your own words to tell me what you know about solid shapes, like cube, sphere and cylinder. We do this because a maths thinker can explain their idea to someone else. By the end, you will be able to say things like "the tin rolls because its side is curved." You need your eyes, your thinking, and someone nearby if you want help typing. Here are the steps. Step 1. Read the first prompt. There are 6 prompts on this page. Each one asks you to explain something, like why a ball cannot be stacked. Under the prompt you will see key ideas — these are the special words you should use, such as face, edge, curved surface, 3D shape or 2D shape. Read the prompt slowly, twice. I expect you to point at each key word and say it out loud before you start writing. Step 2. Write your explanation in the box. Say three things: what you can see, what rule you used, and why your answer makes sense. For example: "The box has flat faces. Flat faces sit still on each other. So the box can stack." Try to use the key words in your writing. Then press Check mathematical ideas. If it asks for more, do not worry — just add one more sentence and press Check mathematical ideas again. Step 3. Press Show model explanation. This opens a good answer so you can compare it with yours. Read it and look for key words you used too. If the model says something you missed, that is fine — mistakes are how we learn. I expect you to tell yourself one thing you did well and one word you could add next time. Then do the same for all 6 prompts. Step 4. Now go to the slides under the page. There is a deck of slides with the same prompts, one on each slide. On the first slide, press Start. Then use the same buttons you already know: write your idea, press Check mathematical ideas, and press Show model explanation to compare. When that slide is done, press the arrow on the right to move to the next slide. The little dots under the slide show you where you are. On the last slide, press the finish button. How you will know you are finished: every one of the 6 prompts has your own explanation, each one uses the key ideas, and you have pressed the finish button on the last slide. Take your time — there's no rush. Start with prompt one, and tell me when you are ready. 😊

overview.label: Unit Overview
overview.text:
Hello! I am your teacher today. 😊

This page is called the Unit Overview. It is like looking at a map before a trip. It tells you what Unit 11 is about: halves. A half is one of two equal parts of a whole. By the end of this page, you will know what we are going to learn together. There are 3 steps. Here they are. Step 1: Read the Unit Overview. Look at the words on your screen. If you see a little speaker picture, press Listen. Then the words are read out loud to you. Listen and follow along with your finger. If a grown-up is near, you can read it with them. I expect you to read or listen all the way to the end — not just the first line. Take your time — there's no rush. Step 2: Say what you will learn, in your own words. Now say it out loud, or type it to me here. You do not need fancy words. Something like "I will learn about halves" or "I will learn how to share things fairly" is great. I expect one or two little sentences from you, in YOUR words — not copied from the screen. That shows me you really understood. Step 3: Press Continue. When you have read the page and said your sentence, find the Continue button and press it. That takes you to The Lesson, where the real learning starts. I expect you to press it only after Step 1 and Step 2 are done. How will you know the page is finished? When you have listened or read, said what you will learn, and pressed Continue and moved to The Lesson. That's it! Let's start with Step 1 now. Read the Unit Overview and press Listen if you see the speaker. Tell me when you are done. 🌟

lesson.label: The Lesson
lesson.text: Hello! Today I am your teacher for The Lesson page in Unit 11: Understanding Halves. This page has 5 short lessons, called concepts. They all teach one big idea: a half is one of two equal parts. We do this so you can share things fairly, halve shapes, and read the symbol ½. Before we start, get a pencil, a piece of paper, and about 10 small things like stones, beans or buttons. A grown-up can sit with you if you like. Here is what I expect from you: read slowly, say things out loud, and touch real objects. Do not rush. Mathematicians think slowly on purpose. Here are your steps. 1. Look at the top of the page. You will see the first concept with a title and a short explanation. Read it slowly, word by word. Then press Listen and hear it read to you while you follow along. I expect you to read it once, then listen once. Take your time — there's no rush. 2. Now find the example in that concept. Say the example out loud in your own voice. Then do it for real: fold a piece of paper so both sides match exactly, or share your stones onto two plates. I expect you to touch something real, not just look at the page. A fold that matches exactly proves the two parts are equal. 3. Do the same for concept 2, then 3, then 4, then 5. For each one: read it, press Listen, say the example out loud, and try it with your own paper or stones. One concept at a time, please. When you get to the number one, share your stones and check: half of 2 is 1, half of 4 is 2, half of 6 is 3, half of 8 is 4, half of 10 is 5. 4. When you have read all 5 concepts, scroll to the bottom of the page. Press the button that says I studied the concepts. Only press it after you have really read every one. I expect you to be honest with yourself here — that button means "I did the work". 5. Now look under the page. There is a deck of slides. The same 5 concepts are there, one on each slide. On the first slide, press Start. This helps the ideas stick in your memory. 6. On each slide, use the same buttons as before, then press the arrow on the right to go to the next slide. Look at the little dots under the slide — they show you where you are and how many are left. I expect you to look at every slide, not skip ahead. 7. On the last slide, press the finish button. That tells the page you have finished the whole deck. You will know the page is finished when the I studied the concepts button is pressed and you have pressed the finish button on the last slide. Ready? Start with step 1, and tell me when you have read the first concept. 🙂

words.label: Math Words & Symbols
words.text:
Hello! Today I am your teacher for the Math Words & Symbols page. This page teaches you the special maths words we use for halves, like whole, half, equal, unequal, fraction, the symbol ½, share equally, and half of. We learn them so that when you read a question or I ask you something, you know exactly what the words mean. By the end, you will be able to say each word, tell me what it means in your own words, and use it in a sentence. You will need your voice, and your fingers ready to type. Take your time — there's no rush. Here are the steps. Step 1. Look at the first word on the page. Read the word, then read what it means. Now press Listen. Listen carefully to how the word sounds. I expect you to listen once, then say the word softly to yourself, the same way you heard it. Step 2. Now say the word out loud, nice and clear. Say it like you mean it, not in a whisper. Say it with me, slowly. Step 3. Now say the meaning in your own words. Do not copy the page word for word. For example, for half you might say, "one of two parts that are the same size." I expect your own little words — that shows me you really understand. Step 4. Now type a sentence with the word in it, then press Check sentence. A good sentence is a real one from your life, like "I gave my brother half of my banana." Make sure the word is inside your sentence. Then read what the checker says to you. If it asks you to fix something, change your sentence and press Check sentence again. Step 5. Do steps 1 to 4 again for every word on the page. One word at a time, please. The words are whole, half, equal, unequal, fraction, ½, share equally, and half of. Remember, when you see ½ you say "one half."

Step 6. When you have finished every single word, press I know these words and symbols at the bottom. Only press it when you have really done them all — that button tells me you are ready. Step 7. Now look under the page. There is a deck of slides with the same words, one word on each slide. Press Start on the first slide. Step 8. On each slide, use the same buttons you already know: press Listen, say the word out loud, say the meaning in your own words, type your sentence, and press Check sentence. Try to make a new sentence this time, not the same one. That helps the word stick in your head. Step 9. When that slide is done, press the arrow on the right to go to the next slide. Look at the little dots under the slide — they show you which slide you are on and how many are left. Step 10. Keep going, slide by slide, until you reach the last slide. On the last slide, press the finish button. You will know the page is finished when the I know these words and symbols button has been pressed, and you have pressed the finish button on the last slide. Then every word has been read, said, and used in your own sentence. Ready? Start with word one and press Listen. Tell me when you have done it, and I will check it with you. 🙂

explore.label: Explore the Concept
explore.text: Hello! Today we are on the Explore the Concept page for halves. This page has 6 little discoveries. Each one shows you a picture or a model, then asks you one thinking question. We do this so you really understand what a half is: one of two equal parts. By the end, you will be able to look at any shape or group and say if it shows halves or not. You will need your eyes, your thinking brain, and a pencil and paper if you want to try folding. Here we go, one step at a time. Step 1. Look at the top of the page. You will see numbered tabs: 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6. Press tab 1. A short story and a picture or model will open. Read the words slowly, or ask your grown-up to read them with you. Look carefully at the picture too — the picture is part of the answer. I expect you to look before you type. Take your time — there's no rush. Step 2. Under the story is the discovery question. Read it twice. Then think in your head: are the two parts equal, or not equal? Say your idea out loud first, if that helps. Step 3. Type your idea in the box. You do not need long, fancy words. A short answer with the important word in it is perfect — words like equal, not equal, half, or a number. I expect one clear idea, in your own words. Step 4. Press Check my idea. If it says Exactly!, well done — the tab gets a tick. If it says Look again, that is fine. Mistakes are how we learn. Step 5. If you saw Look again, press Hint. Read the hint, think again, change your answer a little, and press Check my idea one more time. I expect you to try again yourself — you can do this. Step 6. Now press tab 2 and do the same thing: read, look, think, type, press Check my idea. Keep going like this for tab 3, tab 4, tab 5 and tab 6. Do them in order, one at a time. Step 7. Here is what each one is about, so you know what to expect. Tab 1 is about a biscuit broken into a big bit and a tiny bit. Tab 2 is about a square cut corner to corner. Tab 3 is about sharing 6 dates between two plates. Tab 4 is half of 8. Tab 5 is the symbol one half. Tab 6 is about a fold that matches exactly. In every one, ask yourself the same question: are the two parts equal? Step 8. Check the tabs at the top. Every tab should have a tick. If one is missing a tick, press it and finish that question. The top part of the page is done when all 6 tabs are ticked. Step 9. Now scroll down, under the page, to the deck of slides. These slides show the same discoveries again, one discovery on each slide. This is your practice, so the idea sticks. Step 10. On the first slide, press Start. Then use the same buttons as before: read, type your idea, press Check my idea, and press Hint if you need help. Step 11. When that slide is right, press the arrow on the right side to go to the next slide. Look at the little dots under the slide — they show you which slide you are on and how many are left. Step 12. Keep going, slide by slide, until you reach the last slide. On the last slide, press the finish button. I do not tick this page for you — you press the buttons yourself, and that is how your work gets saved. How will you know the page is finished? Every numbered tab at the top has a tick, and you have pressed the finish button on the last slide. Ready? Press tab 1 and tell me what your first discovery says. I'm right here with you. 🙂

visuals.label: Visual Models
visuals.text:
Hello! Today we are going to look at pictures of halves. This page is called Visual Models. A visual model is a picture that shows a maths idea, so you can see it with your eyes. We are doing this because a half is much easier to understand when you can look at it and move it. By the end, you will be able to point at a picture and say, "That is one half — two equal parts." You need your eyes, your finger for tapping, and your voice for saying the words out loud. Let's start. 1. Find the first model at the top. It is called What a Half Really Means. Look at it carefully. If it moves, drag it with your finger to turn it, and press any buttons on it to change it. I expect you to look for one thing: are the two parts the same size? Say out loud, "equal" or "not equal."

2. Under that model there is a caption. A caption is the little bit of writing under a picture. Read it, then press Listen to hear it read to you. Listen all the way to the end, and try to hear the word equal. 3. Now go to the second model, Halves of Shapes. Drag it and press its buttons to see the different ways a shape can be cut. I expect you to find more than one way — like a line down the middle, and a line corner to corner. Both are still halves! 4. Read the caption under model two, then press Listen. Good listening means keeping your eyes on the picture while you hear the words. Try to spot the word fold or line. 5. Next is the third model, Half of a Set. This one is about sharing a group of things, like dates or stones, between two. Press its buttons and watch the things move into two groups. I expect you to count one group out loud, slowly. 6. Read the caption under model three and press Listen. Then say this sentence to yourself: "Half of a set means sharing it fairly between two."

7. Now the fourth model, Halving Small Even Numbers. Press its buttons to see numbers being halved. I expect you to try saying one fact out loud, like "half of 6 is 3." Take your time — there's no rush. 8. Read the caption under model four and press Listen. Listen for the numbers 2, 4, 6, 8 and 10. These are our special halving numbers. 9. Last one — the fifth model, The Symbol ½. Look closely at the little symbol ½. Press any buttons on it to see it next to a picture of a real half. I expect you to say the words "one half" out loud when you see it. 10. Read the caption under model five and press Listen. Then have one more quick scroll up and down the page, so your eyes see all five models one more time. 11. When you have looked at every model and heard every caption, press the button at the bottom that says I explored the models. That button is how the page knows you are done — I cannot press it for you. You will know the page is finished when you have pressed I explored the models and it is marked done on your screen. Now off you go — start with step 1, and tell me when you have looked at the first model. I'll be right here. 😊

method.label: Learn the Method
method.text: Hello! Today we are on the "Learn the Method" page. A method is a way to do something, step by step, like a little recipe. This page has 6 methods about halves — folding, checking, and putting halves back together. By the end you will know how to make two equal parts and check they match. You need your eyes, your voice, and if you can, a piece of paper to fold. Here we go, one step at a time. 1. Look at the first method. Read its first step. Then press Show me the next step to see what comes after it. I want you to read slowly and think about what your hands would do. 2. Keep pressing Show me the next step until the page says Method complete. Say each step out loud as you read it. Saying it out loud helps your brain remember it, so please really use your voice, even a soft one. 3. Now do the same for every method. There are 6 in all. Press Show me the next step on each one until it says Method complete. Take your time — mathematicians think slowly on purpose. 4. If you have paper, try one method with your hands. Fold your paper so the two sides sit exactly on top of each other. If nothing sticks out, you made two halves. Well done! 5. Now scroll down to the bottom of the page. There is a deck of slides. Each slide has one method on it, the same ones you just read. 6. On the first slide, press Start. Then use the same buttons on the slide to move through the steps, just like before. Say each step out loud again. 7. When that slide is done, press the arrow on the right to go to the next slide. Look at the little dots under the slide — they show you where you are and how many are left. 8. Do every slide the same way: press Start, step through it, then the arrow on the right. Keep going until you reach the last slide. 9. On the last slide, press the finish button. That tells the page you have done all the work. You will know the page is finished when every method has said Method complete, and you have pressed the finish button on the last slide. Now go and do step 1, then come back and tell me what the first step of the first method says. I'll be right here. 🙂

examples.label: Worked Examples
examples.text:
Hello! Today I am your teacher for the Worked Examples page. 🌟

This page shows 12 maths questions about halves. Each one has the full working — that means all the thinking, written out step by step. We do this so you can see HOW a good answer is built, not just the answer. By the end, you will know what a half is, how to check two parts are equal, and how to share things fairly between two. You need a pencil, some paper, and a few small things to count — stones, beans or buttons are perfect. Take your time. Mathematicians think slowly on purpose. Here are your steps. 1. Look at the first worked example. Read the question slowly, all the way to the end. Then read it one more time. I expect you to read before you press anything — reading twice is what good mathematicians do. 2. Now try the question yourself, on your paper. Write your answer, or draw a little picture of it. It does not need to be perfect. I just want to see you have a go first, because trying makes the next part stick in your brain. 3. Now press Show worked solution. Read the solution line by line, slowly, with your finger under the words. I expect you to compare it with your own answer: what did you both do the same, and what did the solution do that you did not? 4. If your answer matches — brilliant work! Say out loud why it is right. If it does not match, that is fine. Mistakes are how we learn. Find the one line where your thinking went a different way, and say that line out loud. 5. Now do the same for the next worked example: read it, try it, then press Show worked solution. Keep going like this, one example at a time, until you have opened all 12. Look at the counter at the top of the page — it tells you how many you have opened. 6. Open every single one, even the easy-looking ones. The page is not finished until all 12 are open. I expect you to try each question before you open the solution — no peeking first! 😊

7. Now scroll under the page. There is a deck of slides with the same examples on them, one example on each slide. Press Start on the first slide to begin. 8. On each slide, do the same three things: read the question, try it on your paper, then press the same buttons to see the working. Same good habit, new place. 9. To move on, press the arrow on the right side of the slide. Look at the little dots under the slide — they show you where you are in the deck. More dots to go means more slides to do. 10. Keep going slide by slide until you reach the last one. On the last slide, press the finish button. That tells the page you are done. 11. Here is how you know the page is finished: the counter at the top shows all 12 worked examples opened, and you have pressed the finish button on the last slide. 12. Last thing, and it matters. Tell me one thing you learned today about halves. That is your reflection, and it helps the learning stay. Take your time — there's no rush. Tell me when you have done step 1 and 2, and I will be right here. 🙂

activities.label: Activities
activities.text:
Hello! Today I am your teacher, and this page is our doing page. Here we do not just read about halves — we make them with our hands. You will fold, draw, and share things into two equal parts. Doing it with real things helps the idea stick in your head. Get a pencil, some paper, and a grown-up or big brother or sister nearby if you can. Step 1. Look at the activity box at the top. It is called "Practise together". It tells you what to use: paper, a pencil, and things from your home like stones, dates, spoons or toys. Press Listen to hear it read out loud. Then go and get those things and put them on the table. I expect you to have real things in front of you, not just the screen. Step 2. Now do the activity. Pick one idea from our unit — folding a shape in half, or sharing a group of things into two equal groups. Draw it or make it with your things. Then show it to someone in your family and tell them, in your own words, why the two parts are halves. Remember the big word: equal. The two parts must be the same size. Step 3. Make up one question of your own, like "What is half of 6?" and answer it. Then write your answer, or what you noticed, in the box on the page. Just one or two lines is perfect. A good answer says what you made and how you knew the parts were equal — for example, "I folded my paper and both sides matched."

Step 4. When you have finished, press Mark complete under the activity. There is one activity here, so when it is marked, press Finish activities at the bottom of the page. Only press it when you really did the folding or sharing — pressing it early would be like saying you ate your food when the plate is still full! Step 5. Now look under the page. There is a deck of slides with the same hands-on activity, one activity on each slide. Press Start on the first slide. Use the same buttons on each slide: Listen, then do it, then write in the box, then Mark complete. Step 6. To move on, press the arrow on the right side of the slide. The little dots under the slide show you where you are — like footprints showing how far you have walked. When you reach the last slide, press Finish activities. You will know the page is done when every activity is marked complete and you have pressed Finish activities at the bottom. Take your time — there's no rush. When you have your paper and things ready, tell me, and we will start Step 1 together. 🙂

guided.label: Guided Practice
guided.text: Hello! Today we are on the Guided Practice page for halves. This page gives you 12 questions about halves — cutting shapes into two equal parts, and sharing things fairly between two. We practise so the big idea sticks: a half is one of two equal parts. By the end you will be able to spot a half, and say half of 2, 4, 6, 8 and 10. Get a pencil and some paper. You can also grab 10 small things, like stones, beans or buttons, to help you share. Here is what I expect from you: think first, then type. Take your time — there's no rush. Mistakes are fine. Mistakes are how we learn. There are 4 steps. Here they all are. Step 1. Read the first question slowly. Read it twice. Then work it out on your paper, or in your head, or with your stones. If the question says "share", deal your stones one at a time: one for this side, one for that side. If it says "half of a shape", draw the shape and draw a line through the middle. I expect you to work it out before you type — that is the important part. Step 2. Type your answer in the box. Then press Check my answer. If you feel stuck, do not worry. Press Give me a hint. You can get up to three hints. If you are still stuck, press Show next step — it shows you one line of the working. I expect you to try a hint first, before Show next step. Hints help you find the answer yourself, and that feels great. Step 3. Do this for every question, all 12 of them. If an answer is not right, read the question again and try once more. Keep going until every question is right. That is when the page is finished. I expect you to fix wrong answers instead of skipping them — that is where the learning happens. Step 4. Now look under the page. There is a deck of slides with the same questions, one question on each slide. Press Start on the first slide. Use the same buttons on each slide: Check my answer, Give me a hint, Show next step. Then press the arrow on the right to move to the next slide. The little dots under the slide show you where you are. On the last slide, press the finish button. I expect you to say your answer out loud before you type it — it makes your thinking stronger. You will know the page is finished when all 12 questions are right, and you have pressed the finish button on the last slide. Press those buttons yourself — that is how your work gets saved. Ready? Tell me what question one says, and let's start together.

games.label: Games
games.text: Hello! Today we are on the Games page for Unit 11: Halves. This is our fun practice time. Each game asks you a few quick questions about halves. Playing them helps the big idea stick in your head: a half is one of two equal parts. By the end, you will be quick and sure at spotting halves and halving numbers like 2, 4, 6, 8 and 10. What I expect from you: think before you tap. Read the question twice. If a question is about sharing, count it out on your fingers or with small things like stones or buttons. It is fine to get one wrong — mistakes are how we learn. There are three steps. Here they all are. 1. Pick one game and press Start game. Then answer each round by tapping the choice you think is right. Take your time — there's no rush. For every round you get right, you earn a star. If you get one wrong, read the little clue and think again next time. I expect you to try every round yourself, and to ask the question in your head each time: are the two parts equal? 2. When the game ends, press Play again to earn more stars. The same game can give you more stars each time you play it well. A game is mastered when it has all its stars. I expect you to keep playing that one game until its stars are full, before you move on. If a question keeps tricking you, tell me and we will work it out together. 3. Now do the same for every game on the page. Choose the next game, press Start game, answer the rounds, and press Play again until that game has all its stars too. Master every game, one at a time. I expect you to go slowly and finish one game before starting another — that way your stars grow fast. How will you know the page is finished? When every game has all its stars, the page finishes by itself. You do not need to press anything extra. I do not mark it done — you do, by playing. Ready? Press Start game on your first game, and tell me how the first round goes. 🌟

problems.label: Solve Real Problems
problems.text:
Hello! Today I am your teacher for "Solve Real Problems."

This page gives you halves from real life — sharing a chapati, cutting a watermelon, pouring water, sharing dates. You already know that a half is one of two equal parts. Now you use that idea in real stories. By the end, you will be able to look at a real problem and say what half is, and why the two parts must be equal. You will need a pencil, some paper, and maybe 10 small things like stones or beans to share out. Here is what I expect from you. Read slowly. Think before you type. And always tell me how you got your answer, not just the answer. Mathematicians think slowly on purpose. 1. Read the first problem out loud, slowly. Ask yourself: what is this problem asking me? Sometimes it asks "how many?" and sometimes it asks "is this fair?" I expect you to know what the question wants before you start working. 2. Now work it out away from the screen first. If it is about a shape or food, think about folding it in the middle. If it is about a group of things, deal them out one at a time — one for this plate, one for that plate — using your stones or beans. Take your time; there is no rush. 3. Type your working and your answer in the box. Do not type only "4". Type how you did it, like "I shared them one at a time and each plate got 4." Then press Check answer. I expect a full little sentence from you every time. 4. If your brain gets stuck, press Hint. That is not cheating — it is being a good learner. Read the hint, then try again yourself. Come and ask me too, and I will give you a small clue. 5. When the page says your answer is right, that problem is done. Then move to the next problem and do the same three things: read it, work it out with your objects, type your working and press Check answer. 6. Keep going until all 6 problems say your answer is right. Some are about food, some are about water, and one is about time — "half past four." That one is tricky, so slow down and picture a clock. 7. Now look under the page. There is a deck of slides with the same problems, one problem on each slide. On the first slide, press Start. 8. On each slide, use the same buttons you already know: type your working, press Check answer, and press Hint if you need help. Same good habits — working first, then the answer. 9. To go to the next slide, press the arrow on the right. Look at the little dots under the slide. They show you where you are and how many slides are left. 10. On the last slide, press the finish button. That tells the page you have done them all. You will know the page is finished when all 6 problems say your answer is right, and you have pressed the finish button on the last slide. Ready? Read problem one and tell me what you think it is asking. I am right here with you. 🙂

fluency.label: Math Fluency
fluency.text: Hello! I am your teacher for this page. Today we do Math Fluency. Fluency means answering quickly, without stopping to think for a long time. This page gives you 12 quick questions about halves. It helps the word "half" become easy and fast in your head — like knowing your own name. You need your eyes, your fingers for counting, and a comfy seat. Take a breath. Here are your steps. 1. Get ready first. Say this to yourself: a half is one of two equal parts. Equal means exactly the same size. If you like, put 10 small things near you — buttons, stones or beans. You can share them into two little groups if a question is tricky. I expect you to be ready before you start, not counting after the timer begins. 2. Start the sprint. Look at the top of the page. You will see your time counting. That is just to show you how fast you go — it is not scary, and no one is watching you but me. I expect you to try your best, not to panic. 3. Read question one carefully. Read it twice in your head. Ask yourself: are the two parts equal, or is one bigger? Or: how many are in one group? I expect you to look at the question before you answer, even in a sprint. Mathematicians think slowly on purpose, even when they go fast. 4. Type your answer, then press Check & continue. Type just the answer, like "3" or "half" or "unequal". Then press Check & continue to go to the next question. I expect one answer at a time, then straight on to the next. 5. Keep going for all 12 questions. Each time: read, think, type, press Check & continue. If a number question comes, share it into two equal groups in your head — one for this plate, one for that plate. I expect you to finish all 12, even if one feels hard. 6. If one question feels hard, do not freeze. Count it out on your fingers or with your stones. Half of a number means both groups get the same. Do your best answer and move on. I expect you to guess bravely rather than stop. 7. When the sprint ends, look at your score. You need most of them right to finish this page. If you got most right — brilliant work! If not, that is fine too. Mistakes are how we learn. 8. If you need another go, press Run the sprint again. The questions come back for more practice. This time, remember the ones that tricked you. I expect you to try again with a calm face, not a sad one. 9. Keep practising until a sprint has enough right. You may need one go, or two, or three. That is normal for everybody. I expect you to keep going — you get faster every single time. How will you know the page is finished? When one sprint has enough answers right, the page counts as done. That is your finish line. Then you can tell me your time and your score, and I will cheer for you. Ready? Start question one now, and come back and tell me how it went. 🌟

explain.label: Explain Your Thinking
explain.text: Hello! I am your teacher today, and this page is called Explain Your Thinking. On this page you do not just give an answer. You say HOW you know. You use your maths words, like whole, half, equal and unequal. Talking about your thinking helps the idea stick in your head for good. You will need your eyes, your brain, and a grown-up nearby if writing feels tricky. Here is what I expect from you: a short answer in your own words, with the word "equal" in it whenever you talk about halves. Two or three sentences is plenty. Take your time — mathematicians think slowly on purpose. There are 4 steps. Here they all are. 1. Read the first prompt. There are 6 prompts on this page, one at a time. Under each prompt you will see the key ideas — those are the words the page wants you to use, like Whole, Half, and Equal. Read the prompt twice, slowly. Then read the key ideas out loud. I expect you to know, before you write, which words you will use. 2. Write your explanation in the box, then press Check mathematical ideas. A good answer has three little parts: what you see, the rule you used, and why it makes sense. Like this: "I see two parts. A half is one of two equal parts. The parts match, so each one is a half." If the page says you need more, do not worry — add one more sentence, maybe the word "equal" or "whole", and press Check mathematical ideas again. 3. Press Show model explanation and compare. This opens a good answer for you to read. Look for words you used too — that is a win! Then look for one word you missed, and remember it for the next prompt. Do not copy it; your own words are the ones that matter. Now do steps 1, 2 and 3 again for prompts two, three, four, five and six. 4. Do the slides at the bottom of the page. Under the page there is a deck of slides with the same prompts, one prompt on each slide. Press Start on the first slide. On each slide, use the same buttons as before: write your answer, press Check mathematical ideas, then press Show model explanation. When that slide is done, press the arrow on the right to move to the next slide. The little dots under the slide show you where you are. On the last slide, press the finish button. You will know the page is finished when all 6 explanations use the key ideas, and you have pressed the finish button on the last slide. Ready? Start with prompt one, and tell me your explanation before you press Check. I would love to hear your thinking. 😊

challenge.label: Unit Challenge
challenge.text: Hello! Today is your Unit Challenge for halves. This is the little quiz at the end of our unit. It shows what you now know about halves — two equal parts, halving shapes, and half of a number. I will be right here as your teacher, but the answers must come from you. Get a pencil and some small things to count, like stones, beans or buttons. Ready? Here are all the steps. 1. Get ready first. Sit somewhere quiet. Put 10 small counters next to you — stones, beans or bits of pasta are perfect. You may also want a piece of paper you can fold. I expect you to have these ready before you start, because good mathematicians get their tools out first. 2. Remember our big idea. Say it out loud with me: "A half is one of two EQUAL parts." Equal means exactly the same size or amount. This one idea helps you with nearly every question. I expect you to keep this sentence in your head the whole time. 3. Start the challenge. There are 12 questions. Read question one, then read it again. Read the question twice before you answer. I expect you to read all the choices before you pick, not just the first one. 4. Think before you tap. For shape questions, picture folding the shape. Ask yourself: "Would both sides match exactly?" If yes, it shows a half. If one part is bigger, it is not a half. I expect you to check the size of both parts every time. 5. For number questions, use your counters. If it asks "half of 8", deal 8 counters onto two spots, one at a time: one here, one there, one here, one there. Then count one spot. That number is your answer. I expect you to count it out, not guess. Take your time — there's no rush. 6. Choose your answer and press Next question. Do this for every question, one at a time, all the way to question 12. If one feels hard, do your best and keep going. Mistakes are how we learn. 7. Look at your score at the end. The page will show how you did. You pass with more than half of the questions right. I expect you to look at any question you got wrong and think about why — that is where the real learning hides. 8. If your score is not high enough, press Try again. This is not a bad thing at all! It just means we practise once more. Before you try again, come and tell me which questions were tricky, and we will work on those together first. 9. When your score is good enough, press Continue. That is the last button on this page. You will know the page is finished when you have answered all 12 questions, seen your score, and pressed Continue. Then come back and tell me one thing you found easy and one thing you found tricky. Good luck — I know you can do this! 🌟

overview.label: Unit Overview
overview.text: Hello! I am Wehel Tutor, and today I am your teacher for Unit 12: Measures (2). This page is our starting page. It tells you what the whole unit is about. In this unit you will find out which things are heavier and lighter, which container holds more, which thing is longer or taller, and what is hot, warm or cold. Doing this page first helps your brain get ready, like warming up before you run. You need your eyes, your ears, and your talking voice. A grown-up can sit near you if you like. There are 3 steps. Here they all are. 1. Read the Unit Overview. Look at the words at the top of the page. Read them slowly. Where you see a little speaker picture, press Listen and let the words be read to you. Listen carefully. If you want, press Listen again. I expect you to read or listen right to the end, not just look at the pictures. 2. Say in your own words what you think you will learn. Now close your mouth for a second and think. Then say it out loud to me, or to your grown-up. A good answer uses your own words, not the page's words. For example: "I will learn which things are heavy." Even one sentence is great. I expect you to try, even if it is not perfect. Mistakes are how we learn. 3. Press Continue to go to The Lesson. When you have read and talked, find the Continue button and press it. That takes you to The Lesson, where we start learning properly. Only press it after step 2, so you do not skip your thinking part. You will know this page is finished when you have listened to the overview, said one thing you will learn, and pressed Continue. Let's start with step 1. Press Listen, read along, then tell me when you are done. Take your time — there's no rush.

lesson.label: The Lesson
lesson.text: Hello! Today I am your teacher for The Lesson page in Unit 12, Measures (2). This page teaches you how to compare things: heavy and light, holds more and holds less, long and tall, and hot, warm and cold. We do it so you can measure and compare real things at home, like cups, pencils and stones. You will need your eyes, your ears, your voice, and maybe a few small things from around you. Here are all the steps, one at a time. Step 1: Look at the top of the page. There are 7 concepts. A concept is one small idea with a short explanation. Read the first one slowly, then press Listen to hear it read to you. Listening and reading together helps the words stick. I expect you to go slowly and not rush past any concept. Step 2: Each concept has an example. Say the example out loud in your own voice. Then try it for real! Hold a stone in one hand and a leaf in the other, or pour a cup of water into a jug. I expect you to try at least one thing with your hands, not just read it. Ask your grown-up to help with water. Step 3: Now say the comparing sentence out loud, both ways. Like this: "The stone is heavier than the leaf. The leaf is lighter than the stone." Say it with me, slowly. I expect a full sentence, not just one word. Step 4: Keep going the same way through all 7 concepts. Read, press Listen, say the example, try it. The concepts are mass, balancing with stones, capacity, length and height, temperature, choosing the right tool, and money with coins. Take your time — there's no rush. Step 5: When you have read every concept, go to the bottom of the page and press the button that says I studied the concepts. Only press it when you really did read them all. That button tells the page you have finished the reading part. Step 6: Under the page there is a deck of slides. The slides show the same concepts again, one idea on each slide. Press Start on the first slide to begin. This part helps you remember what you just learned. Step 7: On each slide, use the same buttons as before. Read the slide, listen if there is a Listen button, and say the idea out loud in your own words. I expect you to talk on every slide, even just one short sentence. Step 8: To move on, press the arrow on the right side of the slide. Look at the little dots under the slide — they show you which slide you are on and how many are left. Do not skip any slide. Step 9: When you reach the last slide, press the finish button. That is the end of the slide deck. Well done! How you will know the page is finished: you have read and listened to all 7 concepts, you have pressed I studied the concepts, and you have pressed the finish button on the last slide. Now start with Step 1, and come tell me what the first concept was about. I will be right here. 😊

explore.label: Explore the Concept
explore.text: Hello! Today I am your teacher for the "Explore the Concept" page in Unit 12: Measures (2). This page has 6 little discoveries. Each one shows you something real — a stone and a leaf, a balance scale, a cup and a jug, two pencils, hot soup, and measuring tools. You think about it, then you type what you found out. By the end, you will be able to say which thing is heavier, which holds more, which is longer, and which tool to use. You need your eyes, your thinking brain, and a grown-up nearby if you want to try it with real things. Here is what I expect from you: try your own idea first, in your own words. A short sentence is perfect. Guessing fast is not the goal — thinking slowly is. Mathematicians think slowly on purpose. Step 1. Look at the numbered tabs at the top. Press tab number 1. Read the little story and look at the picture or model. Take your time looking. I expect you to be able to tell me what you see, like "a stone and a leaf". Step 2. Now read the discovery question under the picture. Read it twice. Ask yourself, what is it really asking? I expect you to think before you type — no rushing. Step 3. Type your idea in the box. Use a full sentence if you can, like "The stone is heavier." Then press Check my idea. I expect your own words, not a copied word. Step 4. If it says Look again, that is fine. Mistakes are how we learn. Press Hint, read it slowly, then change your answer and press Check my idea one more time. Step 5. When it says Exactly!, look at the tab — it gets a tick. Well done! That tick means that discovery is finished. Step 6. Now press tab number 2 and do the very same thing: read, think, type, press Check my idea. Keep going like this for tabs 3, 4, 5 and 6, one at a time. I expect all six tabs to have a tick. Step 7. Now scroll down under the page. There is a deck of slides with the same discoveries, one on each slide. Press Start on the first slide. Step 8. On each slide, use the same buttons as before: read, type your idea, press Check my idea, and press Hint if you need help. Then press the arrow on the right to go to the next slide. Look at the little dots under the slide — they show you where you are. Step 9. On the last slide, press the finish button. That tells the page you are done. You will know the page is finished when every one of the 6 tabs has a tick, and you have pressed the finish button on the last slide. Ready? Press tab number 1 and tell me what you see. 🙂

words.label: Math Words & Symbols
words.text: Hello! Today I am your teacher for the Math Words & Symbols page. This page has the special words we use in Unit 12, Measures. Words like mass, capacity, taller and thermometer. We learn them so that when you measure something, you can say what you found in the right words. By the end, you will be able to say each word, say what it means, and use it in your own sentence. You need your voice, your ears, and your fingers for typing. Take your time — there is no rush. There are four steps. Here they all are. Step 1 — Read and listen. Look at the first word on the page. Read the word, then read what it means. Then press Listen and hear it said out loud. Listen carefully, and say it in your head with the voice. I expect you to look at the word while you listen, not away from the screen. Step 2 — Say it, mean it, write it. First say the word out loud, nice and clear. Next say what it means in your own words, not the words on the screen. For example, for mass you might say, "how heavy a thing is." Then type one sentence with the word in it and press Check sentence. A good sentence is about something real, like "My bag has more mass than my pencil." Then read what the checker says to you. If it asks you to change something, fix it and press Check sentence again. Do Step 1 and Step 2 for every word on the page. Step 3 — Say you are done. When you have finished every word, scroll to the bottom and press I know these words and symbols. Only press it when you really have done them all. That button tells the page you have finished this part. Step 4 — The slides. Under the page there is a deck of slides. Each slide has one of the same words. Press Start on the first slide. Do the same thing here: listen, say the word, say the meaning, and type your sentence. Then press the arrow on the right to go to the next slide. The little dots under the slide show you where you are. Keep going until the last slide, then press the finish button on it. You will know the page is finished when the I know these words and symbols button is pressed, and you have pressed the finish button on the last slide. Ready? Start with Step 1, and tell me which word you are on. I am right here with you. 😊

visuals.label: Visual Models
visuals.text:
Hello! Today we are on the Visual Models page. Visual models are pictures you can look at, touch and move. They show the big ideas of Unit 12: heavy and light, full and empty, long and tall, hot and cold. Looking at them helps the words stick in your head, because you see the idea, not just read it. Here is what I expect from you. Look slowly at each model. Move it with your finger or mouse if it moves. Say the idea out loud in your own words. There are 8 small steps. Take your time — there's no rush. 1. Find the first model, "Mass — Heavier and Lighter". Look at the two objects. If it moves, drag it to turn it around, and press any buttons you see. Ask yourself: which one is heavier? A good look means you can point and say, "This one is heavier, this one is lighter."

2. Now the second model, "Balancing and Non-Standard Units". This one shows a balance scale with stones. Drag it or press its buttons to add stones. Watch which side goes down. I expect you to notice this: the heavy side always goes down. 3. Next is "Capacity — Full, Empty, Holds More". Capacity means how much a container can hold inside. Look at the cups and jugs. Press the buttons to fill or empty them. Tell yourself which one holds more. 4. Now "Length and Height — Longer, Shorter, Taller". Look at how the objects line up at one end. That is our golden rule: line them up first, then it is a fair test. I expect you to say which one is longer and which is shorter. 5. Then "Temperature — Hot, Warm, Cold". Look at the pictures of hot, warm and cold things. Think of one thing in your own home for each word. Say them out loud, like "hot soup, warm bath water, cold ice". 6. Last is "Choosing the Right Tool". You will see the balance scale, the measuring cup, the ruler and the thermometer. Match each tool to its job. Good work here means you can say, "The thermometer tells us how hot something is."

7. Under every model there is a caption — a little sentence that tells you what the picture shows. Read it, then press Listen to hear it read to you. Do this for all six models. Listening while you read helps the words stay in your mind. 8. When you have looked at all six models and pressed Listen on each caption, scroll to the bottom. Press the button that says "I explored the models". You will know the page is finished when you have pressed "I explored the models" at the bottom. That button saves your work, so it must come from you, not me. Then come back and tell me which model was your favourite — I would love to know! 🌟

method.label: Learn the Method
method.text: Hello! I am your teacher today. Let's learn the methods in Unit 12: Measures. A method is a way to work something out, step by step. On this page there are 6 methods. They teach you how to compare things: which is heavier, which holds more, and which is longer. We go slowly, one step at a time. By the end, you will know the steps by heart. You need your voice, and a grown-up nearby is nice. Let's start with something small. Step 1. Look at the top of the page. Find the first method. Read its title and its very first step. Read it out loud, slowly. I expect you to say the words with your mouth, not just your eyes. Mathematicians think slowly on purpose. Step 2. Now press the button that says "Show me the next step". A new step will appear. Read this one out loud too. Ask yourself: what am I doing with my hands in this step? Picture it in your head, like a little film. Step 3. Keep pressing "Show me the next step" again and again. Say every step out loud as it comes. Do not rush. Stop when you see the words "Method complete". That means you have reached the end of that method. Well done — one method finished! Step 4. Now do the same for the next method. Read step one out loud, then press "Show me the next step" until you see "Method complete" again. I expect you to say the steps out loud every time. Saying them helps your brain remember them. Step 5. Keep going until all 6 methods say "Method complete". After each one, try this: tell your grown-up what that method taught you, in your own words. That is how I know it is really in your head. Step 6. Now scroll down to the bottom of the page. There is a deck of slides there. Each slide has one of the same methods on it. This is your practice round — the same steps, one more time. Step 7. On the first slide, press "Start". Then use the same buttons as before to move through the steps, one at a time. Say each step out loud again. It is not boring to say it twice — saying it twice is how it sticks. Step 8. When that slide is done, press the arrow on the right side to go to the next slide. Look at the little dots under the slide. The dots show you where you are, and how many slides are left. Step 9. Do every slide the same way: press "Start", step through to the end, then press the right arrow. Take your time — there's no rush. Step 10. On the last slide, press the finish button. That tells the page you are done. I do not press it for you — you press it, because it is your work. How will you know the page is finished? All 6 methods say "Method complete", every dot under the slides has been visited, and you have pressed the finish button on the last slide. Then you are done! Now go and do Step 1. Come back and tell me the name of the first method, and I will help you with the next bit. 😊

examples.label: Worked Examples
examples.text: Hello! Today we are on the Worked Examples page. A worked example is a question with the answer already worked out for you, step by step. We do this so you can see how a good thinker thinks. By the end, you will know how to compare things by heavy, light, how much they hold, and how long they are. You need your eyes, your brain, and maybe a pencil and paper. Let's go! Step 1: Look at the first worked example. Read the question by yourself, or ask your grown-up to read it with you. Do not press anything yet. Step 2: Try it in your head first. Say your answer out loud, like this: "The stone is heavier than the leaf." I expect you to guess before you look. Guessing first helps your brain grow. Step 3: Now press Show worked solution. Read it slowly, line by line. Ask yourself, "Did I think the same way?" It is okay if you did not. Mistakes are how we learn. Step 4: Do the same for every worked example on the page. Read, guess, then press Show worked solution. There are 12 of them, so take your time. Take your time — there's no rush. Step 5: Look at the counter at the top of the page. It tells you how many you have opened. Keep going until every one is open. The page is finished when all 12 are opened. Step 6: Now scroll down under the page. There is a deck of slides. They have the same examples, one on each slide. Press Start on the first slide. Step 7: On each slide, use the same buttons. Read the question, guess your answer, then press Show worked solution. I expect you to say your answer out loud each time, even if nobody is listening. Step 8: Press the arrow on the right to go to the next slide. Look at the little dots under the slide. They show you where you are in the deck. Step 9: Keep going slide by slide until the last one. On the last slide, press the finish button. You will know the page is finished when the counter at the top shows all of them opened, and you have pressed the finish button on the last slide. Now go and do Step 1. Tell me when you are ready, and I will help you with the first one! 🌟

guided.label: Guided Practice
guided.text:
Hello! I am your teacher today, and this page is our practice time. This page has 12 little questions about measuring. You will say which thing is heavier, which holds more, and which is longer. We do this so the words heavier, lighter, holds more and longer become easy for you. You will need your eyes, your thinking, and maybe a pencil and paper. Here is the whole plan, step by step. Step 1: Read the first question slowly. Read it twice. Then picture it in your head. If it asks which is heavier, imagine holding one thing in each hand. Which hand goes down? That one is heavier. I expect you to think first, before you type anything. Mathematicians think slowly on purpose. Step 2: Type your answer in the box, then press Check my answer. Use the unit words, like heavier, lighter, holds more, holds less, longer or shorter. A good answer is a short sentence, like "The stone is heavier." I expect real words, not a guess typed fast. Step 3: If you feel stuck, press Give me a hint. You can press it up to three times. Each hint tells you a little more. Try again after each hint before pressing for the next one. Being stuck is fine — it means your brain is working. Step 4: If the hints are not enough, press Show next step. That shows you one line of the working. Read it, then finish the rest yourself. I expect you to still type your own answer after that. Step 5: If your answer is not right, do not worry. Mistakes are how we learn. Read the question again, ask what it is really asking, then try once more. Step 6: Do this for every question, from question 1 to question 12. Keep going until each question is marked right. Take your time — there is no rush. Step 7: Now look under the page. There is a deck of slides with the same questions, one on each slide. Press Start on the first slide. Step 8: On each slide, use the same buttons: type your answer, press Check my answer, and press Give me a hint or Show next step if you need help. Say your answer out loud too. Saying it helps it stick. Step 9: When a slide is right, press the arrow on the right to go to the next slide. Look at the little dots under the slide. They show you where you are in the deck. Step 10: On the last slide, press the finish button. That tells the page you are done. How will you know the page is finished? When all 12 questions are marked right, and you have pressed the finish button on the last slide. 🌟

Now start with question 1. Read it twice, then tell me your answer and how you worked it out. I am right here.

activities.label: Activities
activities.text: Hello! Today we are doing our Activities page for Unit 12: Measures (2). This is the fun part where you touch real things — cups, stones, pencils — and see the maths with your own hands. Measuring is not just words on a page; it is feeling which thing is heavier, and pouring to see which holds more. By the end you will be able to show someone at home what you learned, in your own way. You will need a pencil, some paper, and a few things from around your house. Here is what I expect from you: try things for real, use our unit words (heavier, lighter, holds more, holds less, longer, taller, hot, warm, cold), and write down what you noticed. Neat is nice, but honest thinking is better. Step 1. Look at the hands-on activity on the page. There is one activity, called "Practise together". Press Listen to hear it read out loud. Then go and get the things it names: paper, a pencil, and some everyday objects from home. Good work here means you listen right to the end, then bring your things back to your table before you start. Ask your grown-up to help you find the objects if you need. Step 2. Now do the activity. Pick ONE idea from our unit — like heavier and lighter, or holds more and holds less, or longer and taller. Draw it or build it. For example, you could draw a balance scale with a stone going down and a leaf going up. Then explain your picture to someone in your family, out loud. Last, write one question of your own, like "Which holds more, a spoon or a cup?" and write the answer too. Then write in the box what you did and what you noticed. One or two sentences is plenty, and try to use a unit word. Step 3. When you have really done it and written in the box, press Mark complete under the activity. Only press it after you have done it — that button is your promise that the work is finished. When every activity is marked, press Finish activities at the bottom of the page. Step 4. Now look under the page. There is a deck of slides with the same hands-on activity, one on each slide. Press Start on the first slide. Use the same buttons on each slide, just like you did above. Press the arrow on the right to go to the next slide. The little dots under the slide show you where you are. On the last slide, press Finish activities. You will know the page is finished when every activity says complete, you have pressed Finish activities, and you have reached the last dot on the slides. Now, tell me: which idea from our unit will you choose for your model? Take your time — there's no rush.

fluency.label: Math Fluency
fluency.text: Hello! Today we are doing Math Fluency. It is a quick sprint of 12 little questions about Unit 12. You will say which thing is heavier, which is lighter, which holds more, and which is longer. We do this to make your thinking fast and sure. All you need is your eyes, your brain, and a comfy seat. Here are all the steps. 1. Look at the top of the page. You will see a timer. It counts your time while you work. Do not worry about it. Take your time — there's no rush. I expect you to try your best, not to be the fastest. 2. Read question one carefully. It will ask something like which is heavier, a rock or a cotton ball. Read it twice before you answer. I expect you to picture holding one thing in each hand. 3. Type your answer in the box. Short words are fine, like "the rock" or "heavier". Then press Check & continue. I expect one clear answer, not a guess. 4. If your answer is right, cheer inside and keep going. If it is not right, read the little help message. It tells you the common mistake. I expect you to read it, not skip it. 5. Now do the same for every question, one at a time. Read, think, type, press Check & continue. There are 12 questions in all. I expect you to finish all 12, even the tricky ones. 6. Remember our big rule for mass: bigger does not always mean heavier. A big fluffy cotton ball is lighter than a small rock. I expect you to feel it in your mind before you answer. 7. Remember our rule for capacity: ask which one holds more inside. Imagine pouring water from one into the other. I expect you to pour it in your head first. 8. Remember our rule for length: line both things up at one end. Then see which one reaches further. I expect you to check that they start from the same line. 9. When the sprint ends, look at your score. You need most of them right to finish the page. I expect you to be proud of every one you got right. 10. If you got fewer than you need, press Run the sprint again. That is not failing — that is practice. Mistakes are how we learn. I expect you to try once more with a calm mind. You will know the page is finished when you complete a sprint with enough right answers. The page will tell you. Then you can smile — you did it! Now, step 1. Look at the top of your page and find the timer. Tell me when you can see it. 😊

explain.label: Explain Your Thinking
explain.text:
Hello! Today we are doing "Explain Your Thinking."

On this page you do not just give an answer. You tell me HOW you know. That is what real mathematicians do. It helps the words stick, like mass, heavier, lighter, and balance scale. You need your reading eyes, your thinking brain, and maybe a grown-up to help you type. Here is the whole plan. Step 1. There are 6 prompts on this page. Read the first one slowly, then read it again. Under the prompt you will see the key ideas. Those are the special maths words you must use in your answer. I expect you to point at each key idea and say it out loud before you write. Step 2. Now think before you write. Ask yourself three little questions: What do I know? What rule did I use? Why does my answer make sense? For example, the rule might be "the balance scale tips down on the heavier side." Take your time — mathematicians think slowly on purpose. Step 3. Type your answer in the box. Use the key ideas words in your sentences. A good answer has two or three sentences, not just one word. Then press Check mathematical ideas. Step 4. Read what the page says back to you. If it asks for more, do not worry — that just means one idea is missing. Add that idea to your box and press Check mathematical ideas again. I expect you to try again instead of giving up. Step 5. Now press Show model explanation. This shows a good answer so you can compare. Look for words you used and words you missed. You do not need to copy it — your own words are best. Step 6. Do the same thing for all 6 prompts. Read, think, write, press Check mathematical ideas, then Show model explanation. Go one prompt at a time. Take a little rest if your hand gets tired. Step 7. Now look under the page. There is a deck of slides with the same prompts, one prompt on each slide. Press Start on the first slide. Step 8. On each slide, use the same buttons as before: type your answer, press Check mathematical ideas, then press Show model explanation. Say your answer out loud too. Speaking helps the words stay in your head. Step 9. Press the arrow on the right to go to the next slide. Look at the little dots under the slide — they show you where you are. Keep going, one slide at a time. Step 10. On the last slide, press the finish button. That tells the page you are done. You will know the page is finished when every one of the 6 explanations uses the key ideas, and you have pressed the finish button on the last slide. Ready? Start with prompt one, and tell me when you have written your answer. I will be right here. 🙂

games.label: Games
games.text: Hello! I am your teacher today. This page is our Games page for Unit 12, Measures. These games ask you about heavy and light, full and empty, long and short, and hot and cold. We play them so those measuring words stick in your head. By the end, you will answer measuring questions quickly and feel sure about them. You need your eyes, your thinking brain, and maybe a grown-up sitting near you. Here are the three steps. I will tell you what to press and what I expect from you. 1. Find a game on the page and press Start game. A question will pop up with some answers to choose from. Read the whole question first, then think for a moment before you tap. Every round you get right gives you a star. I expect you to think, not to guess fast. If a question is tricky, picture the real thing in your hands, like a stone and a feather. Mathematicians think slowly on purpose. 2. When the game ends, press Play again to try more rounds and earn more stars. A game is mastered when it has all its stars. So keep playing that same game until its stars are full. If you get one wrong, that is fine — read the little explanation, then try again. Mistakes are how we learn. I expect you to finish one game fully before you hop to another one. 3. Now do the same for every game on the page. Press Start game, answer the rounds, press Play again, and fill up the stars. Take them one at a time, from the top. If you get tired, stop and come back later — that is allowed. I expect you to try your best on each one, not to rush to the end. You will know the page is finished when every game has all its stars. The page finishes by itself then — you do not need to press anything extra. Ready? Press Start game on the first game, then tell me how it went. 🌟

challenge.label: Unit Challenge
challenge.text: Welcome to your Unit Challenge! This is the last part of Unit 12: Measures (2). It is like a friendly test. You will answer 12 questions about heavier and lighter, holds more and holds less, longer and taller, hot and cold, and the right tool for each job. We do it to show what your brain has learned. You need your eyes, your thinking, and a comfy seat. I cannot tell you the answers — but I can help you think. Take your time — there's no rush. Here is what to do, step by step. Step 1. Read question one slowly. Read it twice. Ask yourself: is this question about how heavy, how much it holds, how long, or how hot? Knowing that helps you pick the right answer. Step 2. Picture it in your head. If it says heavy, imagine holding one thing in each hand and feel which pulls down. If it says holds more, imagine pouring one into the other. If it says longer, imagine lining both ends up at the same line. I expect you to imagine first, then choose. Step 3. Click the answer you think is right. Only one answer. Do not rush and do not just pick the biggest thing — remember, bigger does not always mean heavier. Step 4. Press Next question. Then do the same thing again for the next one: read twice, picture it, choose, press Next question. Keep going until all 12 are done. Step 5. If a question feels hard, look for the hint on the page, or come and tell me the question. I will give you a small hint, not the answer. The answer needs to come from you — I'll help you get there. Step 6. At the end you will see your score. This tells you how many you got right. You pass when more than half are right. Look at any you got wrong and read why — mistakes are how we learn. Step 7. If your score is not high enough, press Try again. That is not a bad thing! It just means one more turn to practise. Read even more slowly this time. Step 8. When your score is good, press Continue. That finishes the page. You will know the page is finished when you have seen your score, you passed, and you have pressed Continue. Ready? Tell me when you have read question one, and I will help you think about it. 🌟

problems.label: Solve Real Problems
problems.text: Hello! I am your teacher today, and this page is called Solve Real Problems. On this page you use what you learned about measures in real life. You will think about heavy and light, holds more and holds less, and taller and shorter. By the end you will be able to look at a real situation, like a bathtub and a sink, and say which one holds more and why. All you need is your thinking brain, and maybe a grown-up nearby to help you type. Here is what I expect from you. Read slowly. Say your answer in a full sentence, like "The bathtub holds more than the sink." And tell me why you think so. Take your time — there's no rush. Step 1. Read the first problem out loud. Ask yourself: what is this question really asking? Is it about heavy and light, or about how much fits inside, or about tall and short? I expect you to know which one before you answer. Step 2.
