Now work it out in your head. Picture the two things. Imagine holding them, or pouring one into the other, or standing them side by side. Good thinking looks like a picture in your mind, not a guess. Step 3. Type your answer in the box. Write the answer and one short "because". For example: "…holds more, because you could fit a whole child inside it." Then press Check answer. Step 4. If you feel stuck, press Hint. The hint gives you a little push, not the answer. Read it, think again, then type your own answer. Step 5. When the page says your answer is right, that problem is done. Well done! Move on to the next problem and do Steps 1 to 4 again. There are 6 problems in all. Step 6. Now look under the page. There is a deck of slides with the same problems, one problem on each slide. On the first slide, press Start. Step 7. On each slide, use the same buttons as before: type your answer, press Check answer, and press Hint only if you need help. Step 8. To go to the next slide, press the arrow on the right. Look at the little dots under the slide. They show you which slide you are on and how many are left. Step 9. On the last slide, press the finish button. That tells the page you are all done. You will know the page is finished when all 6 problems say your answer is right, and you have pressed the finish button on the last slide. Ready? Tell me the first problem when you have read it, and we will look at that together.

overview.label: Unit Overview
overview.text: Hello! I am your teacher today. Welcome to Unit 13: Working with Numbers to 20. This page is called the Unit Overview. "Overview" means a quick look at the whole unit before we start. It tells you what we will learn and what you will be able to do at the end. We do this so your brain knows what is coming — like looking at a picture of a place before you go there. Here is what I expect from you: read slowly, listen carefully, and use your own voice. You will need a pencil, and maybe 20 small things to count, like beans, bottle caps or stones. There are 3 steps on this page. 1. Read the Unit Overview. Look at the words on the screen and read them, slowly, with your eyes and your mouth. Where you see a little speaker picture, press Listen. Then read along while you listen. Doing it well means you do not rush — you read every line once, and listen once. I expect you to notice the words we will use a lot: add, take away, count on, count back, and number line. 2. Say in your own words what you will learn. Do not copy the words on the screen. Say it like you are telling your grown-up or a friend. For example you might say, "I will learn to add and take away numbers up to 20, and hop on a number line." That is a good answer because it says WHAT you will do. You can say it out loud, or type it here to me. I expect one or two sentences, in your own words. 3. Press Continue to go to The Lesson. When you have read the overview and said what you will learn, find the Continue button and press it. That takes you to The Lesson, where we start counting on and counting back for real. Only press it when you have finished steps 1 and 2 — no skipping! You will know this page is finished when you have read the overview, pressed Listen, told me in your own words what you will learn, and pressed Continue to move on. Now let's begin with step 1. Read the Unit Overview and press Listen. Take your time — there's no rush. Tell me when you are done. 😊

lesson.label: The Lesson
lesson.text: Hello! Today I am your teacher, and this page is called The Lesson. Here is what we are doing. This page teaches you 7 big ideas about adding and taking away numbers up to 20. We do it so you can add fast, take away safely, and check your own work. By the end you will be able to count on, count back, and hop on a number line. You will need a pencil, some paper, and about 20 small things you can count — beans, stones, or bottle caps are perfect. Your voice too! Ready? Here are all the steps. Step 1. Look at the top of the page. Find the first concept, called Adding by Counting On. Read it slowly, all the way to the end. Slow is good — mathematicians think slowly on purpose. Step 2. Now press Listen on that same concept. Listen to the whole thing while your eyes follow the words. I expect your eyes to move along with the voice, not wander away. Step 3. Find the example in that concept. Say it out loud, in a big clear voice. Saying it out loud helps your brain keep it. Step 4. Now try it with your own counters. For counting on, make a pile of 12 beans and a pile of 5. Start at 12 and touch the small pile one at a time: 13, 14, 15, 16, 17. I expect you to say the numbers out loud and land on the last one — that is your answer. Step 5. Do Steps 1 to 4 again for every concept on the page. There are 7 in all: Adding by Counting On, Subtracting by Counting Back, Using the Number Line, Combining and Taking Away in Stories, Part-Whole and Comparing to 20, Bridging Through 10, and Checking Your Answer. Read it, press Listen, say the example out loud, then try it with your counters. One concept at a time, no skipping. Step 6. When all 7 are done, scroll to the bottom of the page. Press the button that says I studied the concepts. Only press it if you really read them all — that button is your promise to yourself. Step 7. Under the page you will see a deck of slides. They show the same 7 ideas, one idea on each slide. On the first slide, press Start. Step 8. On each slide, use the same buttons you see there, just like you did on the first slide. Read the slide, listen if there is a Listen button, and say the example out loud. Then press the arrow on the right to go to the next slide. Step 9. Look at the little dots under the slide. They show where you are in the deck. More dots filled means you are getting closer to the end. Keep going, one slide at a time. Step 10. On the very last slide, press the finish button. That closes the deck nicely. How you will know the page is finished: you have read and listened to all 7 concepts, you have pressed I studied the concepts, and you have gone through every slide and pressed the finish button on the last one. One little job for me: when you finish Step 4 with your beans, come back and tell me what number you landed on. I will check it with you. Take your time — there's no rush.

words.label: Math Words & Symbols
words.text:
Hello! Today I am your teacher for the Math Words & Symbols page. This page teaches you the special words we use in Unit 13, like count on, count back, and number line. We learn the words first, because when you know the words, the maths story makes sense. By the end you will be able to say each word, tell what it means, and use it in your own sentence. You will need your voice, your eyes, and your fingers for typing. A grown-up can sit near you to help. There are four steps. Here they are, all together, so you know the plan. 1. Read and listen. Look at the first word on the page and read what it means. Then press Listen and hear the word said out loud. Do this for every word, one at a time, from the top to the bottom. I expect you to go slowly and really listen — not rush to the end. Take your time — there's no rush. 2. Say it, then write it. For each word, say the word out loud in a big clear voice. Then say the meaning in your OWN words, not the words on the screen. For example, for count on you might say, "It means I start at a number and go forward." Then type one sentence using that word and press Check sentence. A good sentence uses the word the right way, like "I count on from 12 to add 5." Read what the checker tells you. If it says to fix something, change your sentence and press Check sentence again. I expect a real sentence from your own head, even a short one. 🙂

3. Press the big button. When you have done EVERY word — listened, said it, and checked a sentence — press I know these words and symbols at the bottom of the page. Only press it when all the words are done. That button tells the page you are ready. 4. Do the slides. Under the page there is a deck of slides. Each slide has one of the same words. On the first slide, press Start. Then use the same buttons on that slide as you did above: Listen, say it out loud, type your sentence, press Check sentence. When that slide is done, press the arrow on the right to go to the next slide. Look at the little dots under the slide — they show you how far you have come. On the last slide, press the finish button. How will you know the page is finished? When every word has a checked sentence, the I know these words and symbols button has been pressed, and you have pressed the finish button on the last slide. Then you are done! Now begin with step 1. Press Listen on your first word, then tell me which word it is and what it means in your own words. I will be right here. 🌟

explore.label: Explore the Concept
explore.text: Hello! I am your teacher today. Let's look at this page together. This page is called Explore the Concept. It has 6 little discoveries about adding and taking away numbers up to 20. We do it so you can find the ideas yourself, not just be told them. By the end you will know how to count on to add, count back to take away, and hop on a number line the right way. What you need: a pencil, some paper, and about 20 small things you can count — beans, stones, buttons or bottle caps. A grown-up can sit with you. What I expect from you: read slowly, think first, then type your own idea in your own words. A short answer is fine. Guessing fast is not — thinking is the work. Mathematicians think slowly on purpose. Here are the steps. 1. Look at the top of the page for the numbered tabs, 1 to 6. Press tab number 1. Read the little story, and look at the picture or model under it. Say the numbers out loud as you read. I expect you to touch or count your beans to match the story before you answer. 2. Now read the discovery question. Stop and think. Then type your idea in the box and press Check my idea. Write what you think AND why, like "12, because 12 is the bigger number." That "because" is what I am looking for. 3. If the page says Look again, do not worry. Mistakes are how we learn. Press Hint, read it carefully, then change your answer and press Check my idea one more time. When it says Exactly!, that tab gets a tick. Well done — one done! 4. Press tab number 2 and do the same thing: read, think, type, press Check my idea. Keep going through tabs 3, 4, 5 and 6, one at a time. Do not skip any. The page is finished when all 6 tabs have a tick. 5. Now scroll down under the page. There is a deck of slides with the same discoveries, one on each slide. Press Start on the first slide. 6. On each slide, use the same buttons: type your idea, press Check my idea, press Hint if you need help. Then press the arrow on the right to move to the next slide. The little dots under the slide show you where you are. 7. On the last slide, press the finish button. That means you are all done! You will know the page is finished when every one of the 6 tabs has a tick, and you have pressed the finish button on the last slide. Ready? Press tab number 1 and tell me what the story says. I am right here with you. 😊

method.label: Learn the Method
method.text: Hello! Today I am your teacher for the "Learn the Method" page. A method is a way to work something out, step by step. This page has 6 methods for adding and taking away up to 20. We do this so your brain learns the right order of steps, not just the answer. By the end, you will be able to count on, count back, and use a number line all by yourself. You will need a pencil, some paper, and about 20 small things to count — beans, buttons, or bottle caps. You will also need your voice, because we say the steps out loud! Here is what I expect from you: read every step slowly, say it out loud, and try it with your counters before you press the next button. No rushing. Mathematicians think slowly on purpose. 1. Look at the first method on the page. Read the first step out loud. Then press "Show me the next step" to see step two. Do not press fast — read each step first, then press. 2. Keep pressing "Show me the next step" until the page says "Method complete". Say every step out loud as it appears, and do the counting with your fingers or your counters. Good work looks like this: your mouth is moving and your fingers are hopping. 3. Now do the very same thing for every method — all 6 of them. Read, say it out loud, press "Show me the next step", until each one says "Method complete". After each method, tell yourself in your own words what it teaches, like "start at the bigger number and count on". 4. Now look under the page. There is a deck of slides. Each slide has one method on it, the same as before. On the first slide, press "Start". 5. On each slide, use the same buttons you already know. Press to see the next step, until that slide's method is finished. Say the numbers out loud again — saying them helps you not lose count. 6. When one slide is finished, press the arrow on the right to go to the next slide. Look at the little dots under the slide. They show you where you are and how many slides are left. 7. Keep going slide by slide, the same way, until you reach the last slide. On the last slide, press the finish button. You will know the page is finished when all 6 methods say "Method complete", and you have pressed the finish button on the last slide. Off you go with step 1. When you have done the first method, come back and tell me what its steps were — I will be right here waiting. 🙂

visuals.label: Visual Models
visuals.text:
Hello! Today I am your teacher for the Visual Models page. Let me tell you what we are doing. Visual models are pictures of maths. They show adding and taking away so you can SEE them, not just hear them. By the end, you will know how to count on, count back, and hop on a number line. You need your eyes, your finger, and about 20 small things to count — beans, stones, or bottle caps. Grab them now. Here is what I expect from you today. Look at every model slowly. Touch it, drag it, press its buttons. Say the numbers out loud as you count. Slow is good — mathematicians think slowly on purpose. There are 8 steps. Here they all are. Step 1: Find the first model, Adding by Counting On. Look at it carefully. If it moves, drag it with your finger to turn it. Press its buttons to change the numbers. I want you to see the big number first, then the small hops after it. Say each hop out loud: "13, 14, 15..." Good work looks like this: you can tell me which number you started at. Step 2: Under that model there is a caption. A caption is the words that tell you about the picture. Read it. Then press Listen and hear it read to you. I expect you to listen all the way to the end, then say the caption back in your own words. Step 3: Now go to model two, Subtracting by Counting Back. Look at it and press its buttons. Watch which way the hops go. Take away means going backward. Then read the caption and press Listen. I expect you to point with your finger which way "back" is. Step 4: Go to model three, Using the Number Line. A number line is a row of numbers in order, like a ruler for numbers. Put your finger on a number and slide it forward, then backward. Press the buttons to make jumps. Read the caption and press Listen. I expect you to say out loud: "Forward to add. Backward to take away."

Step 5: Go to model four, Combining and Taking Away in Stories. This one shows maths inside a little story. Look at the picture and ask yourself: are things joining, or are things leaving? Press the buttons to see it change. Read the caption and press Listen. I expect you to say "add" or "take away" for the story you see. Step 6: Go to model five, Part-Whole and Comparing to 20. This shows one whole number split into two parts, like 15 is 10 and 5. Press the buttons to see different splits. Use your beans too — put 15 in one pile, then share them into two piles. Read the caption and press Listen. I expect you to find two different ways to split the same number. Step 7: Go to model six. This one shows the mistake of hopping the wrong way. Look at it and find the hop that goes the wrong way. Press its buttons and read the caption, then press Listen. I expect you to tell me why that hop is wrong. Step 8: Now check you have seen all six models and pressed Listen under each one. When you have, press the button at the bottom that says "I explored the models". Only press it after you really looked at them all. You will know the page is finished when you have pressed "I explored the models" at the bottom. That is your work being saved — I cannot press it for you, so it must be you. 🌟

Ready? Start with Step 1, then come back and tell me which number you started at.

examples.label: Worked Examples
examples.text: Hello! Today I am your teacher for the Worked Examples page. A worked example is a maths question with all the working shown. It is like watching someone else count, step by step. We do this so you can see HOW to count on and count back, not just the answer. By the end, you will be able to add and take away to 20 and show your jumps. You need a pencil, some paper, and about 20 small things to count — beans, stones or bottle caps are perfect. Here are your steps. There are 6. Step 1. Look at the first worked example on the page. Read the question slowly, out loud if you can. Do not press anything yet. I expect you to know what it is asking — is it adding (putting together) or taking away? Step 2. Try it yourself first, on your paper. Start at the bigger number and count on for adding, or count back for taking away. Write your answer down. Even a guess is fine — trying first is what makes the next step work. I expect one written answer before you peek. Step 3. Now press Show worked solution. Read the solution line by line and compare it with your paper. Ask yourself: did I start at the same number? Did I count the same number of hops? If you got it right, lovely. If not, that is fine — mistakes are how we learn — just find the one line where yours went a different way. Step 4. Do the same thing for all 12 worked examples: read, try it on paper, then press Show worked solution and compare. Look at the counter at the top — it tells you how many you have opened. I expect it to reach all 12. Take your time — there's no rush. Step 5. Now scroll down to the slides under the page. They have the same examples, one on each slide. On the first slide press Start. Use the same buttons on each slide: read, try it, then show the solution. Press the arrow on the right to move to the next slide. The little dots under the slide show you where you are. Step 6. Keep going until the last slide, then press the finish button. That tells the page you are done. You will know the page is finished when the counter at the top shows all 12 opened, and you have pressed the finish button on the last slide. Ready? Start with Step 1 and tell me when you have read the first question. 😊

guided.label: Guided Practice
guided.text: Hello! Today we are on Guided Practice. This page has 12 questions about adding and taking away numbers up to 20. We practise so that counting on and counting back become fast and easy for you. Get a pencil, some paper, and about 20 small things you can count, like beans or bottle caps. Ready? Here are all the steps. 1. Read the first question slowly. Say it out loud if you like. Then work it out on your paper or in your head. For adding, start at the bigger number and count on. For taking away, start at the bigger number and count back. I expect you to think first, before you type. Mathematicians think slowly on purpose. 2. Type your answer in the box. Then press Check my answer. I expect one number in the box, like 17 — not a whole sentence. If the page says you are right, smile and move on! 3. If you feel stuck, press Give me a hint. You can get up to three hints. Try again after each hint before you ask for the next one. Hints are not cheating — they are like holding a grown-up's hand. 4. If a hint is still not enough, press Show next step. That shows you one line of the working. Read it, then finish the rest by yourself. I expect you to try again after every hint or step, because the answer needs to come from you. 5. If your answer is not right, do not worry. Mistakes are how we learn. Check two things: did you start at the bigger number, and did you hop the right way? Forward to add, backward to take away. Then try again. 6. Do this for every question, from question 1 all the way to question 12, until each one is right. Take your time — there is no rush. 7. Now look under the page. There is a deck of slides with the same questions, one per slide. Press Start on the first slide. 8. On each slide, use the same buttons: type your answer, press Check my answer, and use Give me a hint or Show next step if you need help. I expect you to work it out again, not just remember the answer. 9. To go to the next slide, press the arrow on the right. Look at the little dots under the slide — they show you where you are in the deck. 10. On the last slide, press the finish button. Well done — that is the end! You will know the page is finished when all 12 questions are right and you have pressed the finish button on the last slide. Now go and read question 1. Tell me the question and what you think the answer is, and I will check it with you. 😊

activities.label: Activities
activities.text:
Hello! Today I am your teacher for the Activities page. This page is where you stop reading and start doing. You will use real things you can hold, like beans or bottle caps, to add and take away numbers up to 20. This helps the maths stick in your fingers and your head, not just your eyes. You will need paper, a pencil, and about 20 small objects — dates, stones, beans, buttons or caps. Here is the whole page, step by step. Step 1: Read the activity, then press Listen. There is 1 hands-on activity on this page. It is called "Practise together". Read it slowly. Then press Listen to hear it read out loud — listening is a great way to catch anything you missed. It will name what to get: paper, a pencil, and things from around your home you can count. Go and fetch them now and put them on the table. Step 2: Do the activity with your hands. First, pick one idea from this unit — counting on, counting back, or splitting a number into two parts. Then build it or draw it. For example, put 15 beans in one pile, then share them into two piles and count each one. Next, explain your model to someone at home, out loud. Last, make up your own question, like "13 add 4 is ____", and solve it by counting on. Step 3: Write in the box. In the answer box, write what you did and what you noticed. A good answer has a number sentence in it, like 15 = 10 + 5, or 13 + 4 = 17. Try to add one thing you noticed, such as "I started at the bigger number." I expect neat, small writing and your own words — not a copy of mine. Step 4: Press Mark complete. When your box is filled in, press Mark complete under the activity. Only press it when you really did the doing part with your objects. That button tells the page, "I have finished this one."

Step 5: Press Finish activities. When every activity is marked, scroll to the bottom and press Finish activities. That saves your work for today. Step 6: The slides at the bottom. Under the page there is a deck of slides. Each slide has the same hands-on activity, one per slide. Press Start on the first slide. Use the same buttons on each slide: Listen, write in the box, then Mark complete. Step 7: Move through the slides. Press the arrow on the right to go to the next slide. Look at the little dots under the slide — they show you where you are and how many are left. Take your time on each one. Step 8: Finish the deck. On the last slide, press Finish activities. Now you are done. You will know the page is finished when every activity shows as marked complete, and you have pressed Finish activities at the bottom and on the last slide. Let's start with something small. Go and get your 20 objects, your paper and your pencil, then tell me when they are on the table.

games.label: Games
games.text: Hello! Today we are playing the Games page for Unit 13, Working with Numbers to 20. These games ask you to add, take away, and use a number line. We play them because games help your brain get quick at counting on and counting back. By the end, you will add and subtract to 20 faster and with more confidence. You will need a pencil, some paper, and about 20 small things to count — beans, stones, or bottle caps. Here is what I expect from you: think before you press. Say the counting out loud, like "13, 14, 15, 16, 17." Take your time — mathematicians think slowly on purpose. And if you get one wrong, that is fine. Mistakes are how we learn. There are 3 steps. Here they all are. 1. Pick one game and press Start game. A question will pop up with some choices. Read it twice. Then work it out — if it says add, start at the BIGGER number and count on. If it says take away, start at the big number and count back. Use your beans or your fingers if you like. Then press the choice you think is right. You get a star for every round you get right. I expect you to count it out first, not just guess. 2. When the game ends, press Play again to earn more stars. The questions come back so you can do better this time. Try to fix the kind you got wrong before. Remember the rule: forward to add, backward to take away. A game is mastered when it has all its stars. I expect you to keep playing that game until its stars are full. 3. Now do the same for every game on the page. Press Start game on the next one, answer the rounds, and press Play again until all its stars are filled. Then move to the next game. Go one game at a time — do not rush ahead. I expect you to finish each game's stars before you start a new one. You will know the page is finished when every game has all its stars. The page finishes by itself then — you do not need to press anything extra. Ready? Pick your first game and press Start game. Tell me when you have played your first round, and tell me one question you got. 🌟

fluency.label: Math Fluency
fluency.text: Hello! I am your teacher today. This page is called Math Fluency. It is a sprint — a quick, fun race with 12 small questions about adding and taking away up to 20. We do it so counting on and counting back become fast and easy in your head. Get a pencil, some paper, and about 20 small things you can count, like beans or bottle caps. Take a breath — you know this! 1. Look at the top of the page. You will see a timer counting your time. Do not worry about it. Mathematicians think slowly on purpose. It is only there to show you how quick you are getting, week by week. 2. Read question one carefully. Say it out loud if that helps. Ask yourself: is this an adding question or a taking away question? Adding means putting groups together. Taking away means some go away. 3. For an adding question, start at the BIGGER number. Hold it in your head. Then count on the smaller number, one hop at a time. For 12 add 5, say: 13, 14, 15, 16, 17. The number you land on is your answer. 4. For a take away question, start at the bigger number and count BACK. For 14 take away 6, say: 13, 12, 11, 10, 9, 8. Remember our rule: forward to add, backward to take away. Use your fingers or your beans for each hop so you do not lose count. 5. Now type your answer in the box and press Check & continue. I expect you to type a number, not a guess — even if you counted slowly on your fingers. A slow right answer is better than a fast wrong one. 6. The page will tell you if you were right. If you were right, smile and keep going. If not, read the little help message. It will show you where the count went wrong. Mistakes are how we learn. 7. Keep going the same way for all 12 questions: read, decide add or take away, count the hops, type, then press Check & continue. Some questions ask you to explain or to split a number into two parts, like 14 equals 10 and 4. For those, just type your two parts. 8. When the sprint ends, look at your score. You need MOST of them right to finish this page. That is what I expect from you — not perfect, but most. 9. If you got too few right, do not feel sad. Press Run the sprint again. This time, go a little slower and touch a bean for every hop. You will do better — you always do the second time. 10. You will know the page is finished when you finish a sprint with enough right answers. The page will show you that you have passed and let you move on. That is your green light! Now, are you ready? Press start and tell me question one — I am right here with you.

problems.label: Solve Real Problems
problems.text: Hello! Today I am your maths teacher, and this page is called Solve Real Problems. On this page you will meet 6 little stories about real life — dates in a bowl, mangoes at the market, people on a bus. Your job is to work out each one by counting on to add, or counting back to take away. We do this because maths is not only numbers on paper; it helps us in our real day. By the end, you will be able to read a story, decide add or take away, and find the answer. What you need: a pencil, some paper, and about 20 small things you can count — beans, stones, or bottle caps. What I expect from you: read slowly, count out loud, and always tell me HOW you got your answer, not just the number. Mathematicians think slowly on purpose. Here are all the steps. Step 1. Read the first problem on the page, out loud if you can. Read it twice. Ask yourself one question: are things coming together, or are some going away? "Gives her more" and "joined" mean add. "Sells" and "get off" mean take away. I expect you to say to yourself, "This is an adding story" or "This is a take-away story," before you count anything. Step 2. Now work it out. Find the bigger number and start there. To add, count on forward, one hop at a time. To take away, count back, one hop at a time. Use your beans or your fingers, and say each number out loud so you do not lose your place. Step 3. Type your working and your answer in the box, then press Check answer. Working means the story of your counting, like this: "Start at 11, count on 7: 12, 13, 14, 15, 16, 17, 18. Answer 18." I expect to see your hops, not only the last number. That is how I know your thinking is strong. Step 4. If you feel stuck, press Hint. The hint tells you where to start and which way to hop. Read it, then try again yourself. Getting stuck is normal — it is not a mistake, it is thinking. Step 5. When the page says your answer is right, that problem is done. Well done — tick it in your head and move to the next problem. If it says not right, do not worry. Count again slowly and check two things: did you start at the bigger number, and did you hop the right number of times? Step 6. Do the same for all 6 problems: read, decide add or take away, count, type your working, press Check answer. Take your time. There is no rush. Step 7. Now look under the page. There is a deck of slides with the same problems, one problem on each slide. Press Start on the first slide to begin. Step 8. On each slide, use the same buttons you already know: type your working, press Check answer, and press Hint if you need help. Then press the arrow on the right to go to the next slide. The little dots under the slide show you where you are — the more dots you pass, the closer you are to the end. Step 9. On the last slide, press the finish button. That saves your work for the whole deck. You will know the page is finished when all 6 problems say your answer is right, and you have pressed the finish button on the last slide. Ready? Read problem 1 now, and tell me one thing: is it an adding story or a take-away story? 😊

explain.label: Explain Your Thinking
explain.text: Hello! I am your teacher today, and this page is called Explain Your Thinking. On this page you do not just say the answer. You say HOW you worked it out. Talking about your thinking makes it stick in your brain. By the end, you will be able to say why we count on to add and count back to take away. You will need a pencil and paper next to you, and maybe 20 small things like beans or bottle caps to count. A grown-up can help you type. What I expect from you: a full sentence, not one word. Say the answer, say what you did, and use the key ideas words like count on, count back, and number line. Take your time — mathematicians think slowly on purpose. Here are the steps. Step 1. There are 6 prompts on this page. Read the first prompt slowly. Under it you will see the key ideas — those are the special maths words I want you to use. Read them out loud. If a prompt is a sum, work it out first with your fingers, your counters, or a number line. Step 2. Click in the box and write your explanation. Say three things: what you know, what rule you used, and why your answer makes sense. For example: "I started at the bigger number and counted on, so I landed on the total." Then press Check mathematical ideas. If it asks for more, add another sentence with a key idea word, and press it again. Step 3. Now press Show model explanation. This shows a good answer so you can compare. Do not copy it — just look and see if you used the key idea words too. Then do the same three steps for prompts 2, 3, 4, 5 and 6. Your explanation and mine do not have to match word for word. That is fine! Step 4. Under the page there is a deck of slides. Each slide has one of the same prompts. Press Start on the first slide. Write your explanation, press Check mathematical ideas, then press Show model explanation, just like before. Press the arrow on the right to go to the next slide. The little dots under the slide show you where you are. On the last slide, press the finish button. How you will know you are done: all 6 explanations are written and checked, every one uses the key ideas, and you have pressed the finish button on the last slide. Ready? Read prompt one and tell me what it says. I am right here with you. 😊

challenge.label: Unit Challenge
challenge.text: Hello! I am your teacher today, and this is our Unit Challenge. The Unit Challenge is the last part of Unit 13. It shows what you have learned about adding and taking away up to 20. You will count on, count back, use a number line, and split numbers into parts. Get a pencil, some paper, and about 20 small things you can count, like beans or bottle caps. I will not tell you any answers — but I will help you think well. Here is what I expect from you: read every question twice, count slowly out loud, and try each one yourself before you press anything. Mathematicians think slowly on purpose. Here are all the steps. Step 1. Look at the first question on your screen. Read it twice. Ask yourself: is this putting groups together, or taking some away? Words like "more" and "joined" mean add. Words like "eaten", "sold" and "left" mean take away. Step 2. Now work it out on your paper before you look at the four choices. For adding, start at the bigger number and count on. For taking away, start at the big number and count back. Say each number out loud so you do not lose your place. Step 3. Check your answer. For adding, swap the two numbers and add again — you should get the same total. For taking away, add your answer back on and see if you land on the number you started with. Step 4. Now find your answer in the list of choices and click it. Then press Next question. Do this same way of working for every question — read twice, work it out, check, then choose. Step 5. Some questions are word questions, like "What does count back mean?" There is no counting to do. Read all four choices, then pick the one that says exactly what the word means. Take your time — there's no rush. Step 6. Keep going until you finish all 12 questions. If one feels hard, do your best guess and move on — one tricky question will not spoil your score. Step 7. At the end you will see your score. You pass with more than half of the questions right. Read which ones you got right, and look at the ones you missed. Step 8. If your score is not high enough, press Try again. This is not a bad thing — it is another chance to practise. Go slower this time, and count with your beans or your fingers for every sum. Step 9. When your score is good, press Continue. That takes you on from this page. You will know the page is finished when you have answered all 12 questions, seen a passing score, and pressed Continue. Come back and tell me how it went, or ask me for a hint any time you get stuck. You can do this! 🌟

overview.label: Unit Overview
overview.text:
Hello! I am your teacher today. 🌟

This page is our Unit Overview. It is like standing at the door and looking inside the room before we go in. It tells us what Unit 14 is about: sorting things into groups, and showing them in charts. By the end of this page you will know what we are going to learn. You need your eyes, your ears, and your voice. A grown-up can sit with you if you like. Here are our 3 steps. Step 1. Read the Unit Overview. Look at the words on the page. If you see a little speaker picture, press Listen and let the words be read to you. Listen right to the end. I expect you to look for two things: what we will sort, and what charts we will make. Take your time — there is no rush. Step 2. Say in your own words what you think you will learn. Say it out loud, or tell your grown-up. You do not need long words. A good answer sounds like this: "I will learn to put things in groups and make a picture chart." I expect one or two sentences from you, in your own words, not copied from the page. Step 3. Press Continue to go to The Lesson. This is the button at the bottom. Press it only after you have listened and said your sentence. That button takes us to the next part, where we start learning properly. You will know this page is finished when you have listened, said your own sentence, and pressed Continue. Let's start with Step 1. Press Listen and read along. Tell me when you are done. 😊

lesson.label: The Lesson
lesson.text: Hello! Today I am your teacher, and this page is our lesson. This page teaches us how to sort things into groups and how to show them on a chart. We do this because sorting helps us count and compare — like tidying toys or seeing which fruit most people like. By the end, you will know 7 big ideas about sorting and charts. You will need a pencil, some small things from home (stones, buttons, spoons, toy animals), and your voice for saying things out loud. Here are all the steps. Do them one at a time. Take your time — there's no rush. Step 1: Look at the top of the page. There are 7 concepts. A concept is just one big idea. Read the first one slowly, then press Listen to hear it read to you. Listening while you read helps the words stick. I expect you to read every word, not skip. Step 2: Each concept has an example. Say the example out loud, in your own voice. Saying it out loud helps your brain hold it. I expect to hear real words, not silent reading. Step 3: Now try it with your own things. If the concept is about sorting by colour, get a little pile of buttons or stones and make colour groups. Then count each group out loud: "one, two, three." I expect you to touch each thing once as you count. Step 4: Do steps 1, 2 and 3 again for each concept, all the way to concept 7. The concepts are: sorting by one rule, the sorting circle, the sorting box, reading a pictogram, making a pictogram or block graph, comparing groups with more, fewer, most and least, and finding all the combinations. One at a time, please — not all at once. Step 5: When you have read all 7, scroll to the bottom and press I studied the concepts. Only press it if you really read them all. That button tells the page you have finished the reading part. Step 6: Under the page is a deck of slides. Slides are like little cards. Each card has one of the same concepts on it. On the first slide, press Start. Step 7: On each slide, use the same buttons as before — read it, press Listen, and say the example out loud. Then press the arrow on the right to go to the next slide. The little dots under the slide show you where you are, like footprints. Step 8: Keep going until the last slide. On the last slide, press the finish button. You will know the page is finished when the I studied the concepts button is pressed and you have pressed the finish button on the last slide. Then the whole lesson page is done! Now go and do Step 1. When you have read the first concept, come back and tell me one thing you learned. 🌟

words.label: Math Words & Symbols
words.text: Hello! Today I am your teacher for the Math Words & Symbols page. This page teaches you the words we use in Unit 14: words like data, sort, rule, group, pictogram, block graph, more, fewer, most, least and title. These are our sorting and chart words. When you know them, reading a pictogram becomes easy. You need your eyes, your voice, and your fingers for typing. A grown-up can sit with you if you like. Here is what I expect from you: try every word, say each one out loud, and write your own sentence. Slow and careful is best. Mathematicians think slowly on purpose. Step 1. Look at the first word on the page. Read the word, then read what it means. Now press Listen. Listen carefully to how it sounds. A good job here means you hear the word and you can say it back the same way. Step 2. Say the word out loud. Then say the meaning in your own words — not the same words as the page. For example, for "sort" you might say, "it means put things in groups." I expect your own little words, even short ones. That shows me you really understand. Step 3. Now type one sentence using that word. Make it about your day, like your toys, your food, or your family. Then press Check sentence. Read what the checker tells you. If it says to fix something, change your sentence and press Check sentence again. Step 4. Do steps 1, 2 and 3 again for every word on the page. Go one word at a time. Do not rush. Each word gets Listen, your voice, your own meaning, your sentence, and Check sentence. Step 5. When every word is done, press I know these words and symbols at the bottom. Only press it after you have really done them all. That button tells the page you have finished this part. Step 6. Now look under the page. There is a deck of slides. Each slide shows one of the same words again. This is your practice, so the words stick in your head. Step 7. On the first slide, press Start. Then use the same buttons on the slide: Listen, say the word, say the meaning, type your sentence, and press Check sentence. Step 8. Press the arrow on the right to go to the next slide. Look at the little dots under the slide — they show you where you are. Do every slide the same way. Step 9. On the last slide, press the finish button. Well done — that is the end of the deck. You will know the page is finished when you have pressed I know these words and symbols, and you have pressed the finish button on the last slide. Now go and start with word one, and press Listen. Tell me when you have done it, and I will check it with you. 😊

explore.label: Explore the Concept
explore.text:
Hello! Today I am your teacher, and this page is called Explore the Concept. On this page you will meet 6 little discoveries about sorting things into groups. Sorting means putting things that go together in the same group, like putting all the red toys in one pile. We do this so you can read charts and say which group has more and which has less. You only need your eyes, your thinking, and the box to type in. A grown-up can sit near you if you like. Here is what I expect from you: look carefully first, think before you type, and use your own words. Short answers are fine. If you get it wrong, that is good news, because mistakes help us learn. Now let's go, one step at a time. 1. Look at the top of the page. You will see numbered tabs: 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6. Press tab 1. Read the little story it shows you, and look at the picture or model next to it. Take your time and point at the picture with your finger. I expect you to be able to tell me what you see, like "I see stones" or "I see a circle."

2. Under the picture there is a discovery question. Read it slowly, or ask your grown-up to read it with you. Think first in your head. Then type your idea in the box and press Check my idea. A good answer is short and says the group or the number, like "the white group" or "outside." Do not guess quickly — thinking slowly is what mathematicians do. 3. If the page says Look again, that is okay. Press Hint. The hint tells you where to look, but it does not give you the answer. Read it, think again, and type a new idea. When the page says Exactly!, the tab gets a little tick. That tick means "well done, this one is finished."

4. Now press tab 2 and do the very same thing: read, look, think, type, press Check my idea. Tab 2 is about a sorting circle. Things that follow the circle's rule go inside, and things that do not stay outside. I expect you to check the rule first, then decide. 5. Press tab 3. This one is a sorting box with two sides, like furry and not furry. Ask yourself the yes or no question for the thing. Remember, each thing goes in one side only, never both. Type your answer and press Check my idea. 6. Press tab 4. This one is a pictogram, which is a chart made of pictures. One picture means one thing. Count the pictures in a row by touching each one, so you do not count any picture twice. Then type your answer and press Check my idea. 7. Press tab 5. Here you make a chart. You colour one block for each answer people gave. So count how many people said that thing, and that is how many blocks. Type your answer and press Check my idea. 8. Press tab 6. This one is about comparing. More means the bigger group, fewer means the smaller group. If you are not sure, match them in pairs, one from each group, and see which group has some left over. Type your answer and press Check my idea. 9. Check your tabs. Every tab, 1 to 6, should have a tick. If one has no tick, press it and try that question again. The top part of the page is finished when all six have ticks. 10. Now scroll down under the page. There is a deck of slides with the same discoveries, one on each slide. On the first slide, press Start. Do the slide just like before: read, think, type, press Check my idea, and press Hint if you need help. 11. When a slide is done, press the arrow on the right to go to the next slide. Look at the little dots under the slide. They show you how far you have come and how many are left. 12. Keep going until the last slide. On the last slide, press the finish button. That tells the page you have done them all. How you will know the page is finished: all six tabs have a tick, and you have pressed the finish button on the last slide. I do not tick it for you — you press the buttons yourself, because it is your work. Ready? Press tab 1 and tell me what you see. Take your time — there's no rush.

visuals.label: Visual Models
visuals.text: Hello! Today I am your teacher, and this page is called Visual Models. Here is what it is. A visual model is a picture that shows a maths idea. This page has 6 of them, all about sorting and charts. Some of them move, so you can drag them and press their buttons. Why we do it. Sorting is easier to understand when you can SEE it. By the end, you will be able to point at a picture and tell me the rule, the group, and which group has the most. What you need. Your eyes, your finger or mouse, and your voice for talking to me. A grown-up can sit with you if you like. What I expect from you. Look slowly at each model. Press its buttons and see what changes. Then tell me one thing you noticed. Slow looking is good looking — mathematicians think slowly on purpose. There are 8 small steps. Here they all are. 1. Find the first model, Sorting by One Attribute. Look at the objects in it. Drag it to turn it if it moves, and press any buttons you see. Ask yourself: what is the rule? Colour, size, or shape? I expect you to say the rule out loud, like "the rule is colour". 2. Now the second model, The Sorting Circle (Venn Diagram). This is one circle with one rule. Press its buttons and watch things go inside or outside. I expect you to say why one thing went inside, like "it is red, so it belongs". 3. Next is The Sorting Box (Carroll Diagram). This box has a yes or no rule, like furry and not furry. Press its buttons and watch each thing land in one box. I expect you to notice this: every thing goes in only ONE box, never both. 4. Now Reading a Pictogram. A pictogram uses one picture for one thing. Touch each picture in a row and count along: one, two, three. I expect you to find the longest row and tell me which group has the most. 5. Next is Making a Pictogram or Block Graph. A block graph colours one block for each thing. Press its buttons and watch the blocks fill up. I expect you to see that the blocks start from the same line, with no gaps. 6. Last is Comparing Groups — More, Fewer, Most, Least. Look at two rows side by side. Match one from each row, like partners. I expect you to use the words more and fewer when you tell me what you see. 7. Under every model there is a caption. That is the little writing that tells you what the picture shows. Press Listen to hear it read to you. Do this for all 6 models. Listen once, then look at the picture again — it makes more sense the second time. 8. Now check that you have looked at all 6 models and heard all 6 captions. When you have, press the button at the bottom that says I explored the models. Only you can press it, because it saves your work. How you will know the page is finished. When you have pressed I explored the models, the page is done. Then come and tell me your favourite model of the six, and one thing it showed you. Take your time — there's no rush. Start with model 1 and tell me what rule you see. 😊

method.label: Learn the Method
method.text: Hello! Today I am your teacher, and this page is called Learn the Method. A method is a way to work something out, step by step. This page has 6 methods about sorting and charts. You will learn how to sort things by a rule, how to use a sorting circle, how to use a sorting box, how to read a pictogram, how to make one, and how to compare rows. By the end, you will know the steps by heart. You need your eyes, your voice, and maybe a pencil. Here is what I expect from you: press one button at a time, say each step out loud, and take your time. Take your time — there's no rush. Here are your steps. Step 1: Look at the first method on the page. Read its first step, or ask your grown-up to read it with you. Then press the button that says Show me the next step. I expect you to read before you press — not press quickly to get to the end. Step 2: Keep pressing Show me the next step until you see the words Method complete. Say each step out loud in your own voice as it appears. Saying it out loud helps your brain keep it. That is my one big rule for today. Step 3: Now do the same for every method on the page. There are 6 altogether. Go through each one from its first step to Method complete. I expect all 6 to be finished, not just the first one. Step 4: Look under the page. There is a deck of slides with the same methods, one method on each slide. On the first slide, press Start. Then use the same buttons to walk through the steps, just like before. Step 5: When a slide is done, press the arrow on the right side to go to the next slide. The little dots under the slide show you where you are. Do this until you reach the last slide, then press the finish button on that slide. You will know the page is finished when all 6 methods say Method complete, and you have pressed the finish button on the last slide. Ready? Start with Step 1, then tell me when your first method says Method complete. 🙂

examples.label: Worked Examples
examples.text: Hello! Today we are on the Worked Examples page. A worked example is a question with all the thinking shown, step by step. We are doing this so you can see HOW a good maths brain sorts things and counts pictures — not just the answer. By the end, you will be able to look at a pictogram row and say how many, and say which group has more. You will need a pencil, some paper, and your counting finger. Let's begin! Step 1. Look at the very first worked example on the page. Read the question, or ask your grown-up to read it with you. Do not press anything yet. Try it yourself first on your paper — draw the stones, or the animals, or the pictures. I expect a try, not a perfect answer. A try is always enough. Step 2. Now press the button that says Show worked solution. Read it slowly, line by line, and put your finger on each line as you read. Compare it with your paper. Ask yourself: did I do the same thing? If you did something different, that is fine — that is how we learn. Step 3. Do the same for every worked example on the page. There are 12 of them. Each time: read the question, try it on your paper, then press Show worked solution and check. Take your time — there's no rush. Mathematicians think slowly on purpose. Step 4. Look at the top of the page. There is a little counter there. It tells you how many examples you have opened so far. Keep going until every single one is open. The page is finished when all 12 are open, so do not leave any closed. Step 5. Now scroll down, under the page. There is a deck of slides there. They have the same examples, one example on each slide. On the first slide, press Start. Step 6. On each slide, use the same buttons as before. Read the question, think about it, then press the button to see the worked solution. Say the answer out loud to yourself or to your grown-up. Saying it out loud helps it stick in your head. Step 7. To move on, press the arrow on the right side of the slide. Under the slide there are little dots. The dots show you where you are in the deck, so you can see how many slides are left. Step 8. Keep going, slide by slide, until you reach the last slide. On the last slide, press the finish button. That tells the page you are done. How will you know the page is finished? Two things: the counter at the top shows all the worked examples are open, and you have pressed the finish button on the last slide. Then you are done! Off you go with Step 1. When you have tried the first one, come back and tell me what you got, and we will look at it together. 🙂

guided.label: Guided Practice
guided.text: Hello! Today we are doing Guided Practice for Unit 14: sorting and organising data. That means putting things into groups and reading picture charts. We do it so you get quick and sure at counting rows, finding the most and the least, and knowing where each thing belongs. You need a pencil, some paper, and your thinking brain. Here are all the steps — take your time with each one. 1. Look at the first practice question on the page. Read it slowly, twice. Ask yourself: what is this question asking me? Some ask you to sort, some ask you to count a row, some ask which group has more. I expect you to work it out on paper or in your head first, before you type anything. You can draw little dots or pictures to help — drawing is smart, not cheating. 2. Now type your answer in the box and press Check my answer. Type just the answer, like "3" or "goat" — short and clear. If a green tick comes, lovely work. If not, do not worry. Mistakes are how we learn. 3. If you feel stuck, press Give me a hint. You can get up to three hints. Read one hint, then try again before you ask for the next one. I expect you to think between hints — that is where the learning happens. 4. If the hints are still not enough, press Show next step. That shows you one line of the working, like counting the first row. Then you finish the rest yourself. The answer needs to come from you — the button just helps you start. 5. Do this for every one of the 12 questions: read, work it out, type, press Check my answer. Keep going on a question until it is right. Getting it right after a wrong try counts as a win. 6. When all 12 are right, the top part of the page is done. Then scroll down to the deck of slides under the page. It has the same questions, one question on each slide. 7. On the first slide, press Start. Then answer that slide the same way: type your answer, press Check my answer, and use Give me a hint or Show next step if you need help. 8. When a slide is right, press the arrow on the right to go to the next slide. Look at the little dots under the slide — they show you how far along you are. Do every slide, one at a time. 9. On the last slide, answer it, then press the finish button. I expect you to press it yourself, because that is what saves your work. You will know the whole page is finished when all 12 questions have a tick and you have pressed the finish button on the last slide. Ready? Start with question one, and tell me your answer — I am right here with you. 🙂

activities.label: Activities
activities.text: Hello! Today I am your teacher, and this is our Activities page. On this page you do maths with your hands, not just in your head. You will sort real things into groups and make a little chart. Sorting means putting things that are alike together. Doing it with real objects helps the idea stick in your mind. You will need paper, a pencil, and some small things from home, like buttons, stones, spoons or toys. A grown-up can sit with you and help. Here is what I expect from you: try it for real, say your groups out loud, and write something in the box even if it is just a few words or a number. Neat is nice, but honest thinking is better. Step 1. Look at the hands-on activity card at the top of the page. There is 1 activity. Read it, then press Listen to hear it read to you. Listen all the way to the end. Then go and fetch the things it names, like your paper, your pencil, and a handful of small objects. Do not start yet — first have everything on the table in front of you. Step 2. Now do the activity. Pick one idea from our unit, such as sorting by colour. Put your objects into groups, one group for each colour. Then count each group out loud: one, two, three. If you like, draw a block graph — one block for each object, all starting from the same line, with no gaps. Step 3. Show your work to someone at home and tell them your rule. Say something like, "My rule is colour. This group is red. It has four." Explaining out loud is part of the activity, so please do not skip it. Step 4. Write in the box on the page. Write your rule and how many are in each group, like "colour: red 4, blue 2". You can also write what you noticed, such as which group has the most. One or two short lines is plenty for Grade 1. Step 5. Think of one question of your own about your groups and answer it. A good one is "How many more red than blue?" Write your question and your answer in the box too. That is the best part — you become the teacher! Step 6. Press Mark complete under the activity when you have really done it. Only press it after the objects are sorted and your writing is in the box. Then, at the bottom of the page, press Finish activities once every activity is marked. Step 7. Now look under the page. There is a deck of slides with the same hands-on activities, one activity on each slide. Press Start on the first slide. Do the activity on that slide, use the same buttons as before, then press the arrow on the right to go to the next slide. The little dots under the slide show you where you are. Step 8. Keep going slide by slide until you reach the last one. On the last slide, press Finish activities. Take your time — there is no rush. You will know the page is finished when every activity has Mark complete pressed, and you have pressed Finish activities at the bottom and on the last slide. When you have done step 1, come back and tell me what objects you chose. I will be right here waiting for you.

fluency.label: Math Fluency
fluency.text: Hello! Today I am your teacher for Math Fluency. This is a sprint. That means twelve quick questions about sorting and charts, one after the other. We do it so your brain gets fast at counting rows, sorting into groups, and using the words more, fewer, most and least. By the end, you will answer these questions without stopping to think for long. You need your eyes, your fingers for counting, and a comfy seat. A grown-up can sit near you if you like. What I expect from you: try every question yourself, count carefully by touching each picture once, and keep going even if one feels tricky. Fast is nice, but right is better. I will not give you answers — I will give you hints, and you will find the answer. Here are all the steps. 1. Look at the top of the page. There is a timer that counts your time. Take one big breath first. The timer is only there to cheer you on, not to scare you. You do not need to rush like a race car. 2. Read question one slowly, all the way to the end. Ask yourself, what is this really asking? Some questions say count. Some say which has the most. Some say how many more. 3. Now answer it. If it asks you to count pictures, touch each picture once as you count: one, two, three. If it asks which group has more, match them in pairs and see which one has some left over. 4. Type your answer in the box. Then press Check & continue. That sends your answer and brings the next question. 5. Do the same for every question, one at a time. Twelve questions in all. If one question feels hard, do your best guess and keep going. Coming back to it later is fine. 6. Watch out for two little traps. Do not count a picture twice. And when a question says how many more, take away the smaller number from the bigger one, do not add. 7. When you finish all twelve, the page will show how you did. Look at how many you got right and how long you took. 8. You need most of them right to pass. If you got fewer than that, do not worry at all. Mistakes are how we learn. Press Run the sprint again and try one more time. 9. On your second try you will be faster, because you have met the questions before. Go slower on the ones that tripped you up last time. Mathematicians think slowly on purpose. 10. You will know the page is finished when a sprint has enough right answers. The page will tell you it is done. That is your finish line. When you are ready, start question one and tell me how it goes. If you get stuck on any question, type it here and I will give you a small hint. 🙂

games.label: Games
games.text: Hello! Today we are playing the Games on this page. These games are all about sorting and charts — the things we learned in this unit. Playing them helps the ideas stick in your head, and it is fun too. You need your eyes, your thinking brain, and maybe a grown-up sitting near you. Here is our plan, step by step. 1. Find a game and press Start game. Read the question slowly, or ask your grown-up to read it with you. Think first, then tap the answer you believe is right. Take your time — there's no rush. Each game has a few rounds, and you earn a star for every round you get right. I expect you to think before you tap, not tap fast. 2. When a game ends, press Play again. This gives you more chances to earn stars. If you got one wrong before, read the little explanation and try to remember it this time. Keep playing that game until it has all its stars — then it is mastered. I expect you to try again with a smile, because mistakes are how we learn. 3. Now do the same for every game on the page. Press Start game, answer the rounds, press Play again if you need more stars. Master one game, then move to the next one. If a question feels hard, tell me and I will give you a hint — but the answer must come from you. You will know the page is finished when every game has all its stars. The page finishes by itself once they are all mastered — you do not need to press anything extra. Ready? Pick your first game and press Start game. Tell me which one you chose!

problems.label: Solve Real Problems
problems.text: Hello! Today I am your teacher for the Solve Real Problems page. This page has 6 little story problems about sorting and charts. They are about real life: fruit bowls, toys, animals at the market. We do them so you can use what you learned about sorting, counting rows, and the words more, fewer, most and least. By the end, you will be able to look at a real-life story and say which group has more and how many more. You need your eyes, your fingers for counting, and a grown-up nearby if you want help typing. Take your time — there's no rush. Here is what to do, step by step. Step 1. Read the first problem slowly. Read it twice. Ask yourself: what is it really asking? Is it asking "how many?", or "which has the most?", or "how many more?" I expect you to say the question out loud in your own words before you answer. Step 2. Work it out with counting. Touch each thing as you count, one at a time, so you do not count one twice. If the question says "how many more", match them in pairs and count the ones left over. Step 3. Type your working and your answer in the box, then press Check answer. Do not just type a number — type how you got it too, like "I counted 4 mangoes and 1 banana, so banana is least." Show your working — every step counts. Step 4. If you feel stuck, press Hint. The hint gives you a little push, not the answer. Read it, then try again yourself. Being stuck is normal — mistakes are how we learn. Step 5. When the page says your answer is right, that problem is done. Move on to the next problem and do steps 1 to 4 again. Keep going until all 6 problems say right. Step 6. Now look under the page. There is a deck of slides with the same problems, one problem on each slide. Press Start on the first slide to begin. Step 7. On each slide, use the same buttons: type your working and answer, press Check answer, and press Hint if you need help. Do the slides carefully, just like before — this is your practice. Step 8. To go to the next slide, press the arrow on the right. Look at the little dots under the slide. They show you where you are and how many are left. Step 9. On the last slide, press the finish button. That tells the page you have finished the whole deck. You will know the page is finished when all 6 problems say your answer is right, and you have pressed the finish button on the last slide. Then you are done! Ready? Read problem 1 and tell me what you think it is asking. I am right here with you. 😊

explain.label: Explain Your Thinking
explain.text:
Hello! Today I am your teacher for the "Explain Your Thinking" page. On this page you do not just give an answer. You say HOW you got it. That is what mathematicians do — they tell their thinking out loud. By the end, you will be able to explain a sorting rule and a pictogram in your own words. You will need your eyes, your voice, and a grown-up nearby to help you type. Take your time — there's no rush. Here is what I expect from you. Each explanation should say three things: what you see, what rule you used, and why your answer makes sense. Try to use the key words: data, sort, rule, group, pictogram, more, fewer, most, least. Two or three sentences is plenty for a Grade 1 mathematician. Step 1. Look at the first prompt on the page. Read it slowly, or ask your grown-up to read it to you. Under the prompt there are some key ideas — little word cards. Read those too. They are your helpers, so try to use them in your answer. Step 2. Now think before you type. Ask yourself: what am I counting or sorting? What is the rule? For example, if the prompt shows three camel pictures, you might think, "I touch each picture and count: one, two, three."

Step 3. Type your explanation in the box. Say what you did, then say why. A good answer sounds like this: "I counted each picture one at a time and got 3. Each picture is one child, so 3 children chose camel." That is what I am looking for. Step 4. Press the button that says Check mathematical ideas. If the page asks for more, do not worry. Just add one more sentence — often the missing bit is the WHY. Then press Check mathematical ideas again. Step 5. Now press Show model explanation. This shows a good answer so you can compare. Look for ideas you missed, not for words you got wrong. Mistakes are how we learn. Step 6. Do the same for all 6 prompts: read, think, type, press Check mathematical ideas, then Show model explanation. One prompt at a time. Every explanation should use at least one key idea word. Step 7. Now look under the page. There is a deck of slides with the same prompts, one prompt on each slide. Press Start on the first slide. Step 8. On each slide, use the same buttons as before: type your explanation, press Check mathematical ideas, then press Show model explanation. Step 9. When a slide is done, press the arrow on the right to go to the next slide. Look at the little dots under the slide — they show you where you are and how many are left. Step 10. On the last slide, press the finish button. That tells the page you are done. You will know the page is finished when all 6 explanations use the key ideas, and you have pressed the finish button on the last slide. Ready? Start with Step 1, then tell me what your first prompt says. I will help you build your answer. 😊

challenge.label: Unit Challenge
challenge.text: Welcome to your Unit Challenge! This is the last page of Unit 14. It is a little quiz about sorting and charts. It shows you what you have learned. You do not need a pencil — just your eyes, your thinking, and your finger to press the buttons. Take your time. Mistakes are okay. Here is what I expect from you: read every question twice, think first, then choose. No guessing quickly. I will not give you answers — but I will help you think. Step 1. There are 12 questions. Read the first one carefully. Ask yourself, what is the rule? Some questions ask about sorting by colour, size or type. Some ask you to count pictures in a row. Some ask which group has the most or the least. Step 2. For sorting questions, say the rule out loud first. If the rule is colour, look only at colour. Then ask, does this thing match the rule? If yes, it belongs in that group. If no, it goes somewhere else. Step 3. For circle and box questions, remember one thing goes in one place only. Ask a yes or no question, like "Is it furry?" Yes goes in one side. No goes in the other side. Never both. Step 4. For pictogram questions, one picture means one thing. Touch each picture as you count: one, two, three. Do not count a picture twice. Do not skip one. Step 5. For "most" and "least" questions, look at all the rows. The longest row has the most. The shortest row has the least. If it asks "how many more", count the extra ones left over. Step 6. Now choose your answer, then press Next question. Do this for every question, one at a time. Twelve times in all. Take your time — there's no rush. Step 7. At the end you will see your score. You pass with more than half right. That means 7 or more out of 12. Step 8. If your score is not high enough, press Try again. That is not a bad thing! Going again helps your brain remember. Read even more slowly the second time. Step 9. When your score is good, press Continue. That is the last button on this page. You will know the page is finished when you have pressed Continue. Then Unit 14 is done. Good luck — I know you can do this! 🌟

overview.label: Unit Overview
overview.text: Hello! I am Wehel Tutor, and today I am your teacher for Unit 15: Time (2): Days, Months and Clocks. This page is called the Unit Overview. It is like looking at a map before a trip. It tells you what this unit is about, and what you will be able to do at the end. In this unit you will learn the seven days of the week, the twelve months of the year, and how to read a clock. All you need is your eyes, your ears, and your voice. A grown-up can sit with you if you like. There are 3 small steps on this page. Here they all are. Step 1. Read the Unit Overview. Look at the words at the top of the page. Where you see a little speaker, press Listen. Then listen carefully while the words are read to you. You can read along with your finger under the words. I expect you to listen all the way to the end, and to spot at least one thing you will learn, like days, months, or clocks. Take your time — there's no rush. Step 2. Say in your own words what you think you will learn. Do not copy the page. Just say it out loud, like you are telling a friend. You can start like this: "In this unit I will learn..." One or two sentences is plenty. A good answer names something real, such as the days of the week, or reading the clock. I expect you to use your own words, even if they are simple words. That is exactly right for Grade 1. Step 3. Press Continue to go to The Lesson. When you have looked at the page and said your sentence, find the button that says Continue and press it. That takes you to the next part, where the real teaching begins. I expect you to press it only after you have done Step 1 and Step 2, so nothing is skipped. How will you know the page is finished? You have listened to the overview, you have said your own sentence about what you will learn, and you have pressed Continue and landed on The Lesson. When that happens, this page is done. Now go ahead and start with Step 1: press Listen and read along. Tell me when you are done, and we will talk about what you noticed. 🙂

lesson.label: The Lesson
lesson.text: Hello! Today I am your teacher for The Lesson page in Unit 15: Time. This page teaches you six big ideas about time: the days of the week, the words yesterday, today and tomorrow, the months of the year, reading o'clock, reading half past, and putting your day in order. We do this so you can look at a clock or a calendar and know what it says. By the end you will be able to say the days and months in order, and read two kinds of clock times. You need your eyes, your voice, and maybe a pencil and paper. A grown-up can sit near you to listen. Here are your steps, one at a time. Step 1. Read the first concept slowly. Then press Listen and hear it read to you. Do this for all six concepts, one by one. Do not rush. I expect you to read each one, then listen to each one, so your eyes and your ears both learn it. Step 2. Say the example out loud. For the days, chant them: Monday, Tuesday, Wednesday, Thursday, Friday, Saturday, Sunday. Clap once for each day. For the clock, say it like this: long hand on 12, short hand on 3, so it is 3 o'clock. I expect to hear your own voice saying it, not just reading in your head. Step 3. Now try it with your own things. Put seven small stones or blocks in a line, one for each day, and touch each one as you say its name. Then look at a real clock at home and say what the two hands are doing. I expect one try of your own for each idea. Step 4. When you have read all six concepts, go to the bottom of the page and press I studied the concepts. Only press it after you have really read them all. That button tells the page you are done reading. Step 5. Under the page there is a deck of slides. They have the same six ideas, one idea on each slide. Press Start on the first slide. Read that slide out loud to yourself. Step 6. Use the same buttons on each slide, just like you did on the first one. Then press the arrow on the right to go to the next slide. The little dots under the slide show you where you are, so you can see how many are left. Step 7. Keep going until the last slide. On the last slide, press the finish button. I expect you to look at every slide, not skip ahead. You will know the page is finished when you have pressed I studied the concepts and pressed the finish button on the last slide. Now go and do Step 1. Come back and tell me when you have read and listened to the first concept, and tell me one thing you remember from it. Take your time — there's no rush.

words.label: Math Words & Symbols
words.text: Hello! I am your teacher today. This page is called Math Words & Symbols. It is our word page for Unit 15 about time. Here we learn the special time words, like week, o'clock and hour hand. When you know the words, the clock and the calendar become easy. You need your voice, your eyes, and your typing finger. Let's start! 1. Look at the first word on the page. Read the word, then read what it means underneath. Now press Listen. Listen carefully to how the word sounds. I expect you to listen with quiet ears, then say the word back to yourself the same way. Do this for every word on the page, one at a time. 2. Now say the word out loud in a big clear voice. Then say the meaning in your own words, not the words on the screen. For example, for "week" you might say, "a week is seven days." Next, type a sentence with the word in the box, then press Check sentence. A good sentence uses the word properly, like "There are seven days in a week." Then read what the checker tells you. If it says to fix something, change your sentence and press Check sentence again. Do this for each word: Week, Yesterday, Today, Tomorrow, Month, Year, O'clock, Half past, Hour hand, Minute hand. 3. When you have done every single word, scroll to the bottom and press I know these words and symbols. Only press it when you really have done them all. That button tells the page you are ready. 4. Under the page there is a deck of slides. Each slide shows one of the same words. Press Start on the first slide. Use the same buttons on each slide: listen, say it, and make your sentence. Then press the arrow on the right to move to the next slide. Look at the little dots under the slide — they show you how far you have come. When you reach the very last slide, press the finish button. You will know the page is finished when every word has a green tick from Check sentence, you have pressed I know these words and symbols, and you have pressed the finish button on the last slide. Take your time — there's no rush. Tell me when you have done step 1, and I will help you with the next one. 🙂

visuals.label: Visual Models
visuals.text: Hello! Today I am your teacher, and this page is our picture page. Visual Models means pictures that show our time ideas. We have six of them. Looking at pictures helps time feel real, not just words. By the end, you will see the days, the months and the clock hands with your own eyes. You need your eyes, your voice, and a grown-up nearby if you want one. Here is what I expect from you. Look slowly. Say each picture out loud. Touch and move the ones that move. There is no rush. Step 1: Find the first model, The Days of the Week. Look at the seven days going round like a wheel. If it moves, drag it with your finger or mouse to turn it. Press any buttons on it too. Say the seven days out loud as you look: Monday, Tuesday, Wednesday, Thursday, Friday, Saturday, Sunday. I expect you to say all seven, with none missed. Step 2: Under that model there is a caption, which means the little words that tell you about the picture. Read it. Then press Listen and hear it read to you. I expect you to listen right to the end, then tell yourself one thing you noticed. Step 3: Go to model two, Yesterday, Today and Tomorrow. Look at the three days in a row. Drag it if it moves. Now say it about you: "Today is..., yesterday was..., tomorrow will be..." I expect you to fill in your own real days. Step 4: Read the caption under model two, then press Listen.
