Listen carefully for the words yesterday, today and tomorrow. I expect you to hear all three words. Step 5: Go to model three, The Months of the Year. The twelve months sit in a circle. Drag it round and press its buttons. Say the months in order and clap once for each one. I expect twelve claps, ending at December, then back round to January. Step 6: Read the caption under model three and press Listen. I expect you to notice one thing, like the two months that start with A: April and August. Step 7: Go to model four, Reading O'Clock Times. This is a clock face. Look for the short hand, which is the hour hand, and the long hand, which is the minute hand. Move the hands if you can. Put the long hand straight up on the 12 and read the hour. I expect you to say a time out loud, like "3 o'clock". Step 8: Read the caption under model four and press Listen. I expect you to remember the rule: short hand for hours, long hand for minutes. Step 9: Go to model five, Reading Half Past Times. Move the long hand from the 12 all the way down to the 6. Watch the short hand slide between two numbers. Say "half past" and then the number the short hand has just gone past. I expect you to say a half past time out loud, like "half past 2". Step 10: Read the caption under model five and press Listen. I expect you to hear why we say the number the hand has just passed, not the one ahead. Step 11: Go to model six, Putting Events in Order. Look at the pictures of the day. Say your own day using first, next, then and last. I expect four or five events in the right order, from waking up to bedtime. Step 12: Read the caption under model six and press Listen. This is your last caption, so listen well. Step 13: Check you have seen all six models. Then press the button at the bottom that says I explored the models. Only press it when you really have looked at every one. You will know the page is finished when you have pressed I explored the models. That press is your record, so it must come from you, not me. Take your time — there's no rush. Tell me when you finish a step, and I will be right here. 😊

explore.label: Explore the Concept
explore.text: Hello! Today I am your teacher for the Explore the Concept page in Unit 15, Time. This page has six little discoveries about time. You will look at days, months, and clock hands, and you will work out the answer yourself. That is why we do it — thinking it out makes it stick in your head much better than being told. All you need is your eyes, your thinking brain, and maybe a grown-up sitting near you. Take your time — there's no rush. Here is what I expect from you: read every question twice, think before you type, and always try your own idea first, even if you are not sure. A wrong try is fine. Mistakes are how we learn. Step 1: Look at the top of the page. You will see numbered tabs, 1 to 6. Press tab number 1. A little story and a picture or model will open. Read it slowly, or ask your grown-up to read it with you. I expect you to look at the picture properly before you answer — the picture is a big clue. Step 2: Now read the discovery question under the story. Stop and think first. Say the answer out loud to yourself before you type it. For days and months, say them in order in your head, like a chant, until you reach the right one. Step 3: Type your idea in the box, then press Check my idea. Write just the answer, like a day name, a month name, or a time such as 3 o'clock. Spelling does not have to be perfect, but try your best. Step 4: If it says Look again, do not worry. Press Hint, read it, and try once more. When it says Exactly!, that tab gets a little tick. A tick means that discovery is done. Step 5: Now press tab number 2 and do the same thing again: read, think, type, press Check my idea. Keep going for tabs 3, 4, 5 and 6. Discovery 4 and 5 are about the clock, so remember this rule: the short hand tells the hour, the long hand tells the minutes. Step 6: The page is finished when all six tabs have a tick. Six ticks means every discovery question was answered right. Well done if you get there! Step 7: Now look under the page. There is a deck of slides with the same six discoveries, one on each slide. Press Start on the first slide. Step 8: On each slide, use the same buttons as before: read, think, type your idea, press Check my idea, and press Hint if you need help. Then press the arrow on the right to go to the next slide. The little dots under the slide show you how far you have come. Step 9: On the last slide, press the finish button. That tells the page you are done. Remember, I cannot tick it for you — you must press the buttons yourself so your work is saved. How will you know the whole page is finished? Two things: all six tabs have a tick, and you have pressed the finish button on the last slide. Ready to begin? Press tab number 1 and tell me what the story says.

method.label: Learn the Method
method.text:
Hello! Today I am your teacher for the Learn the Method page. 🙂

This page shows 6 methods. A method is a way to work something out, step by step. Our methods are about days, months, and reading a clock. By the end, you will know how to find the next day, the next month, and how to read o'clock and half past times. You need two things: your voice, and a pencil and paper if you like. Here is what I expect from you: say every step out loud, and do not rush. Mathematicians think slowly on purpose. Here are your steps. 1. Look at the first method on the page. Read its first step. Say that first step out loud, in your own voice. Then press the button that says Show me the next step. A new step will appear. 2. Keep pressing Show me the next step. Say each new step out loud as it comes. Keep going until the page says Method complete. That tells you this method is finished. I expect you to say every step out loud, not just look at it — your ears help your brain remember. 3. Now do the same for the next method, and the next, until all 6 are done. Read, say it out loud, press Show me the next step, and stop when it says Method complete. Take your time — there's no rush. Six methods is a lot, so it is fine to have a little stretch in the middle. 4. Under the page there is a deck of slides. The same methods are there, one method on each slide. On the first slide, press Start. Then use the same buttons you used before to move through the steps of that slide. 5. When a slide is done, press the arrow on the right side. That takes you to the next slide. Look at the little dots under the slide — they show you where you are in the deck. More dots ahead means more slides to go. 6. Keep going slide by slide, saying each step out loud. On the very last slide, press the finish button. That is you telling the page, "I did them all!"

You will know the page is finished when all 6 methods say Method complete, and you have pressed the finish button on the last slide. Off you go with step 1. When you finish the first method, come back and tell me one step you remember from it — I would love to hear it! 🌟

examples.label: Worked Examples
examples.text: Hello! Today we are working on the Worked Examples page. A worked example is a question with all the thinking shown, step by step. We do this so you can see how a good answer is built, and then copy that way of thinking yourself. By the end you will be better at days, months, and reading clocks. You need a pencil, some paper, and your thinking voice. Here are the steps. Take your time — there's no rush. 1. Look at the first worked example. Read the question out loud, slowly. Do not press anything yet! First, try it yourself on your paper. Say your answer out loud too, like "Today is Wednesday, so tomorrow is Thursday." I expect you to try first, even if you are not sure. A good try is what matters here. 2. Now press Show worked solution. Read it line by line, from the top. Compare it with your own working. Ask yourself: did I say the same thing? Did I miss a step? If your answer was different, that is fine — mistakes are how we learn. Just find the line where your thinking changed. 3. Do the same for every worked example. There are 12 of them. Read, try, then press Show worked solution. At the top of the page there is a counter — it tells you how many you have opened. Watch that number grow. The page is done when all 12 are open. I expect you to try each one before you open it, not just click them all quickly. 4. Now scroll down to the slides at the bottom. This is a deck of slides with the same examples, one on each slide. Press Start on the first slide. Use the same buttons on each slide: read the question, try it, then show the solution. 5. To move on, press the arrow on the right side of the slide. That takes you to the next one. Look at the little dots under the slide — they show you where you are in the deck. Take one slide at a time. 6. Keep going until you reach the last slide. On that one, press the finish button. That tells the page you are done. You will know the page is finished when the counter at the top shows all 12 examples opened, and you have pressed the finish button on the last slide. Ready? Start with step 1, and tell me when you have tried the first example. I'll be right here. 😊

guided.label: Guided Practice
guided.text: Hello! Today we practise time together. This page has 12 questions about days, months and clocks. We do it so you can say the days in order, say what comes next, and read o'clock and half past on a clock. Get a pencil and paper, and sit somewhere quiet. Here are your steps. 1. Read the first question slowly. Read it twice. Then work it out on paper or in your head. You can count days on your fingers, or draw a little clock. Take your time — there's no rush. I expect you to think first, not guess. 2. Type your answer in the box. Then press Check my answer. Write it in full, like Wednesday or 5 o'clock or half past 3. If you feel stuck, press Give me a hint. You can press it up to three times, and each hint helps a bit more. If you are still stuck, press Show next step and it shows you one line of the working. I expect you to try first, then use a hint — that is good thinking, not cheating. 3. Do this for every question, one at a time, until each one is right. If an answer is wrong, that is okay. Mistakes are how we learn. Read the question again, use a hint, and try once more. When all 12 are right, this part is done. 4. Now look under the page. There is a deck of slides with the same questions, one on each slide. Press Start on the first slide. Answer it the same way, with the box, Check my answer, Give me a hint and Show next step. Then press the arrow on the right to go to the next slide. The little dots under the slide show you where you are. Keep going, slide by slide, and on the last slide press the finish button. You will know the page is finished when all 12 questions are right and you have pressed the finish button on the last slide. Ready? Start with question one and tell me your answer. I'm right here. 🙂

activities.label: Activities
activities.text: Hello! I am your teacher today. Let's do our Time activity together. This page is a doing page. You will not just read about time — you will make something and talk about it. Our unit is Days, Months and Clocks. So you will pick one time idea, like the seven days, the twelve months, or a clock with a short hand and a long hand. Why do we do this? Because when you build a thing with your own hands, your brain remembers it much better. Making a clock helps you read a clock. Get these ready: paper, a pencil, and some small things from home like stones, buttons or bottle tops. A grown-up nearby can help. Here is what I expect from you: try your best, use your own words, and say your answer out loud before you write it. Take your time — there's no rush. 1. Find the hands-on activity. There is 1 activity on this page. Read it, then press Listen to hear it read to you. Listen carefully. It tells you what to use and what to do. Now go and get those things — your paper, your pencil, and your small objects. I expect you to have them on the table before you start. 2. Do the activity, then write in the box. Pick one time idea. You could draw a clock face and put the numbers 1 to 12 on it. You could lay out seven stones for the seven days. You could lay twelve stones in a circle for the twelve months. Then show it to someone in your family and tell them about it. Then make up one question of your own, like "what day comes after Tuesday?", and answer it. Now type in the box what you made and what you noticed. One or two sentences is plenty. A good answer names your idea and tells me one thing you learned. 3. Press Mark complete, then Finish activities. When you have really done the activity and written in the box, press Mark complete under it. Only press it after you have done it — that button is your promise that the work is real. When it is marked, go to the bottom of the page and press Finish activities. 4. The slides at the bottom. Under the page there is a deck of slides. Each slide shows the same hands-on activity, one per slide. Press Start on the first slide. Do the same buttons on each slide: Listen, do it, write in the box, Mark complete. Then press the arrow on the right to move to the next slide. The little dots under the slide show you where you are. On the last slide, press Finish activities. How will you know the page is finished? Every activity has Mark complete pressed, you are on the last dot of the slides, and you have pressed Finish activities. Then you are done! Now go and get your paper and pencil, then tell me which time idea you chose. 😊

fluency.label: Math Fluency
fluency.text:
Hello! Today I am your teacher for the Math Fluency page. 🌟

This page is a sprint. A sprint means we go fast! You will get 12 quick questions about days, months, clock hands, and what comes first. You already know these — this page helps you say them quickly, without stopping to think for a long time. What I expect from you: try your best on every question, keep going even if one feels tricky, and be honest with your answers. Fast is nice, but right is better. Here are all the steps. 1. Get ready first. Sit up, have your grown-up nearby if you like, and get your fingers ready to type. Say the days of the week in your head once: Monday, Tuesday, Wednesday, Thursday, Friday, Saturday, Sunday. That little warm-up wakes up your brain. 2. Start the sprint. Look at the top of the page — you will see your time counting. That is fine! Do not worry about the clock. Read question one, then type your answer in the box. 3. Answer one question at a time. After you type your answer, press Check & continue. Then question two comes. Keep doing this: read, type, press Check & continue, over and over, until all 12 questions are done. 4. Remember the clock rule while you answer. Short hand tells the hour. Long hand tells the minutes. Long hand on 12 means o'clock. Long hand on 6 means half past. Say this quietly to yourself if a clock question comes up. 5. Remember the day and month rule too. For "after", go forward one. For "before", go back one. Say the list in order in your head and listen for the next name — do not skip. 6. Do not stop if you get one wrong. A wrong answer just tells us what to practise. Keep going to the end of all 12 questions. I expect you to finish the whole sprint, not to be perfect. 7. Look at your score at the end. You need most of them right to pass this page. If you got enough right — brilliant work! Move on. 8. If you did not get enough right, press Run the sprint again. This is not a punishment. It is another turn, like a game. Say the days and months out loud once before you start again. 9. Try the sprint as many times as you need. Each time, you will be a little faster and a little surer. That is exactly what fluency means. You will know the page is finished when one whole sprint has enough right answers. The page will tell you, and then you can smile — you did it! 😊

Come back and tell me your score, and we will look at any tricky ones together. Take your time — there's no rush.

games.label: Games
games.text: Hello! Today we are playing the games for Unit 15: Time. This page is full of little quiz games about days, months and clocks. Games help your brain remember things without it feeling like hard work. You will need your thinking brain, and it helps to say the days and months out loud as you play. Here is what we will do, step by step. Step 1: Pick one game and press Start game. Read the question slowly. Then look at all four choices before you tap one. I expect you to think first, then choose — not tap fast. Every round you get right earns you a star. If you get one wrong, that is fine. Mistakes are how we learn. Read the little explanation, and say it back to yourself in your own words. Step 2: When the game ends, press Play again. This gives you more chances to earn stars. A game is mastered when it has all its stars. I expect you to keep playing that same game until its stars are full. Playing again is not because you failed — it is how the answers stick in your memory. Step 3: Now do the same for every game on the page. Go one game at a time, from the first to the last. Master each one before you move on. I expect you to try each game yourself, even the clock ones that feel trickier. Remember: short hand tells the hour, long hand tells the minutes. How will you know the page is finished? When every game has all its stars, the page finishes by itself. You do not need to press anything extra. Ready? Press Start game on the first game, and tell me how your first round goes. 🌟

problems.label: Solve Real Problems
problems.text: Hello! I am your teacher today. This page is called Solve Real Problems. On this page you meet 6 little story problems about time. They are about real life — a special meal on Friday, a trip to the market, a spelling test day. Your job is to read the story, work out the day, month or time, and say how you knew. We do this so time words help you in your real day, not just in a book. Here is what I expect from you. Read slowly. Think first. Then write your answer AND one short line telling me how you worked it out. Take your time — there's no rush. You will need your eyes, your thinking, and a grown-up nearby if you want help reading. Here are all the steps. 1. Look at the first problem at the top of the page. Read the story twice. Read it out loud if you can — that helps a lot. Then ask yourself: what is this question really asking? Is it asking for a day, a month, or a time on a clock? I expect you to know what the question wants before you answer. 2. Now work it out in your head. For days, say the week in order: Monday, Tuesday, Wednesday, Thursday, Friday, Saturday, Sunday. For months, say them in order from January. Use your fingers, one for each day. This is good thinking, not slow thinking. Mathematicians think slowly on purpose. 3. Type your answer in the box. Write the answer word, like "Friday". Then write one short line of working, like "Today is Thursday, so the next day is Friday." I expect both parts — the answer and the how. Then press Check answer. 4. If your mind goes blank, press Hint. The hint gives you a little push, not the answer. Read it, then try again yourself. Pressing Hint is smart, not cheating. 5. When the page says your answer is right, that problem is done. Give yourself a little cheer! If it says not quite, read the story again and look for the day or month word hiding inside it. Then fix your answer and press Check answer again. 6. Now do the same for problem 2, then 3, 4, 5 and 6. Same way every time: read twice, think, type your answer and your working, press Check answer. Do them in order so you do not miss one. 7. Under the page there is a deck of slides. It has the same problems, one problem on each slide. On the first slide, press Start. This is your practice round, so you get the ideas twice. 8. On each slide, use the same buttons you already know: type your answer, press Check answer, and press Hint if you get stuck. Answer out loud first if you like — saying it helps you hear if it sounds right. 9. To move on, press the arrow on the right side of the slide. Look at the little dots under the slide. They show you where you are and how many slides are left. 10. On the last slide, press the finish button. That tells the page you have done them all. You will know the page is finished when all 6 problems say your answer is right, and you have pressed the finish button on the last slide. Ready? Read problem 1 now, and tell me what you think it is asking for — a day, a month, or a time. I am right here. 😊

explain.label: Explain Your Thinking
explain.text: Hello! Today we are going to talk like little mathematicians. This page is called Explain Your Thinking. You will not just say the answer — you will say HOW you know it. That is the big skill today: telling me your thinking in words. It helps because when you can explain a day, a month or a clock, you really understand it. You need your eyes, your voice, and your typing finger. Ready? Here are all the steps. Step 1. Look at the first prompt on the page. Read it slowly, out loud if you can. Under the prompt there are Key Ideas — little words like week, today, tomorrow, hour hand. Those are the words I want to hear in your answer. Read the prompt twice before you write anything. Take your time — there's no rush. Step 2. Now write your answer in the box. Tell me three things: what you know, what rule you used, and why your answer makes sense. Like this: "Today is Saturday. The days of the week always go in the same order. After Saturday comes Sunday, so tomorrow is Sunday." That is a full, lovely answer. Step 3. When your writing is done, press Check mathematical ideas. If the page says you need more, do not worry! Mistakes are how we learn. Just add one more sentence, put in a key word you missed, and press Check mathematical ideas again. Step 4. Now press Show model explanation. This shows a good answer so you can compare. Look for one thing that answer has and yours does not. You do not copy it — you just learn from it, like looking at a friend's neat handwriting. Step 5. Do steps 1 to 4 again for every prompt. There are 6 prompts in all. Some are about days, some about months, some about the clock hands. Go one at a time, and keep using the key words in every answer. Step 6. Now look under the page. There is a deck of slides with the same prompts, one prompt on each slide. On the first slide, press Start. Step 7. On each slide, do the same as before: read the prompt, write your explanation, press Check mathematical ideas, then press Show model explanation. Same job, new slide. Step 8. To move on, press the arrow on the right side of the slide. Look at the little dots under the slide — they show you where you are, like footprints on a path. Step 9. On the last slide, press the finish button. That tells the page you are all done. You will know the page is finished when all 6 prompts have your own explanation with the key ideas in them, and you have pressed the finish button on the last slide. I will be right here. Start with prompt one, and tell me when you have written your first explanation — I would love to hear it! 🌟

challenge.label: Unit Challenge
challenge.text: Hello! I am your teacher today, and this page is our Unit Challenge. The Unit Challenge is 12 questions about everything in Unit 15: the days of the week, the months of the year, yesterday, today and tomorrow, and reading o'clock and half past on a clock. We do it to see what you have learned all by yourself. This one is a quiz, so I really can't give quiz answers — but I promise you can get this. I will show you how to think about each kind of question. Get a pencil and paper if you like, sit somewhere quiet, and take your time — there's no rush. Here are all the steps. Step 1. Get ready. Before you start, whisper the days of the week to yourself: Monday, Tuesday, Wednesday, Thursday, Friday, Saturday, Sunday. Then whisper the months, from January to December. I expect you to say them in order, with no day or month skipped. This wakes up your memory before question one. Step 2. Read question one twice. Read the question, then read it again. Ask yourself: is this question about days, months, or a clock? Then look at the four answer choices. I expect you to read all four before you pick, not just the first one. Step 3. Choose your answer and press Next question. Click the answer you think is right, then press Next question to move on. Do this for every question, one at a time. If you are not sure, pick the one that feels closest — a good guess is better than no answer. Step 4. For day questions, count on your fingers. If a question says "what day comes after Friday?", start at Friday and step forward one day. If it says "before", step back one day. Watch out: after and before are different, so read the word carefully. Step 5. For yesterday, today and tomorrow, remember the picture. Today is now. Yesterday is the day that has gone. Tomorrow is the day still coming. So if today is named in the question, just step one day back for yesterday, or one day forward for tomorrow. Step 6. For month questions, chant from January. Say the months in order in your head until you reach the month in the question, then stop and hear the next one. That is much safer than guessing from memory. Step 7. For clock questions, look at the long hand first. If the long hand points straight up to the 12, it is an o'clock time, and the short hand tells you the hour. I expect you to check the long hand before you say the time. Step 8. For half past questions, the long hand points straight down to the 6. Then the short hand sits between two numbers. Say the number it has just passed, not the one it is going to. That is the tricky bit, so go slowly. Step 9. Keep going to question 12. Answer them all, one at a time, pressing Next question after each. If one feels hard, do your best and move on — do not stop. Step 10. Look at your score. At the end you will see how you did. You pass with more than half of the questions right. Look at which ones you got wrong, because that tells us what to practise together. Step 11. Press Try again if your score is not high enough. That is not a bad thing at all — mistakes are how we learn. Read each question slowly the second time, and use my tips from steps 4 to 8. Step 12. Press Continue. When your score is good enough, press Continue to finish the page. You will know the page is finished when you have answered all 12 questions, seen your score, and pressed Continue. Now go and start with question one. Come back and tell me your score, and tell me which question felt hardest — we will practise that one together. 😊
